BEFORE THE GEORGIA PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION

GEORGIA POWER COMPANY
DOCKET NO. 55378

Data Request No. STF-PIA-10-1

BASIS FOR THE ASSERTION THAT THE 
INFORMATION SUBMITTED IS A TRADE SECRET

As part of Georgia Power Company’s 2023 Integrated Resource Plan Update filed in Docket No. 55378 (“2023 IRP Update”), Georgia Power Company (“Georgia Power” or the “Company”) submits to the Georgia Public Service Commission its response to STF-PIA-10-1 (“Response”). In the Response, the Company has provided engineering and construction timelines for new technology options. All of such information (the “Information”) constitutes trade secret information of Southern Company, Georgia Power, and its affiliates and is therefore protected from public disclosure under Commission Rule 515-3-1-.11.

 The Information derives economic value from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable by proper means by other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use. Specifically, the Information contains competitively sensitive details on the construction timeline and schedule for generic technology options assumed in the Company’s Resource Mix Study. Publicly disclosing these timelines would allow bidders in future solicitations to tailor their proposals and potentially set an artificial schedule and potential in-service date, which would harm customers by not allowing the Company to conduct a proper solicitation and obtain the best cost estimates that will also meet schedule timelines. In addition, the Company’s competitors are not required to disclose this type of information and to require the Company to do so would place it at an economic disadvantage.

The Information is subject to substantial procedures to maintain its secrecy. Only select Georgia Power and Southern Company Services personnel are granted access to the Information. Those personnel receive access only on a “need to know” basis. Parties outside the Company who have been granted access to the Information, if any, have been required to sign confidentiality agreements with respect to the Information.

BEFORE THE GEORGIA PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION

GEORGIA POWER COMPANY

BASIS FOR THE ASSERTION THAT THE 
INFORMATION SUBMITTED IS A TRADE SECRET

As part of Georgia Power Company’s 2023 Integrated Resource Plan Update filed in Docket No. 55378 (“2023 IRP Update”), Georgia Power Company (“Georgia Power” or the “Company”) submits to the Georgia Public Service Commission its response to STF-PIA-10-3 (“Response”). In the Response, the Company has provided information related to a potential wholesale power purchase agreement. All of such information (the “Information”) constitutes trade secret information of Southern Company, Georgia Power, and its affiliates and is therefore protected from public disclosure under Commission Rule 515-3-1-.11.

 The Information derives economic value from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable by proper means by other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use. Specifically, the Information contains specifics around capacity pricing involved in potential capacity and energy sales for defined periods of time. Publicly disclosing this information would allow competitors, other public utilities, and market participants to potentially disrupt and undercut the Company in negotiations resulting in no sale or otherwise artificially distort the pricing for the proposed sale, which would hurt customers who will benefit from the sale of the remarketed capacity. Further, the Company’s competitors are not required to disclose this type of information and to require the Company to do so would place it at an economic disadvantage.  

The Information is subject to substantial procedures to maintain its secrecy. Only select Georgia Power and Southern Company Services personnel are granted access to the Information. Those personnel receive access only on a “need to know” basis. Parties outside the Company who have been granted access to the Information, if any, have been required to sign confidentiality agreements with respect to the Information.

                                Comments of The Southern Company on
                            Environmental Protection Agency Proposed Rule;
                    Supplemental Effluent Limitations Guidelines and Standards for the

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


          The Southern Company1 (Southern or the Company) is committed to building the future of energy for the

          advancement of our customers and communities. Through industry-leading innovation and a commitment

          to a net zero future, we are delivering the customized sustainable and resilient energy solutions our

          customers and communities require to help drive growth and prosperity. Our uncompromising values put

          the needs of those we serve at the center of everything we do. With these values in mind, we are focused

          on transitioning our generating fleet to net zero greenhouse gas emissions and making the necessary related

          investments in our transmission and distribution grids, while maintaining reliability and affordability for

          our customers.


          The Southern Company system’s compliance plan for the 2020 ELG Reconsideration Rule2 (2020 Rule)

          reflects our continued commitment to comply with all environmental rules and regulations, to responsibly

          transition our system’s generating fleet, and to continue to research and develop emerging wastewater

          treatment technologies. The 2020 Rule, and the associated compliance options, are now key components to

          facilitate the orderly fleet transition for both replacement generation resources as well as necessary

          transmission project completion. However, in the midst of the energy transformation that is underway at

          Southern, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s or the Agency’s) recently proposed


                  1 The Southern Company is a holding company that conducts its business through its subsidiaries,
          accordingly, unless the context otherwise requires, references in this letter to The Southern Company’s operations,
          such as generating activities, refer to those operations conducted through its subsidiaries.
                  2 85 Fed. Reg. 64,650 (Oct. 13, 2020).


                                                                  2

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          Supplemental ELG Rule3 (“the proposal” or “the 2023 Rulemaking”) threatens to disrupt the orderly fleet

          transition by increasing risks to reliability while burdening customers with undue costs. EPA has heavily

          underestimated both the costs and necessary timeframes for complying with this proposed rule, which will

          result in a tremendous cost burden to customers and negative impacts to our ability to provide clean, safe,

          reliable, and affordable energy to customers.


          The impacts of this proposed rule are apparent when considering the cascading and unaccounted for impacts

          to Georgia Power’s Plant Bowen. Plant Bowen, located in Cartersville, Georgia serves as a key dispatchable

          reliability asset for the Metro Atlanta and North Georgia load center. EPA’s proposed Best Available

          Technology Economically Achievable (BAT) (membrane filtration) for flue gas desulfurization (FGD)

          wastewater treatment has not been adequately demonstrated as suitable for all plants and raises significant

          feasibility concerns for Plant Bowen due to site-specific characteristics. Notwithstanding those concerns,

          not only would installation of membrane filtration at Plant Bowen increase the capital costs of the ELG

          compliance strategy by hundreds of millions of dollars and eliminate the environmentally friendly

          beneficial use of operational fly ash at the site, but EPA’s basis for how facilities would meet the zero liquid

          discharge (ZLD) requirement could also result in unacceptable consequences for operations, such as the

          forced operation of the plant just to prevent discharge of treated permeate.


          Further, the 2029 compliance deadline does not allow for sufficient time to complete necessary transmission

          and replacement generation to consider alternatives to installation of controls. Whereas Georgia Power has

          anticipated the eventual retirement of Plant Bowen by the end of 2035, Plant Bowen remains critical to


                  3 Supplemental Effluent Limitations Guidelines and Standards for the Steam Electric Power Generating Point
          Source Category, 88 Fed. Reg. 18,824 (Mar. 29, 2023).


                                                                  3

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          maintaining electric service in north Georgia during the time that both replacement generation and new

          transmission projects are being completed. Through the state regulatory framework in Georgia, the Public

          Service Commission (PSC or the Commission) governs generation resource decisions and approves the

          transmission plans to ensure the utility can meet its obligation to serve its customers. Georgia Power is

          required under Georgia law and PSC regulation to complete comprehensive and long-term integrated

          resource planning every three years. This thorough and fully litigated process ensures decisions are made

          in the best interest of customers but necessarily takes time. A compliance deadline of 2029 does not allow

          for the appropriate time to complete these necessary projects, and the proposed rule does not offer the

          appropriate flexibility to alleviate the disparate costs to aging units and accommodate the time necessary to

          replace generation.


          These impacts are not limited to Plant Bowen. Alabama’s Plant Miller has already proceeded with the

          installation of EPA’s 2020 Rule BAT and has been named by EPA in this rulemaking as an “early adopter”

          of the 2020 Rule. Yet, the early adopter subcategory allows plants like Miller with the option to retire

          earlier than anticipated, as opposed to recognizing the environmental benefits of having operated a more

          stringent FGD wastewater treatment plant and allowing the plant to both maximize the environmental

          benefits of EPA’s recently established BAT and allow for adequate time to recover costs of these

          investments and properly evaluate the impacts of other potentially significant power sector rulemakings

          before abandoning the biological treatment system for EPA’s newly proposed membrane technology. This

          membrane technology is significantly more expensive than EPA has estimated, and EPA has not fully

          evaluated the extent of non-water quality impacts, including the elimination of beneficial fly ash use to the

          local concrete market and the resulting negative impacts on economic development and infrastructure

          projects dependent on this resource.


                                                               4

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          In addition to EPA’s revisions to effluent limitations for both bottom ash transport water (BATW) and FGD

          wastewater, EPA is also proposing to establish new effluent limits for both legacy wastewater (LWW) and

          combustion residual leachate (CRL). EPA has solicited comments for a multitude of compliance options

          for these waste streams, some of which are unnecessarily complicated and do not reflect current practices

          that are already in place to treat these waste streams. The Southern Company’s electric operating companies

          are currently dewatering ash ponds across the system under state regulatory oversight with treatment that

          is protective of state water quality standards. These treatment system configurations are very site-specific

          and are integral to an efficient and protective closure process. We are concerned that finalizing the rule as

          proposed could negatively impact the progress of ash pond closures being conducted to comply with

          aggressive timelines under the coal combustion residuals (CCR) Rule4 (CCR Rule).


          While the Company is committed to installation and operation of wastewater treatment under the ELG Rule,

          the realities of cost and reliability concerns in serving our customers cannot be ignored. We encourage EPA

          to finalize a Supplemental ELG Rule that can protect the environment, promote resiliency and reliability of

          the electric power system, and help to alleviate a significant cost burden to customers. In these comments,

          The Southern Company provides detailed review and recommendations to EPA regarding the following

          issues:


          EPA’s failure to pause implementation of the 2020 Rule has created important reliance interests that
          need to be protected:
              •     EPA’s failure to pause implementation of the 2020 Rule has created important reliance interests

                    that need to be protected. EPA should acknowledge the consequences to customers of requiring


                    4 80 Fed. Reg. 21,301 (Apr. 17, 2015).


                                                               5

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                 continued compliance with its recently finalized 2020 Rule while it simultaneously proceeded with

                 its revision to more costly compliance options that render certain 2020 compliance investments

                 obsolete. To address these interests more adequately, EPA must either reject its newly proposed

                 BAT for FGD wastewater or finalize a rule with appropriate time to comply with the new BAT and

                 flexibilities for aging units to either comply with the new BAT, retire or repower under an

                 appropriate timeframe.


          EPA’s proposed BAT for FGD wastewater:
             •   As EPA correctly concluded in 2015 and 2020 and as has been confirmed by The Southern

                 Company wastewater treatment experience and research results provided to EPA, membrane

                 filtration is still not the BAT and ZLD is not a realistic effluent limit for FGD wastewater across

                 the industry.

             •   As was done in both 2015 and 2020, we urge EPA to again reject membrane filtration and paste

                 encapsulation as industry BAT for FGD wastewater. EPA has not adequately demonstrated that

                 the newly proposed BAT is feasible beyond a limited number of plants and has not adequately

                 considered specific data and information submitted previously to the Agency explaining why the

                 technology is not suitable at every plant. Furthermore, EPA’s proposed BAT for FGD wastewater

                 imposes substantial and significantly underestimated new costs to customers and renders costly

                 investments made in EPA’s 2020 Rule as obsolete in as little as four years after they will have been

                 installed. Additionally, EPA has not adequately considered the significant non-water quality

                 impacts associated with the proposed BAT, particularly the negative consequence of eliminating


                                                              6

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                 beneficial use of operational fly ash at both Alabama Power’s Plant Miller and Georgia Power’s

                 Plant Bowen.


          Compliance timeframes:
             •   If EPA finalizes the proposed BAT despite the concerns outlined above, we urge EPA to extend

                 the late applicability date to December 31, 2032, to account for the additional time needed for site-

                 specific planning requirements and/or research and development of the emerging technology.

                 Requiring compliance by no later than December 31, 2029, would prematurely obsolete the

                 biological treatment systems installed to comply with the 2020 Rule and increase cost impacts to

                 customers by shortening the useful life of the equipment. Furthermore, EPA should maximize the

                 environmental benefits associated with these investments by extending the date to comply with any

                 new BAT.


          Retirement and repowering subcategories:
             •   Existing Permanent Cessation of Coal Combustion (PCCC) by 2028 Subcategory: EPA should

                 maintain the existing PCCC by 2028 subcategory without modification. As mentioned, the 2020

                 Rule PCCC by 2028 subcategory is now a key component of our planning process to transition the

                 fleet and modifications to this subcategory, such as any new or more stringent requirements, could

                 disrupt the orderly fleet transition.

             •   New PCCC by 2035 Subcategory: If EPA finalizes the proposed BAT despite the aforementioned

                 concerns, EPA should create a new PCCC by 2035 subcategory that allows facilities the option to

                 continue operating under the 2020 Rule BAT and opt to either comply with the new BAT by

                 December 31, 2032, or retire by December 31, 2035. This subcategory would allow facilities that

                 are nearing retirement the appropriate timing and opportunity to alleviate unnecessary cost burdens


                                                              7

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                 to customers and ensure continued reliable and resilient delivery of energy while replacement

                 generation and associated transmission is completed.

             •   Early Adopter Subcategory: If EPA finalizes the proposed BAT, EPA should make key

                 modifications to the early adopter subcategory to ensure an equitable treatment of those that do and

                 should qualify as early adopters.

                     o   First, EPA should modify the subcategory criteria cutoff date and expand the definition of

                         early adopter to include those facilities that have made financial commitments to

                         compliance with the 2020 Rule.

                     o   Second, EPA should not require that early adopters retire by December 31, 2032, but

                         should instead allow early adopters to comply with the new BAT by December 31, 2032,

                         or retire by December 31, 2035.


          Legacy Wastewater and Combustion Residual Leachate:


             •   Legacy Wastewater (LWW): EPA has proposed several changes to LWW requirements in the

                 proposal, including subdividing LWW into new categories, new definitions, and requiring different

                 management requirements for the new categories. While we support best professional judgment

                 (BPJ) limits for LWW, we also urge caution with any revision to the LWW requirements or the

                 imposition of permitting constraints that could impose unnecessarily costly or stringent

                 requirements or that could complicate, delay, or derail ongoing dewatering and closure activities

                 required by the CCR Rule.

             •   Combustion Residual Leachate (CRL): Southern does not object to the proposed BAT limits for

                 arsenic and mercury for this waste stream but believes EPA must constrain the scope of regulated

                 CRL to that which is collected from engineered leachate collection systems and then discharged

                 via surface outfalls from active landfills at active generating plants. Subjecting numerous


                                                              8

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                  unidentified and uncharacterized sources of water to an improper regulatory definition completely

                  unbalances any underlying determinations or assumptions of cost-effectiveness. This rulemaking

                  should not establish effluent limits or permitting requirements for functional equivalent discharges

                  of CRL because unlined landfills and surface impoundments are not point sources.


          In assessing the potential impacts of the proposed Supplemental ELG Rule, Southern Company’s focus is

          on managing the transition of our generation fleet in a way that protects both the environment and the best

          interests of our customers. We believe the suggestions provided herein are critical to maintaining clean,

          safe, reliable, and affordable energy for the communities we serve as we transition to a net-zero future.

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


        I.    INTRODUCTION


                  A.      The Southern Company is committed to an orderly fleet transition.

          The Southern Company is committed to reducing our greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to provide our

          customers and communities with a clean energy future. Southern has set an interim goal to reduce direct

          system-wide GHG emissions by 50% by 2030 (from 2007 levels) and a long–term goal of net zero

          emissions by 2050. To reach our net zero by 2050 GHG goal, Southern is focused on transitioning our

          generating fleet and making the necessary related investments in our transmission and distribution grids,

          while maintaining reliability and affordability for our customers.


          Southern continues to reduce the number of generating units in our coal fleet, lowering emissions, and

          retiring uneconomic resources. When considering the retirements and conversions that have already been

          implemented by our electric operating companies, as well as expected future retirements or conversions

          that have been filed with state environmental and/or regulatory agencies, we currently expect to have just

          six coal units5 remaining in our generating fleet with a nameplate capacity of less than 3,000 MWs by the

          end of 2035. The addition or retirement of generation resources, transmission capacity, and expansion plans

          for load growth are closely related, and our electric operating companies must consider these elements

          together in their comprehensive planning processes within their respective state regulatory constructs.


                  5 Miller Units 1-4 and Scherer Units 1-2.


                                                              13

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                   B.       The 2020 ELG Reconsideration Rule provided robust wastewater treatment

                            while facilitating orderly fleet transition to net zero greenhouse gas emissions.

          Sound environmental policies play a critical role, not only in protecting our environment, but also in

          maintaining a resilient and reliable electric power system. The EPA and the Department of Energy (DOE)

          recently issued the Joint Memorandum on Interagency Communication and Consultation on Electrical

          Reliability, which stated, “With the sound application of existing authorities and policy tools, the EPA and

          DOE can continue to support the reliability of the electric power system.”6 The Southern Company agrees

          that there are solutions EPA can implement through environmental rules that can protect the environment,

          promote resiliency and reliability of the electric power system, and help to alleviate a significant cost burden

          to customers.


          As an example, the 2020 Rule, and the associated compliance options, are key components to facilitate the

          orderly fleet transition for both replacement generation resources and necessary transmission project

          completion. In 2020 and 2021, the Company’s planning processes were used to evaluate the 2020 Rule and,

          as a result of that evaluation, we determined that the rule would impact most of the coal-fired generating

          units across The Southern Company system. Notices of Planned Participation (NOPPs) were filed with state

          environmental agencies in October 2021 indicating our intent to repower two coal units with natural gas


                   6 DOE & EPA, Joint Memorandum on Interagency Communication & Consultation on Electric Reliability,
          at 2 (Mar. 9, 2023).

                                                                14

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          and retire 10 coal-fired generating units on or before December 31, 2028, in accordance with the 2020

          Rule’s PCCC by 2028 subcategory.7

        II.    EPA’S      DECISION           TO     CONTINUE              COMPLIANCE       WITH        THE       2020

               RECONSIDERATION RULE DURING THIS RULEMAKING PROCESS CREATED

               IMPORTANT RELIANCE INTERESTS THAT NEED TO BE PROTECTED.

           EPA first established ELGs for the steam electric industry in 1974, 1977, and 1982. Then, 35 years later,

           EPA promulgated comprehensive and significant revisions to the then-existing ELGs to reflect technology

           changes in the industry sector over the three prior decades (2015 Rule)10, as well as widespread

           implementation of air pollution controls under the Clean Air Act (CAA). Litigation followed the 2015

           Rule, with some effluent limits being vacated by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals11 and others being

           reconsidered by EPA.12 EPA twice postponed compliance deadlines for other portions of the 2015 Rule,

          In October 2020, EPA’s updated effluent limits for two waste streams (BATW and FGD wastewater)

          reconsidering every agency action taken by the prior administration. In July 2021, EPA announced that it

          was initiating a rulemaking to “strengthen” the effluent limits promulgated in the 2020 Rule.15 At the same

          As discussed in more detail below, EPA’s current proposal significantly changes many aspects of the 2020

          Rule. Because EPA never paused or delayed implementation of the 2020 Rule, EPA’s actions created

          important reliance interests for industry that need to be meaningfully addressed, and protected, as part of

          the 2023 Rulemaking.17


                  A.       EPA should have paused or delayed implementation of the 2020 Rule, but did

                           not, thereby creating reliance interests that need to be protected now.

          When EPA first announced in 2021 that it was planning to make the ELG rule more stringent than the 2020

          Rule, it should have paused or delayed the then-applicable compliance dates to prevent significant and

          unnecessary expenditures. Instead, EPA chose to continue requiring compliance with the 2020 Rule. As a

          result, many facilities made significant investments in biological treatment systems that will now be

          rendered obsolete through the 2023 Rulemaking. To avoid this outcome, EPA’s final rule should include

          specific additional flexibilities that reflect the good faith efforts that have been undertaken to comply with

          the 2015 and 2020 Rules, and at a minimum, consider the costs associated with these continued efforts to

          comply with the rules in the Agency’s BAT analysis.


                           1.       EPA needs to consider reliance interests.


          As a matter of both good public policy and procedural protections of the Administrative Procedures Act,

          EPA must consider how proposed rule revisions will affect the regulated community. For the 2023

          Rulemaking, this means EPA must consider the impact to facilities that have already made—or are in the


                  17 See Dep’t of Homeland Sec. v. Regents of the Univ. of California, 140 S. Ct. 1891, 1915 (2020) (the
          agency “was required to assess whether there were reliance interests, determine whether they were significant, and
          weigh any such interests against competing policy concerns.” (emphasis in original)).

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment

          mentions the word “reliance” only three times and substantively only in a footnote where EPA states:

                  explanation, where a prior policy has engendered serious reliance interests, those

                  interests must be taken into account. FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556

                  U.S. at 515 (citation omitted). EPA has taken reliance interests into account in this

                  rulemaking, as is clear from EPA’s proposal in Section VII.C.4 of this preamble,

                  below, to create a new subcategory for early adopters who relied on certain of

                  EPA’s past determinations. EPA also notes that no NPDES permittee has certainty

                  of its limitations beyond its 5-year NPDES permit term, as reissued permits must

                  See 40 CFR 122.44(a) & (d).18 88 FR 18839, fn. 23.

          landscapes, program staffing shortages, and other complications. EPA’s statement also ignores the fact that

          it typically takes decades for the Agency to revisit and promulgate updated effluent limitations guidelines

          ignoring these practicalities, EPA still must consider the effect of proposed changes on permittees. Indeed,

          this is why the NPDES permit program includes a provision for compliance schedules to enable permittees

          In the 2023 Rulemaking, EPA appears to have made little effort to investigate costs incurred by those

              communications35 to EPA before the 2019 proposed ELG Reconsideration Rule (2019 proposal),36 and as

              recently as April 1, 2022.37 Even so, we recognized in 2019 that EPA left the door open for further analysis

              of membranes due to its suggestion that membranes could become BAT by the year 2028. In response, we

              stated in comments:


                      Southern Company agrees membrane filtration is not BAT for FGD wastewater. However,

                      we do not agree that this technology will be available in 2028 and think it is imprudent to

                      make that determination almost nine years in advance. EPA’s proposed prediction is not

                      supported. Southern Company believes significant research is left to be done and that

                      demonstration of this technology at commercial scale is needed prior to determining it will

          rule, EPA is not establishing BAT limitations for FGD wastewater based on thermal technologies.” (internal citaton

          This is especially true given the significant reliance interests implicated by the proposal and the numerous

          facilities and units that continue, at the Agency’s insistence, working toward compliance with the 2020 rule

          and installation of biological treatment.


          Although EPA has discretion in how it weighs the statutory factors, EPA’s consideration of those factors is

          mandatory.42 The statutory factors are particularly important in this rulemaking, as many affected facilities

          will have recently installed new technology to comply with the 2020 Rule. This fact informs the “age of

          equipment” factor and should weigh against EPA requiring those facilities to replace recently installed

          biological treatment technology with new membrane-based ZLD technology. This fact also informs the

          “cost of achieving effluent reductions” factor because replacing biological treatment with new membrane

          technology is extremely costly (when properly estimated and amortized). EPA must weigh these against

          the other factors in its determination that membrane-based ZLD is BAT less than three years after EPA

          determined that biological treatment was BAT. It is not sufficient for EPA to rely solely on pollutant

          reduction estimates; EPA must consider the statutory factors in its BAT decision.


          At a minimum, if EPA no longer believes it is required to consider the statutory factors in its selection of

          BAT, or in its decision not to select a technology as BAT, it must say so, provide a rationale, and explain

          why it changed its position from the 2015 and 2020 Rules.

                  D.      EPA has not adequately addressed significant non-water quality impacts

                          associated with membrane filtration-based ZLD.

          In the 2020 Rule, EPA concluded in part that membranes are not BAT because of the significant non-water

          quality impacts. In the proposed rule, EPA has not demonstrated that these non-water quality impacts have

          been resolved, but rather raises more questions about the practical viability of membrane treatment plus

          ZLD. As EPA knows, membranes alone are not a compliance technology but instead are a volume-

          reduction process that needs to be coupled with additional wastewater treatment technology, as well as

          processes and equipment for managing the brine concentrate. Managing these concentrate streams poses

          significant technical and economic challenges that EPA identified in the 2020 Rule, which are still under

          evaluation, and that EPA has not effectively resolved or addressed in the 2023 proposed rule.


                          1.       Paste encapsulation eliminates beneficial use.


          Less than three years ago, EPA stated in its 2020 Rule:


                 58 Southern Company, Third Quarter 2021 Earnings Conference Call, at Slide 15 (Nov. 4, 2021) (Docket ID
          No. EPA-HQ-OW-2009-0819-9231).

                                                               40

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                  EPA also rejects membranes as the technology basis for BAT for all existing plants because

                  it could discourage more valuable forms of beneficial reuse of FA (such as replacing

                  Portland cement in concrete), causing more FA to be disposed of as waste.59


          The impact to beneficial use remains a significant problem for membrane filtration and paste encapsulation.

          Beneficial use of fly ash provides significant environmental and economic benefits which could be largely

          lost with industry-wide implementation of membrane technology. Beneficial use of fly ash results in

          reduction of land needed for disposal, reduction in the need to mine and process virgin materials and

          provides a local source of raw material for the production of durable products like concrete. Installing

          membrane filtration and utilizing paste encapsulation as a waste disposal method for the resulting brine, as

          the proposal envisions, would mean that fly ash that would otherwise have been beneficially used is instead

          consumed in the brine encapsulation process and landfilled, indefinitely. EPA fails to acknowledge or

          adequately consider these significant losses in the proposed rule.


          Presently, the beneficial use market in the Company’s footprint is approximately twice the amount of fly

          ash produced. As such, the Company currently markets approximately 95% of its generated fly ash.

          Removing ash availability from the local market will increase the carbon footprint resulting from the use

          of Portland cement and will create a lower value life cycle of infrastructure as the concrete would be less

          durable and would need to be replaced sooner than if it were produced with fly ash.


          To further illustrate the site-specific impacts of this proposal, the membrane filtration feasibility evaluation

          at Alabama Power’s Plant Miller concluded that the brine management solution would consume all

          available fly ash produced at the site, eliminating 100% of the beneficial use of fly ash at a site that currently


                  59 85 Fed. Reg. at 64,666.


                                                                 41

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          sells all available produced fly ash to the concrete industry, producing approximately $8.5M in revenue and

          significant avoided costs each year that flows to utility customers. Rather than providing the local economy

          and environment a valuable raw ingredient for concrete production, Plant Miller would instead become an

          on-site producer of a concrete-like waste material with no productive benefit to the community or the

          economy. This concrete would have to be disposed of in a landfill. EPA assumes there is available on-site

          permitted and constructed landfill capacity when, in fact, there is none. Plant Miller, for example, does not

          have an on-site landfill. Constructing a new landfill would come at a significant cost and could require

          acquisition of nearby properties or blasting and clearing of surrounding topography to achieve a suitable

          landfill location if there is available space at all.


          This site-specific impact on beneficial use is not unique to Plant Miller. Georgia Power’s Plant Bowen

          currently sells over 90% of its fly ash. While the ash sales generate approximately $5 million in associated

          annual revenue, this practice avoids significant handling and disposal costs for operational ash, resulting in

          an economic benefit to customers. In addition to the lost revenue from eliminating fly ash sales, it is

          expected that Plant Bowen would need to build additional landfill capacity to accommodate the new brine

          mixture or resort to off-site disposal at substantially increased costs.


          In addition to the site-specific impacts, EPA’s conclusion that the industry would retain enough available

          fly ash to supply the beneficial use market is not practical. There is no nationwide distribution system for

          fly ash beneficial use. EPA understood this in 2020 when it explained the very site-specific nature of fly

          ash availability to the local market, which remains valid now:


                   But, while these assumptions are appropriate for nationwide cost estimates which are

                   needed to demonstrate economic achievability for the industry as a whole, this does not

                   necessarily mean that these assumptions should be used for analyzing the non-water quality

                   environmental impacts associated with the resultant brine from membrane use, and in

                                                                  42

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                  particular, estimating what plants are likely to do with this by-product in relation to

                  available FA.60


          Whether sufficient fly ash is present on site or available in the local market is a site-specific question. There

          is still no national depot or distribution system of fly ash to which users come for supply. Furthermore,

          EPA itself has recently further reinforced the idea of a limited potential future supply of available ash for

          beneficial use. In its recent Legacy CCR Surface Impoundments proposal61, EPA states that “[o]lder,

          closed impoundments or other CCR storage areas are less likely to have CCR material of a known and

          reliable composition,” thus limiting their potential value for future beneficial use.62 Therefore, any assertion

          that CCR from storage sites could be used to fill the market supply is contradicted by EPA’s recent

          statement regarding the future value of such CCR for beneficial use.


          It is evident that EPA has not adequately addressed the significant non-water quality impact of its preferred

          brine management solution. Once the supply of fly ash from plants like Miller and Bowen is removed from

          the local market, it will not likely be replaced, and a highly valuable local resource will instead reside, as

          waste, in a landfill. EPA has not explained how it assessed local or site-specific impacts from the loss of

          fly ash for beneficial use in its non-water quality impacts analysis but should do so.

                           2.      The regulatory classification of a paste encapsulation mixture under the

                                   federal CCR Rule is unclear.


          Since 2019, EPA has actively advanced amendments to the CCR Rule, some of which could impact whether

          membrane filtration with brine encapsulation is legally, technically, or economically feasible. It is not clear

          whether brine encapsulation, such as paste encapsulation or ash conditioning will be considered a beneficial

          use of the CCR. EPA states in the 2020 Rule: “While EPA considers FA use for waste solidification and

          stabilization as beneficial use, the CCR waste being solidified or stabilized must still be disposed of in

          accordance with 40 CFR 257.”63 Beneficially used CCR should not on the one hand be exempt from federal

          CCR regulation by definition, and on the other, be fully subjected to requirements in 40 C.F.R. Part 257.

          EPA should leave regulation and disposal of fly ash to the current and any future requirements of 40 C.F.R.

          Part 257 and not overcomplicate long-term facility CCR compliance by upsetting established on-site ash

          handling practices. We encourage EPA to simply avoid these unnecessary future conflicts with the CCR

          Rule and reject membrane filtration as BAT for FGD wastewater.


                           3.      Crystallization and deep well injection (DWI) technologies alternatives to

                                   paste encapsulation are not solutions for facilities that do not have enough

                                   available fly ash.


          In the proposed rule, EPA evaluated alternatives “for handling the resulting brine that do not involve FA

          and thus would have no impact on the beneficial use of FA in other settings.” 64 EPA evaluated two

          alternatives to paste encapsulation – deep well injection (DWI) and crystallization to a salt for disposal.


                  63 85 Fed. Reg. at 64,666 n.50.

                  64 88 Fed. Reg. at 18,842.


                                                                44

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          EPA proposes to find that both crystallization and DWI have acceptable non-water quality environmental

          impacts65 and that, while the costs are higher, they would be economically achievable.66


          With respect to DWI, it is not available to every facility. As EPA knows, the ability to inject wastewater

          into a deep well is dependent upon both the site geology and the ability to permit an injection well in that

          facility’s state. For example, Class I UIC wells (also known as DWI) are currently prohibited by regulation

          in the State of Alabama.67 While there is no prohibition on Class I UIC wells in the State of Georgia, there

          have been none permitted to date.


          EPA’s other alternative, crystallization, is a high-energy evaporative process that requires heat from either

          the operating unit or some external source to concentrate the brine to a salt. The industry’s limited

          experience with using this technology for FGD wastewater has been problematic. EPRI evaluated five

          existing ZLD wastewater treatment systems at Redhawk, Navajo, Iatan, Mayo, and Merrimack Generating

          Stations. The findings from these case studies and site interviews demonstrate that crystallizer systems are

          complex and challenging to operate. Common challenges for a crystallizer system include scaling and line

          plugging, system foaming, flow obstructions, salt dewatering, energy transfer impedance, and chemical and

          mechanical cleaning.68

          Impacts for the Proposed Steam Electric ELGs – DCN SE10244 (Feb. 27, 2023) (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2009-

                  67 See Ala. Admin. Code r. 335-6-8-.05(1)(f).

          EPA states that none of the facilities that currently generate brine as part of a ZLD system elects to

          encapsulate and dispose of that brine.69 “Rather, these facilities send the concentrated brine to a crystallizer,

          and these resulting salt crystals can then be disposed of without the use of [fly ash].”70 There are only a

          few facilities in the U.S. that have installed crystallization as a component of their FGD wastewater

          treatment system to generate a salt from the brine concentrate. These facilities have had significant scaling

          and corrosion problems with the crystallizer, and in some cases have abandoned it in favor of different

          treatment systems. For example, the Iatan Generating Station in Weston, Missouri initially installed two

          vapor compressor evaporators for treating FGD wastewater, but experienced so many operational problems

          since its commissioning that the facility abandoned the system and installed a Spray Dryer Evaporator

          (SDE) based on site-specific conditions.71


          The other facility that has experienced significant scaling and corrosion issues with its FGD wastewater

          treatment system is Granite Shore’s Merrimack Power Station in Bow, New Hampshire. Merrimack Station

          installed one brine concentrator and a two-stage multiple-effect crystallizer in 2011 to treat FGD

          wastewater. The system experiences significant scaling and corrosion issues even though it employs

          softening as a pretreatment step to remove suspended solids and scaling compounds.72 The system, to this

          day, cannot operate without a small liquor purge to keep its crystallizer chemistry in balance, to manage

          In addition, we are not aware that EPA has cited any evidence to suggest that salts produced from

          crystallization will be physically and chemically stable for handling and long-term disposal. Available

          evidence strongly suggests that salts produced from the evaporation of FGD wastewater can be highly

          hygroscopic and can create a liquid upon atmospheric exposure that could potentially be included in the

          leachate discharge from the landfill.75 Hygroscopic salts wreak havoc on equipment and could pose

          environmental and structural risk to landfills, especially if those salts migrate to the leachate collection

          system. In this situation, pumps and other appurtenances would need replacement to avoid corrosive failure

          and associated compliance risks. In the proposed rule, EPA cites one plant in China that takes its brine

          down to salts and then sells them for industrial use as opposed to disposal in a landfill.76 We are unaware

          of any established or readily available domestic market for these salts. In sum, there are significant practical

          uncertainties regarding the handling and disposal of any salts produced from FGD wastewater.

          to the costs of membranes. Specifically, since Plant Miller sells all its operational fly ash for beneficial use

          Volume Reduction Technologies, 3002024773 (Jan. 2023).
                  76 88 Fed. Reg. 60 at 18,843.
