STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          in the concrete market, EPA proposes the facility could use crystallization of the brine as an alternative to

          paste encapsulation. EPA’s cost estimates for a crystallizer at Plant Miller 1-4 are $61.5 million capital and

          $1.9 million annual O&M costs. For Plant Bowen, which also uses nearly all (90%) of its operational fly

          ash for beneficial use, EPA’s cost estimates for a crystallizer are $120.3 million capital and $5.4 million

          annual O&M costs.77 For Plant Bowen, the crystallizer cost would be in addition to the cost of a membrane

          system, which based solely on EPA’s own cost estimates (which we know are low), would be a total of

          $210.3 million in capital costs. The same is true for Plant Miller. It is not clear whether EPA has taken these

          additional costs into account, since fly ash is already used for other purposes at Plants Miller and Bowen.


          The significant non-water quality impacts of eliminating beneficial use of operational fly ash, coupled with

          the significant uncertainties of the two alternative technologies EPA identifies that would allow continued

          beneficial use of fly ash, supports EPA’s conclusion in the 2020 Rule that membrane filtration is not BAT

          for FGD wastewater.


                  E.       EPA ignores practical limitations of achieving ZLD.

          EPA’s proposal to set membrane treatment as BAT is further complicated by the requirement that such

          systems achieve ZLD. EPA arbitrarily makes this assertion by assuming that the treated permeate can

          simply be used for either FGD or boiler make-up without any technical challenge and at a reasonable cost.

          This assumption may be accurate for some facilities, but in the case of Plant Bowen and Plant Miller, there

          is a significant additional cost to install infrastructure to support this type of process. Significant

          engineering, piping, pumps, and potentially even water storage would be necessary to accomplish a closed

          loop system. In the case of Plant Bowen (and likely many other similar plants), it is also incorrect to assume


                  77 Eastern Research Group, Inc., FGD Wastewater Proposed Rule Cost Database, supra note 52.

                                                                48

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          that only FGD wastewater requires treatment when units are dispatched. NPDES discharges from power

          plants are not limited to process wastewater but instead include industrial stormwater that is also sometimes

          managed through the wastewater treatment systems. This ensures that stormwater that contacts exposed

          materials is more thoroughly controlled prior to discharge. However, this results in water entering the

          wastewater treatment system even when there is no makeup water demand for treated FGD wastewater,

          and therefore, no operational water consumption processes to achieve ZLD. This problem is even greater

          at sites that have gypsum landfills/ponds for dewatering. In the case of Georgia Power’s Plant Scherer, this

          results in the greatest FGD wastewater flow occurring when the site receives high rainfall, but all units are

          offline. Plant Bowen has mechanical gypsum dewatering, but also has the same challenges with the FGD

          water balance. A comprehensive evaluation of the water balances necessary to achieve ZLD has yet to

          occur, but it is possible that generating units may need to dispatch solely for purposes of water consumption

          to achieve the ZLD requirement in this proposal. In fact, Mississippi Power’s Plant Daniel has had to

          dispatch units due to a build-up of water in the pond at the gypsum storage facility due to heavy rains and

          low dispatch of the units.


       IV.    COMPLIANCE TIMING AND SUBCATEGORIES

          The Southern Company supports regulations that facilitate the continued delivery of clean, safe, reliable

          and affordable energy to customers. The Company’s planning process provides customers with reliable and

          affordable electric service from a diverse portfolio of demand-side and supply-side resources. This portfolio

          – comprised of demand response, energy efficiency, nuclear, natural gas, oil, coal, hydro, solar, wind,

          landfill gas, and biomass generation – maximizes value for customers in a wide variety of future economic

          and regulatory scenarios.


                                                               49

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          The Company considers retirement options for generating units as a part of the overall resource strategy. If

          environmental controls are mandated for a unit, then the economic value of the unit, including future

          operating costs, changes. The Company must then consider through thorough economic and planning

          evaluations whether it is in the best interest of customers to install the required control technology or to

          retire the unit and replace it with another resource. Accordingly, any compliance deadlines set by the

          proposed Supplemental ELG rule and other environmental rulemakings must consider the costs associated

          with any new rulemaking as well as the process and timing requirements of state regulatory processes,

          especially the integrated resource planning processes for the retail electric operating companies governed

          by the state PSCs.


          As proposed, the FGD wastewater treatment requirements, compliance applicability date, and "early

          adopter” subcategory pose significant challenges to the Company’s traditional electric operating

          companies. As explained in more detail below, we urge EPA to create additional flexibilities to alleviate

          the disparate costs associated with procuring and optimizing new biological treatment technology by 2025,

          and then immediately procuring and optimizing new membrane treatment technology and prematurely

          retiring the new biological system by 2029. We also urge EPA to evaluate any subcategories finalized under

          this rule with the subcategories in the CAA Section 111 rulemakings addressing GHG emissions from new

          and existing sources.


          In this section, we present the following proposals in more detail for EPA’s consideration:


              •   EPA should modify the FGD wastewater “no later than” applicability date to avoid disparate costs

                  and avoid premature retirement of new treatment equipment.

              •   EPA should retain the existing PCCC by 2028 subcategory and create a new PCCC by 2035

                  subcategory.

              •   EPA should make modifications to the early adopter subcategory; and

                                                              50

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


              •   EPA should align compliance timing and subcategory options with other impactful proposed

                  environmental rules.


                  A.       EPA should modify the FGD wastewater “no later than” applicability date to

                           avoid disparate costs and avoid premature retirement of new treatment

                           equipment.

          Should EPA finalize membrane filtration based ZLD as BAT, then EPA should extend the “no later than”

          applicability date for all facilities until December 31, 2032. EPA should allow operation of the 2020 BAT

          for at least eight years to allow cost recovery for investments in 2020 Rule compliance, after which a facility

          can opt to either retire, repower, or continue operating with the new BAT. Reducing the useful life of a new

          biological treatment system to only four years places an acute cost recovery burden on customers and is a

          waste of resources. Modifying the “no later than” applicability date would allow continued operation of

          units that are, or may become, necessary for reliability due to load growth or other market changes; and it

          would allow facilities to evaluate the impacts of a multitude of relevant factors, including additional

          environmental rulemakings, affecting their continued operation and continue to operate by implementing

          the new BAT if they determine it to be the most cost-effective option. Therefore, EPA should extend the

          “no later than” applicability date for all facilities until December 31, 2032.


                  B.       EPA should retain the existing PCCC by 2028 subcategory and create a new

                           PCCC by 2035 subcategory.


                           1.      EPA should retain existing PCCC by 2028 subcategory, as finalized in 2020.


          EPA solicits comment on the proposal to retain the PCCC by 2028 subcategory. We agree that the existing

          PCCC by 2028 subcategory continues to be warranted and we urge EPA to not retroactively impose any


                                                                51

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          new requirements on facilities that have opted into this subcategory. The Southern Company’s traditional

          electric operating companies submitted NOPPs for a combined total of 12 units stating their intent to retire

          or repower using alternative fuel by December 31, 2028. Of these 12, 10 units have received regulatory

          approval to retire or repower by 2028. Georgia Power requested to retire Plant Bowen Units 1&2 by 2028;

          however, in consideration of the reliability needs of customers in North Georgia, the Georgia PSC deferred

          a decision on the retirement of Plant Bowen Units 1&2 until the Georgia Power’s next regularly scheduled

          Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) in 2025. EPA also requests comment on whether a more stringent

          technology already existing on site should be required for FGD wastewater at facilities in the PCCC

          subcategory. The imposition of any additional requirements to these facilities only adds corresponding

          disparate costs. Additionally, because some existing treatment systems may be utilized for treatment of ash

          pond dewatering activities, it is imperative that EPA not impose any complications or delays to the timely

          dewatering and closure of ash ponds, which are already under prescriptive closure deadlines under 40

          C.F.R. § 257.102(f), with extremely limited extension options. We suggest that avoiding this unintended

          consequence would best support EPA’s stated goal of harmonization with the CCR Rule.


                          2.      EPA should establish a new PCCC subcategory allowing units the option to

                                  comply with the generally applicable limitations by the “no later than”

                                  applicability date in the facility’s permit or retire or repower by December

                                  31, 2035.


          EPA should finalize a new subcategory that would allow facilities the option to comply with the 2020 BAT

          no later than December 31, 2025, and, by a certain date, opt to either comply with the new membrane

          filtration BAT for FGD wastewater no later than the finalized applicability date or opt to retire or repower

          no later than December 31, 2035. In the proposed rule, EPA reaffirms its support for the PCCC by 2028

          subcategory: “EPA established this subcategory in the 2020 rule based on the statutory factors of cost (the


                                                              52

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          cost burden on these facilities is greater because they have less time to recoup investments); the age of the

          equipment and plants involved (the remaining useful life of the plants and their pollutant control equipment

          is shorter than for typical plants); potential non-water quality environmental impacts, including energy

          requirements (early retirement of these plants could affect energy supply); and harmonization with the CCR

          Rule alternative closure provisions.”78 This subcategory approach is supported largely by the same factors

          EPA relied upon for the PCCC by 2028 subcategory and is necessary for the same reasons outlined in our

          discussion regarding modifications to the early adopter subcategory.


          In the following sections, we present additional factors for EPA to consider in finalizing a new PCCC

          subcategory that most appropriately addresses the timing associated with the planning, regulatory approval

          and implementation of any necessary replacement generation for generation units impacted by this proposed

          rulemaking. Based on factors presented below, we urge EPA to establish a new PCCC subcategory

          allowing retirement or repowering by December 31, 2035.


                                   a. A retirement subcategory should appropriately consider the
                                      planning and regulatory approval process.

          As an illustration of the critical timing considerations of state regulatory processes, Georgia Power is

          required to complete extensive planning analyses as a vertically integrated utility regulated by the PSC

          under O.C.G.A. § 46-2-20(a). The PSC oversees and must approve of planning and resource decisions to

          ensure Georgia Power can meet its obligation to serve its customers, including ensuring the Company

          maintains sufficient capacity to serve during periods of peak energy demands. Georgia Power is required

          under PSC regulations to act prudently in its investment and compliance decisions. Those decisions are


                  78 88 Fed. Reg. at 18,857; see also 40 C.F.R. §§ 257.71(d), 257.103.


                                                                 53

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          reviewed as part of statutorily required, triennial IRP proceedings, subject to Commission review and

          approval, which comprehensively evaluate Georgia Power’s plans for the next 20 years. The IRP process

          allows interested members of the public the right to participate in multiple ways, including engaging in the

          thorough review of the Company’s plans by intervening in the case or providing comments during a public

          hearing.


          Decisions on how best to meet the needs of customers are not relegated to a singular analysis. Georgia law

          acknowledges this by requiring a planning process that is truly integrated and recognizes the supply-side

          dynamics of forecasted needs, transmission, environmental compliance, and generation. The development

          of the IRP is a complex process requiring coordination from across the Company that takes significant time

          to complete. As a part of the three-year planning cycle, planning for and preparing the IRP takes a year or

          more, the IRP and any associated rate case proceedings take another year, and implementation of the

          Commission decisions is the focus of the following year and beyond. Through the IRP process, the

          Company ultimately submits to the Commission its long-term plan to meet the needs of customers by

          providing reliable, cost-effective electricity while also complying with a range of environmental laws.


          Given this regulatory framework, Georgia Power must carefully evaluate the implications for operations,

          reliability, and the impacts on customers through the IRP process while considering environmental

          compliance strategy decisions to control or retire and replace generating resources. By way of example,

          Georgia Power is procedurally required to submit to its PSC an IRP at least every three years that details

          its long-term plans for its energy resources to meet customer energy demands. To modify its generation

          portfolio, Georgia Power must follow Commission rules and, for large resources, would be required to issue

          a request for proposals (RFPs), evaluate RFP bids, and apply for certification of the new resource(s) with

          the PSC. To receive approval of a certification request, the utility must ensure prudency of the RFP process,

          which necessitates a thorough and equitable evaluation. Georgia Power typically requires between 19 and


                                                               54

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          30 months before resources are certified or activities associated with building a new resource are initiated.

          Up to six months of additional time may also be required prior to the certification filing depending on the

          level of activity at the Commission and whether certification requests will be included as part of an

          upcoming triennial IRP filing. Of special note is the fact that the state law prohibits an electric utility from

          commencing construction until a certificate is obtained from the PSC. With the robust regulatory process

          that is required by law, any decision to retire a generating unit necessarily follows a multi-year evaluation

          to ensure that customers’ best interests are fully considered. EPA must consider these state regulatory

          process requirements in setting any guidelines around timelines for unit retirement commitments.


                                   b. A retirement subcategory should appropriately consider the timing
                                      required for replacement generation and transmission.

          In the Southern Company’s January 2020 comments to EPA79, Southern provided support for a timeframe

          of at least 8 years for a utility to obtain necessary regulatory approvals to retire coal units and complete the

          construction of new generation. This timeline was largely based on a historical example illustrating the

          approval and construction of three new gas-fired units at Georgia Power’s Plant McDonough. In these

          comments, we also noted the following key issues that may also affect the actual timing that may be required

          to replace generation: 1) transmission constraints are an important and critical component for new or retiring

          generation, and that significant transmission upgrades may be needed to support reliable operations and

          resiliency of the system, depending on the location of the generation; and 2) these updates may require long

          lead-time planning, land acquisition, design, and construction efforts in order to support the new generation

          or accommodate future retirements.


                  79 Comment Letter from Jeffrey A. Burleson, Senior Vice President, Environmental and System Planning,
          Southern Company, supra note 38, at 49-53.

                                                                55

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          In the case of Georgia Power, because this rulemaking more specifically impacts the potential economic

          viability of Georgia Power’s Plant Bowen, more current and site-specific impacts must be considered. Plant

          Bowen presents a different scenario than Plant McDonough in that the existing generating capacity of Plant

          Bowen represents the largest single facility that will have been retired to date. Due to its location and size,

          to replace the generation capacity of Plant Bowen, both very significant new transmission development and

          generation replacement are required. Georgia Power currently anticipates that the necessary transmission

          projects and additional generation to replace Plant Bowen while maintaining reliability could require

          timelines through the end of 2035, including completion of the robust regulatory approval process and

          associated RFP and certification process. While certain extensive transmission projects are already

          underway to allow for the eventual retirement of Plant Bowen, the acceleration of the timeline required to

          meet the 2029 compliance deadline is not possible. With numerous individual transmission projects

          required, planning for the timing of construction and outages is critical to maintain reliability for customers

          throughout the process. Even if critical factors such as supply chain, labor and transmission and generation

          outage planning needs are ignored, the acceleration of the timeline would require even more extensive

          transmission work than currently planned, almost doubling the cost (from about half a billion dollars to

          about one billion dollars). And yet, doubling the cost still does not make the timeline achievable when all

          factors are appropriately considered. Until the completion of this transmission work, Plant Bowen remains

          critical to maintaining electric service reliability in Georgia.


          Further, procuring and/or building replacement generation to prepare for the eventual retirement of over

          3,000 megawatts of capacity at Plant Bowen has critical timing considerations. Currently, Georgia Power

          is in the process of deploying generation capacity through power purchase agreements (PPAs) of about

          2,300 megawatts to prepare for currently approved plant retirements (which does not include Plant Bowen)

          through 2028. Planning for the 2019 IRP, which included the proposed RFP process, began before 2018,

          the proposed RFP process was approved by the Commission in the 2019 IRP, selected resources from the

                                                                 56

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          RFP process were approved during the 2022 IRP, and the resources are anticipated to begin serving

          customers between 2024 and 2028. Thus, full deployment of these resources, which are all existing

          resources with no new construction required, will take at least 10 years from start to finish. Meanwhile,

          additional coal plant retirements beyond those already approved through 2028 will only increase the

          complexities of market supply and demand for electricity and are expected to further challenge and prolong

          these timeframes.


          Taking all of these relevant factors into consideration, the end of 2035 is the earliest feasible and responsible

          date to consider for the retirement of Plant Bowen in order to maintain reliability and resiliency of the

          electric grid in north Georgia and affordability for customers. If EPA finalizes the proposed BAT, EPA

          should finalize a new subcategory that allows plants such as Plant Bowen the time necessary to construct

          replacement generation and transmission necessary to accommodate its retirement without the addition of

          disparate costs to customers that would be imposed by the proposed new BAT for FGD wastewater. This

          new subcategory must consider the multi-year planning and evaluation process before unit retirements can

          be approved, as well as the complex planning and coordination necessary prior to construction of

          transmission and replacement generation for coal plants that are expected to remain after 2028. In the case

          of Plant Bowen, this subcategory should allow the plant to continue operating the 2020 BAT, and by a

          certain date no earlier than December 31, 2028, to align with the constructive state regulatory processes

          required by law, commit to either install the newly required BAT by December 31, 2032, or commit to

          retire or repower by December 31, 2035. This option mirrors the successful PCCC by 2028 subcategory

          and ensures resource decisions can be made in the best interest of customers.


                  C.       EPA should make modifications to the early adopter subcategory.

          EPA has proposed a new subcategory for plants that have achieved compliance either with the 2015 or 2020

          rule limitations on FGD wastewater and BA transport water by the publication of this proposed rule, and

                                                                 57

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          which elect to retire no later than December 31, 2032. As a condition of being eligible for this subcategory,

          EPA proposes that permitting authorities include the BAT limitations in these sources’ permits after

          December 31, 2032. EPA reasons that such a subcategory is warranted on the basis of cost (disparate costs

          to facilities with these units), age (both the age of the new pollution treatment technology and the remaining

          useful life of the plant), non-water quality environmental impacts (air pollution), and other factors the

          Administrator deems appropriate (impacts to early adopters who relied on the identification of biological

          treatment as BAT for FGD wastewater in the 2015 and 2020 Rules). EPA also reasons that utilities that

          have “avoided incurring any cost for as long as possible” may be better poised to adjust to this proposed

          rule.


          As proposed, the “early adopter” subcategory inadequately assesses the entirety of effort and investments

          made toward compliance with the 2015 and 2020 rules across the industry, as well as the projected

          retirement horizons of those assumed to be “early adopters;” and therefore produces an unfair and

          unequitable outcome for both those that are included as early adopters but have no plans to retire by 2032

          as well as those who are excluded from the subcategory even though they may have already converted to

          dry ash handling systems and/or made substantial and irreversible financial commitments to comply with

          the 2020 BAT for BATW and FGD wastewater (which could also include the early operation of a physical

          chemical treatment system).


          In our comments, we have presented site-specific cost estimates for Plants Miller and Bowen, illustrating

          that the projected costs to comply with the newly proposed BAT are far greater than EPA has estimated.

          Further, EPA’s limited review of projected retirement horizons has likely excluded retirement commitments

          that extend beyond the December 31, 2032, date, by only a few years. Expanding this review to include

          units that may retire by the end of 2035 would both alleviate disparate costs to a wider population of aging

          units and weigh in favor of EPA’s consideration of non-water quality environmental impacts, such as


                                                               58

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          reduced air emissions. Finally, the other factors EPA relies upon (impacts to early adopters who relied on

          the identification of biological treatment as BAT for FGD wastewater in the 2015 and 2020 Rules) unfairly

          penalizes facilities that also fully complied with the law and made decisions in the best interests of

          customers.


          Accordingly, we present solutions for EPA to consider in finalizing the early adopter subcategory to

          produce fair and equitable outcomes while maximizing the environmental benefits of complying with the

          2015, 2020 and this Supplemental ELG rulemaking.


                           1.       EPA should revise the “cut-off” date or qualification date to include facilities

                                    that have entered into a contract with a vendor to install technologies to

                                    comply with the 2020 Rule BAT.


          EPA’s proposed eligibility “cut-off” date or qualification date for this subcategory should be changed. EPA

          requested comments on this issue. EPA’s proposed March 29, 2023, qualification date creates fair notice

          and equitable concerns. EPA never previously identified the March 29, 2023, date as one from which

          regulatory consequences would flow. The first notice anyone may have had of this date and its significance

          was disclosed in the pre-publication version of the proposed rule, released by EPA on March 8, 2023.

          However, that pre-publication version was also internally inconsistent, referring to the Federal Register

          date of the proposed rule in certain instances, while referring to a date after publication of the final ELG

          rule in other instances. Accordingly, the industry had no opportunity to conform its conduct to this new

          legal standard. Many facilities are currently in the process of contracting for and constructing a biological

          treatment system to comply with the 2020 Rule. The only fair and just approach would be to extend the

          eligibility date to one that’s after the effective date of a final rule. Only then will a party considering whether

          to opt-in to this subcategory have the ability to conform its conduct and also have full knowledge of its

          legal obligations and options to make a fully informed compliance decision.

                                                                  59

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                          2.       The early adopter subcategory eligibility should not be limited to only those

                                   that have completed installation and demonstrated compliance with the 2020

                                   Rule requirements.


          The early adopter subcategory eligibility should not be limited to only those that have completed installation

          and demonstrated compliance with the 2020 Rule requirements. It is enough that companies and facilities

          have made sizeable (and sometimes irreversible) commitments to install a treatment system to comply with

          the 2020 Rule. EPA has recognized in 2015, 2020, and in this proposed rule that the installation of these

          complex treatment systems is a multi-year process. Despite this, the Agency is proposing to establish an

          eligibility criterion that ignores the fact that many companies and facilities may have spent millions of

          dollars to achieve compliance with the 2020 Rule but may be one or two years away from achieving

          compliance; while other facilities may have executed a contract with a vendor for the installation of a 2020

          ELG rule-compliant treatment system but may not be able to meaningfully amend or void that contract.


          For example, the proposed qualification date for the early adopter subcategory will prevent Plant Bowen

          from qualifying for the subcategory. Plant Bowen has entered a contract with a vendor for the installation

          of a biological treatment system and has already incurred more than $50 million to pursue, plan, finance,

          and design how it will comply with the 2020 Rule, because its NPDES permit requires the new biological

          treatment system to be in service to meet the 2020 Rule limits by December 31, 2025. Depending on when

          a final rule is issued, Plant Bowen’s current compliance costs will likely increase another $30-40 million.


          A reasonable and workable subcategory needs to provide relief to permittees that initiated actions to comply

          with the 2020 Rule. Stated simply, the early adopter subcategory needs to provide relief not only for those

          facilities that have completed the installation and optimization process to achieve compliance, but also for

          those that have taken meaningful steps toward complying with 2020 Rule. To address these concerns, the

          only fair and just approach would be to revise the eligibility criteria and include units that have already

                                                               60

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          contracted for but not yet installed biological treatment to comply with the 2020 Rule, i.e., entered into a

          contract by the signature date of the final rule.


                           3.       EPA should not require retirement for early adopters.


          As mentioned previously, the proposed early adopter subcategory unfairly treats even those that would

          qualify by requiring retirement. This requirement is largely unexplained by EPA (which makes it arbitrary

          and capricious) and misses the point on why the “early adopter” subcategory is necessary and equitable.

          The subcategory is warranted because: (1) of the reliance interests of early adopters (as explained herein);

          (2) these units should not be forced to abandon these new treatment technologies after only a few years

          (when their useful life is well-established as 20+ years); and (3) customers should not be immediately

          subjected to additional (or even overlapping) rate increases because of EPA’s changing regulatory

          positions. EPA’s proposal also fails to adequately take into consideration the environmental benefits already

          experienced at such facilities by installing and operating the 2020 BAT earlier than December 31, 2025

          (Plant Miller), installing and operating a physical chemical treatment system as progress toward compliance

          with the 2020 BAT (Plant Bowen), and/or converting to dry bottom ash handling systems well in advance

          of this proposed rulemaking (Plants Miller and Bowen). Requiring retirement to qualify for this subcategory

          seems punitive. As opposed to penalizing these facilities with an early retirement option that is neither

          feasible nor coordinated with simultaneously proposed environmental rulemakings, EPA should simply

          remove the requirement for early adopters to commit to retirement and should instead allow early adopters

          to either retire or continue operating under the new BAT no later than December 31, 2032.


                                                               61

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                           4.      If EPA’s early adopter subcategory requires a retirement commitment, then

                                   EPA should allow early adopters to either comply with new generally

                                   applicable limits by December 31, 2032, or commit to retire by December 31,

                                   2035.


          While we believe EPA should not require retirement for early adopters, if EPA ultimately decides to finalize

          an early adopter subcategory that requires a retirement commitment, then EPA should: 1) as discussed

          above, require compliance with the new generally applicable limits no later than December 31, 2032, and

          2) extend the retirement date from December 31, 2032 to December 31, 2035. As discussed previously,

          EPA’s review of facilities that may soon retire fell short of including a potentially substantial number of

          units that may elect to retire no later than the end of 2035, including Plant Bowen. EPA cited retirement

          plans made by utilities beyond December 31, 2032, but, without full explanation, excluded these units as

          early adopters by establishing a retirement date that is not achievable. In doing so, EPA has set up a potential

          outcome that not only fails to capture the full scope of non-water quality benefits that could be associated

          with an expanded subcategory (e.g., reduced air emissions), but also results in an untenable situation for

          units that: 1) should qualify as early adopters based on progress toward 2015 and 2020 Rule compliance,

          and 2) would experience disparate costs and potential reliability concerns due to the age of the units and

          associated timelines for completing necessary generation replacement and transmission infrastructure

          upgrades. In our preceding sections, we presented a scenario for Georgia Power’s Plant Bowen that strongly

          supports both the need for such a retirement subcategory and an associated date to retire by December 31,

          2035. We recommend that the timing of a retirement commitment under the early adopter subcategory

          should mirror that which we have recommended for a new PCCC by 2035 subcategory.


                                                                62

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                  D.      EPA should align compliance timing and subcategory options with other

                          impactful proposed environmental rules.

          As a general matter, whether through establishment of an early adopter subcategory or with stand-alone

          subcategories that allow flexibilities in compliance timing and associated requirements, EPA should take

          steps to ensure harmonization with other impactful environmental rules, including, but not limited to, CAA

          Section 111 rulemakings. Given the substantially underestimated costs of the proposed new BAT in this

          rulemaking and the proposed expedited timeframe to achieve compliance, utilities should have the

          appropriate time to evaluate the impact of multiple rulemakings on the generation fleet and make decisions

          that are protective of the environment and in the best interests of customers. Extending the time to comply

          with any new proposed BAT until at least December 31, 2032, and extending the date by which units must

          commit to retire to December 31, 2035, under any new retirement subcategory best achieves this outcome.


        V.    LEGACY WASTEWATER (LWW)

          In spring of 2016, The Southern Company announced that operating companies would stop sending coal

          ash to unlined ponds by spring of 2019, except for one facility. By spring of 2019, the Company’s operating

          companies fulfilled this commitment through an aggressive ash and wastewater management program. By

          the end of 2020, all the Company’s operating companies had completely discontinued sending both CCR

          and non-CCR waste streams to our ash ponds – ahead of EPA’s April 11, 2021, deadline. Twenty-one units

          across six sites (Plants Barry, Bowen, Gaston, Miller, Scherer, and Wansley) converted to dry/closed loop

          ash handling (even as early as August 2018) and the water treatment functionality of the ash ponds was

          replaced at 12 sites, comprising a $2.6 billion program.


          EPA has proposed several changes to LWW requirements in the proposal, including subdividing LWW

          into new categories, new definitions, and requiring different management requirements for the new

                                                              63

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          categories. As a general matter, Southern urges caution with any revision to the LWW requirements that

          could complicate, delay, or derail ongoing dewatering and closure activities required by the CCR Rule.


                  A.       EPA should not subdivide LWW.

          EPA is proposing in this rule to segregate LWW into two main categories of separately regulated

          discharges, which would each be subject to separate case-by-case technology-based effluent limitations

          established by the permitting authority. These two main categories are described as follows:


          1) Wastewater continuously or intermittently generated and discharged to a pond after the issuance of the

              first permit implementing the 2015 or 2020 Rule but before the compliance date specified in the permit

              (the “as soon as possible” date required by the rule), and


          2) Wastewater that was discharged to the pond previously and will be discharged when the pond is

              dewatered for closure.


          The Southern Company believes these proposed definitional changes to be unnecessary. While there is

          value in acknowledging the current status of waste streams in the context of how the CCR and ELG Rules

          have impacted the on-site management and treatment of these waste streams, as proposed, EPA’s

          subdivision of LWW is problematic. The proposed subdivision allows for a scenario where a wastewater

          may have been sent to the pond after permit issuance but before its late applicability date in the permit. The

          definition becomes retroactive in a manner that is impossible to achieve. If a facility were to discharge

          wastewater continuously or intermittently to a pond after the issuance of a permit, then this wastewater

          would not be separable, physically, or otherwise, from wastewater that was discharged to that same pond

          prior to the issuance of the permit. In this scenario, there is no significant difference in composition between

          the two categories of LWW. The only difference is when the LWW was generated. If separated by time,

          both categories of LWW with similar composition will be treated to meet the existing ELGs and any water


                                                                64

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          quality-based effluent limits in the NPDES permit prior to discharge. Therefore, EPA does not need to

          propose separate subcategories of LWW separated by time or propose that the permit writer conduct a

          separate ELG BAT determination on each category to set BPJ limits. This is unnecessary, creates

          confusion, and adds an extra burden to the permit writer.


                  B.      If EPA chooses to subdivide LWW, then EPA should do so based on the

                          following temporal marker: the later date of either when a pond stopped

                          receiving these waste streams (i.e., the “cease receipt” date of CCR and non-

                          CCR wastes for unlined ponds) or the issuance of the first permit

                          implementing the 2015 or 2020 Rule.

          If EPA does subdivide LWW into different categories, then EPA could instead consider establishing a more

          practical temporal marker to subdivide these waste streams: the later date of either when the pond stopped

          receiving these waste streams (i.e., the “cease receipt” date of CCR and non-CCR wastes for unlined ponds)

          or the issuance of the first permit implementing the 2015 or 2020 Rule either renewal or modification. In

          this scenario, there would be no instance where the subdivided wastewater would have already been sent to

          the pond, and a facility that stopped sending wastewater to ponds earlier than the issuance of the NPDES

          permit would not be subject to these requirements any earlier than the date of issuance of the first permit

          implementing the 2015 or 2020 Rule.


          Even if EPA can establish a practical subdivision, there may be little practical effect for any LWW other

          than FGD wastewater, as it is likely that facilities would have implemented the 2015 BAT for fly ash

          transport water (FATW) prior to, or at latest, concurrent with, the date that they stopped sending LWW to

          the pond. Presuming EPA issues a final rule in 2024, many facilities would be well underway toward

          installation and testing of the 2020 BAT to meet the applicability date established in the permit, no later


                                                              65

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          than December 31, 2025. At Plants Bowen and Miller, both FATW and BATW are already meeting the

          2020 BAT, and FGD wastewater is being treated by either chemical precipitation (Plant Bowen) or the

          2020 BAT (Plant Miller). Even in the case where FGD wastewater were re-rerouted from an unlined CCR

          impoundment to a lined settling pond, the effluent would still be discharged through an NPDES permitted

          outfall and subject to meeting existing ELGs and state water quality standards. Therefore, there is no reason

          to separate this waste stream as a subdivision of LWW for purposes of this rulemaking since EPA’s

          objective of achieving a more effective treatment for FGD wastewater until the 2020 BAT applicability

          date is likely already occurring in many cases.


                  C.      EPA should not subcategorize LWW that was discharged to the pond

                          previously and will be discharged when the pond is dewatered for closure.

          EPA is proposing to further subcategorize the second major proposed category of LWW: that which was

          discharged to the pond previously and will be discharged when the pond is dewatered for closure. This is

          effectively the wastewater that remains in the pond after the pond has ceased receipt of both CCR and non-

          CCR wastes. This wastewater may exist above the settled CCR solids within the pond or as interstitial water

          surrounding the settled CCR solids. EPA’s proposed subdivision of this category is as follows:


              •   Surface impoundment (SI) decant wastewater: surficial water located above the CCR solids

                  (hereafter referred to as ‘‘surface impoundment (SI) decant wastewater’’), or the layer of a closing

                  surface impoundment’s wastewater that is located from the water surface down to the level

                  sufficiently above any coal combustion residuals that, when drained, does not resuspend the coal

                  combustion residuals; and


              •   Surface impoundment (SI) dewatering wastewater: Pore water in the saturated CCR layer at levels

                  beyond that needed for conditioning, or the layer of a closing surface impoundment’s wastewater


                                                               66

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                  that is located below surface impoundment decant water due to its contact with either stationary or

                  resuspended coal combustion residuals.


          Since the beginning of dewatering efforts, our facilities have recognized and addressed the potential

          differences in pollutant levels associated with progressive dewatering. This is evident from the dewatering

          data the Company voluntarily provided to EPA in April 2022. In practice, a single technology can be used

          to treat both types of surface impoundment wastewaters with modifications to the treatment process (e.g.,

          addition of chemicals to remove pollutants) to protect receiving stream water quality. Therefore, we suggest

          that this specific subcategorization is unnecessary and irrelevant for purposes of establishing effluent limits

          for dewatering wastewater. If there is water removed from an impoundment during closure through

          dewatering, then it should be referred to collectively as “dewatering wastewater.”


          Importantly, EPA’s definition of this LWW refers to wastewater within an impoundment that is in the

          process of being closed (i.e., “a closing surface impoundment”). We support EPA’s decision to limit this

          definition to wastewater that is removed from within the impoundment to facilitate closure. We question,

          however the intent of EPA’s description of surface impoundment dewatering wastewater in the preamble

          as that which is present “in the saturated CCR at levels beyond that needed for conditioning.” For purposes

          of this ELG rulemaking, knowing whether a wastewater is present “at levels beyond that needed for

          conditioning” serves no purpose.


          As stated above, EPA should not further subcategorize LWW that was discharged to the pond previously

          and will be discharged when the pond is dewatered for closure. Our experience and information/data

          provided to EPA has shown that this subcategorization is not necessary.80 However, should EPA ultimately


                  80 Letter from Donna Hill, Southern Company Services, Inc., supra note 9.


                                                                67

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          choose to define these two subcategories, then EPA should remove any reference regarding the degree to

          which the wastewater is present “in the saturated CCR at levels beyond that needed for conditioning.”


                  D.       EPA should not establish more stringent LWW treatment requirements that

                           hinder pond closure.

          As described above, the Company’s operating companies have moved aggressively to replace surface

          impoundments as wastewater treatment units, rerouting LWWs to robust treatment systems that protects

          receiving water quality and facilitates pond closure activities. EPA is correct in its stated uncertainty as to

          whether more stringent systems (chemical precipitation, biological treatment, membrane filtration, thermal

          evaporation, spray dryer evaporation) could be used nationwide “without disrupting some plants’ already

          commenced (and contracted for) closure process, thereby possibly jeopardizing the ability of those plants

          to meet their closure deadlines under the CCR Rule.”81 We agree that EPA should avoid establishing

          requirements (either through more stringent technologies or through permitting constraints) that would

          interfere with the closure progress or become a linchpin of the pond closure schedule. To account for this,

          EPA could specifically instruct permit writers to take into consideration in their BPJ analyses a facility’s

          current dewatering treatment system, dewatering status, and CCR closure timeline, and establish effluent

          limitations accordingly. It is imperative that, given the already stringent deadlines for completing closure,

          these activities proceed expeditiously and without delays associated with the imposition of an unnecessarily

          stringent technology, even if it is perceived as readily available at the site.


                  81 88 Fed. Reg. at 18,853.


                                                                 68

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


       VI.    COMBUSTION RESIDUAL LEACHATE (CRL)

          EPA has maintained the definition for CRL from the original 2015 rulemaking, which defines CRL as

          “liquid, including any suspended or dissolved constituents in the liquid, which has percolated through or

          drained from waste or other materials placed in a landfill, or that passes through the containment structure

          (e.g., bottom, dikes, berms) of a surface impoundment.”82 EPA is proposing chemical precipitation as the

          technology basis for establishing BAT limitations to control pollutants discharged in CRL. EPA proposes

          that this technology is available, is economically achievable, and has acceptable non-water quality

          environmental     impacts.    Specifically,    the       proposed   BAT   basis   consists   of   chemical

          precipitation/coprecipitation employing the combination of hydroxide precipitation, iron coprecipitation,

          and sulfide precipitation. The Company does not object to the proposed BAT limits for arsenic and mercury

          for this waste stream but believes EPA should constrain the scope of regulated CRL to that which is

          collected from engineered leachate collection systems and then discharged via surface outfalls from active

          landfills at active generating plants. Subjecting numerous unidentified and uncharacterized sources of water

          to an improper regulatory definition completely unbalances any underlying determinations or assumptions

          of cost-effectiveness. In particular, this rulemaking should not establish effluent limits or permitting

          requirements for functional equivalent discharges of CRL because unlined landfills and surface

          impoundments are not point sources.


                  82 80 Fed. Reg. 67,838, 67,847 (Nov. 3, 2015).


                                                                   69

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                  A.      EPA’s proposed BAT limits for functional equivalent discharges of CRL

                          represents a regulatory overreach and should not be finalized.

          As part of the proposal, EPA has included new guidance to implement the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision

          in County of Maui.83 The proposed guidance is presented as having limited applicability, but it actually

          represents a significant regulatory overreach. Notably, in 2020, EPA published for comment a proposed

          standalone guidance document that would help inform how to broadly incorporate County of Maui into

          existing NPDES permit programs. EPA finalized that guidance in January 2021, only to rescind it several

          months later. Now, years later, EPA proposes new County of Maui guidance but has tucked it into a larger,

          industry-specific rulemaking. As described below, the substance of EPA’s proposed County of Maui

          guidance is flawed, as is the Agency’s decision to propose it, for the first time, as part of this industry

          specific ELG rulemaking.


                          1.       Unlined landfills and surface impoundments are not point sources.


          In County of Maui, the existence of a “point source” was both a necessary predicate and undisputed (there,

          wastewater was injected directly into groundwater through an engineered underground injection control

          system). However, unlined landfills and surface impoundments are not point sources. In the only cases

          directly on point, both the Fourth Circuit and Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected all arguments to the

          contrary.


                  83 Cty. of Maui v. Haw. Wildlife Fund, 140 S. Ct. 1462 (2020).


                                                                 70

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          In the Fourth Circuit case, Sierra Club v. Virginia Electric & Power Company,84 Sierra Club argued that

          seepage of CRL from an unlined landfill and settling ponds at the Chesapeake Energy Center in Virginia

          constituted unpermitted point source discharges under the CWA. But the court disagreed, ruling that they

          did not function as conveyances and thus did not meet the statutory definition of point source. The court

          went on to explain that in regulating discharges of pollutants from point sources, Congress clearly intended

          to target the measurable discharge of pollutants.

                   When a source works affirmatively to convey a pollutant, the concentration of the pollutant
                   and the rate at which it is discharged by that conveyance can be measured. But when the
                   alleged discharge is diffuse and not the product of a discrete conveyance, that task is
                   virtually impossible.85
          The court concluded that the scenario presented by the unlined landfill and settling ponds at Chesapeake

          Energy Center “indicates circumstances that are incompatible with the effluent limitation scheme that lies

          at the heart of the Clean Water Act.”86


          In Ky. Waterways Alliance. v. Kentucky Utilities Company, the Sixth Circuit reached the identical

          conclusion in a case involving two coal ash ponds at the E.W. Brown Generating Station in Kentucky.


                   Here [plaintiffs] contend that the coal ash ponds are point sources. We doubt the
                   correctness of that position. A point source, by definition, is a “conveyance.” 33 U.S.C. §
                   1362(14). Coal ash ponds are not conveyances – they do not “take or carry [pollutants]
                   from one place to another.” . . . In fact, ash ponds are quite the opposite; they are designed
                   to store coal ash in place.87


                   84 903 F.3d 403 (4th Cir. 2018).

                   85 Id. at 411 (emphasis in original).

                   86 Id.

                   87 905 F.3d 925, 934 n.8 (6th Cir. 2018), abrogated by Cty. of Maui, Hawaii v. Hawaii Wildlife Fund, 140
          S. Ct. 1462 (2020) (internal citations omitted) (emphasis in original).

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          EPA fails to reconcile or even acknowledge the existence of these controlling cases in its proposal. Instead,

          EPA purports to dodge the point source requirement altogether: “EPA, through this action, is not addressing

          the definition of any terms in the CWA (such as ‘point source’ or ‘discharge of a pollutant’) that governs

          when a discharge is subject to NPDES permitting requirements . . . .”88        EPA’s position is untenable and

          any attempt to regulate CRL through groundwater from unlined landfills and surface impoundments must

          be rejected.


                           2.       EPA has not yet taken the steps necessary to implement County of Maui.


          Even assuming, for the sake of argument, that a point source exists, EPA’s proposal would still be

          inappropriate. In the three years since the Supreme Court issued County of Maui, EPA has not yet taken

          the required regulatory steps necessary to bring functional equivalent discharges into the NPDES permit

          program. First, EPA has not amended the NPDES regulations at 40 C.F.R. Part 122 to implement County

          of Maui, either in terms of the scope of the NPDES permit requirements in § 122.1(b) or the application

          requirements in § 122.21 et seq. Second, EPA has not revised the required application forms to encompass

          the types of data and information needed to determine the existence of, and develop the limitations and

          conditions applicable to, functional equivalent discharges. Indeed, across EPA’s complete set of forms and

          instructions for the entire universe of regulated NPDES discharges, there is not a single reference to

          functional equivalent discharges.89 Third, EPA has not issued any guidance that interprets or applies


                  88 88 Fed. Reg. at 18,850.

                  89 See EPA, National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES), NPDES Application Forms,
          available at https://www.epa.gov/npdes/npdes-application-forms (last visited May 28, 2023).

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          County of Maui or, for that matter, instructs delegated states on how to do so.90 In the absence of any of

          these necessary predicate actions, EPA’s recommendations in the preamble for applicants to submit

          extensive “supplemental information” on potential CRL in groundwater, and thereafter to provide annual

          CRL monitoring reports, are wholly unsupported and inappropriate.


          EPA claims that much of the supplemental data and information to be submitted with applications and

          included in annual reports is already available and thus “the incremental burden to facilities should be

          minimal,”91 but this is not accurate. The recommended technical information extends far beyond what is

          required under EPA’s CCR Rules. For example, EPA’s CCR Rules do not require any of the information

          required to apply the Supreme Court’s County of Maui factors (as proposed here), including travel time,

          pathway(s), or chemical fate and transport, as part of routine operational compliance. Moreover, EPA’s

          CCR Rules only require characterization of the nature and extent of groundwater impacts for units that are

          subject to corrective action (i.e., those exceeding groundwater protection standards for Appendix IV

          constituents by statistically significant levels and for which an alternative source such as natural variability

          has not been identified). Therefore, the supplemental data and information EPA identifies for inclusion

          with applications is, in fact, not readily available.

                           3.      CRL ceases to be a waste stream—by definition—when it exits a unit.


          As noted above, EPA proposes to maintain the 2015 definition of CRL, which is leachate that exits a CCR

          landfill or surface impoundment. CRL clearly is not the same as groundwater, which EPA defines as “water

          that is found in the saturated part of the ground underneath the land surface.”92 If CRL exits a unit and

          ends up in groundwater, then it necessarily becomes impacted groundwater.


          EPA seems to assume that CRL retains some independent identity even after it mixes with groundwater,

          but this defies logic and lacks any limiting principles, the most obvious of which would be both spatial and

          temporal. In other words, CRL ceases to exist as a unique waste stream subject to the ELG program (or the

          CWA for that matter) once it exits a unit (e.g., through migration into groundwater). Similarly, CRL can

          no longer be considered CRL when it mixes with other media before, during or after the closure process.

          Otherwise, CRL-impacted groundwater could be subject to BAT limits (and EPA’s presumptive pump-and-

          treat technology) long after a unit closes or at substantial distance from the unit. This proposal does not

          contemplate these definitional and practical limitations.


                           4.      CRL in groundwater is governed by RCRA, not the CWA.


          EPA’s approach to CRL in groundwater also conflicts with – and threatens to undermine – EPA’s

          comprehensive regulation of groundwater quality at CCR units through the CCR regulatory program under

          RCRA. In fact, EPA’s proposal is fundamentally inconsistent with RCRA. In 2015, EPA adopted the first

          national regulations governing CCR as RCRA solid waste.93 These regulations impose location restrictions,


                   92 88 Fed. Reg. at 18,895 (Appendix A to the Preamble: Definitions, Acronyms and Abbreviations Used in
          this Preamble).
                  93 See 80 Fed. Reg. 21,301 (Apr. 17, 2015).


                                                                74

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          design and operating criteria, groundwater monitoring and corrective action requirements, and closure and

          post-closure care requirements for regulated CCR units, including landfills and surface impoundments, as

          well as extensive recordkeeping, notification and public posting requirements, all of which are designed to

          meet the RCRA protectiveness standard of “no reasonable probability of adverse effects.”94 With respect

          to groundwater monitoring and corrective action, in particular, EPA’s CCR Rules require compliance with

          groundwater protection standards and require remedial measures whenever Appendix IV constituents are

          detected in groundwater at statistically significant levels above those standards.95 EPA’s proposed BAT

          limits for CRL in groundwater bear no relation to these CCR groundwater protection standards, and EPA’s

          presumed pump-and-treat approach96 (assuming the groundwater is pumped for purposes of corrective

          action) circumvents the more comprehensive corrective action process required by the CCR rules.

          Furthermore, establishing effluent limits for groundwater impacted by CCR units could unnecessarily

          complicate or prolong corrective action under the federal CCR Rule at the site. Should EPA establish

          effluent limits for groundwater impacted by CRL, then EPA would introduce unnecessary uncertainty to

          the remedy selection process.


          More fundamentally, EPA’s proposed ELGs for CRL in groundwater threaten to disrupt the foundation of

          the RCRA CCR program. Congress defined “solid waste” in the statute to exclude point sources subject to


                  94 42 U.S.C. § 6944(a).

                  95 See 40 C.F.R. §§ 257.95 – 257.98.

                    96 Included in the record for EPA’s proposed supplemental ELGs is a memorandum dated March 2, 2023,

          be pumped and treated to meet the proposed BAT limits. See Memorandum from U.S. EPA, Evaluation of Potential
          CRL in Groundwater – DCN SE10250 (Mar. 2, 2023) (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2009-0819-9678). It is clear
          from this memo that EPA assumes pump-and-treat systems will be required to meet those limits.

          NPDES permits under the CWA.97            If EPA determines that CRL in groundwater is subject to ELGs

          implemented through NPDES permits, then CRL in groundwater will no longer be considered solid waste

          subject to RCRA, or more specifically, to the comprehensive CCR regulatory program (including

          groundwater corrective action). Congress could not possibly have intended for EPA to usurp its legislative

          EPA cannot possibly impose BAT limits on CRL-impacted groundwater from unlined landfills and surface

          impoundments without fully understanding – or explaining to the public – the scope of the potentially

          regulated universe (which will not be determined, at the earliest, until items 1 and 2 above are proposed

          and finalized). Nor can EPA draw rational conclusions about how its proposed ELGs will affect units that

          are in the closure process – or the timing of closure – without fully understanding the outcome of items 3,

          4, and 5 above. This is particularly problematic since the CCR Rules impose prescriptive closure deadlines

          with limited extension opportunities, all of which are directly implicated by EPA’s newly proposed BAT

          limits and pump-and-treat requirements for CRL in groundwater. For all these reasons, EPA should

          withdraw its proposal to regulate CRL in groundwater. Doing so would be entirely consistent with EPA’s

          approach to the landfill point source category in 2000.


                  B.       EPA should not establish BAT or set effluent limits for CRL based upon the
                           characteristics and treatment methods for FGD wastewater.
          EPA solicits comment on whether it should establish BAT and set effluent limits for CRL based upon the

          characteristics and treatment methods for FGD wastewater. There are two key reasons why EPA should

          not pursue such an approach: 1) the two waste streams exhibit key differences that warrant different

          treatment; and 2) these two waste streams occur in entirely different settings, and for much different

          durations, relative to the life expectancy of the power plant itself.


          Ultimately, both FGD wastewater and CRL result from combustion of coal. Therefore, there will be some

          similarities in the chemical composition of the waste streams. However, there are key differences in the

          waste stream chemical makeup that would allow a more cost-effective solution for CRL than is required

          for FGD wastewater. From a chemical standpoint, CRL is typically a much lower TDS waste stream than

          FGD wastewater with much lower concentrations of constituents that could necessitate different levels of

          treatment, such as selenium or nitrate. CRL typically contains selenium and nitrate at levels orders of

          magnitude lower than FGD wastewater, specifically making biological treatment a poor solution for CRL

                                                                77

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          compared to FGD wastewater. Unlike FGD wastewater, the production of CRL will long outlive the

          production of electricity at the plant. This fact should lead EPA toward considering more cost-effective

          options to effectively treat CRL. For at least these reasons, EPA should view the supporting basis for FGD

          wastewater limits and CRL limits as separate and distinct and should collect additional data as necessary to

          establish an appropriate BAT for CRL.


                  C.      EPA should not pursue more stringent technology than chemical precipitation

                          and should avoid establishing ZLD limits for CRL.

          EPA should not pursue the use of more stringent technology such as biological or thermal systems for the

          treatment of CRL. As discussed, CRL should be viewed as separate and distinct from waste streams

          produced only during the operating life of the power plant itself, such as FGD wastewater. CRL is different

          in that the waste stream will be produced long into the future beyond the plant’s active life of producing

          electricity. Biological and thermal systems pose significant operating, maintenance, and economic burdens

          to an operating plant, and even more so after a plant’s retirement. Similarly, spray dryer evaporator (SDE)

          systems, which evaporate water by a heat source (typically from a slipstream of hot flue gas) are known to

          create hygroscopic salts from power plant waste streams that can quickly become a liquid under

          atmospheric conditions.


          EPA is soliciting comment on whether ZLD limits should apply to CRL, and, if so, whether they should be

          based upon membrane filtration. As stated previously, we strongly encourage EPA to study and consider

          CRL as a separate waste stream from FGD wastewater and not simply transfer limitations from FGD

          wastewater to CRL. As a practical matter, we are not aware that EPA’s technical administrative record

          would support such an approach. Additionally, achieving ZLD for a waste stream with a long-anticipated

          duration is an energy-intensive proposition. The energy required to maintain a ZLD of CRL will have to

          come from somewhere, even after a plant has ceased generating electricity. Landfills don’t always exist

                                                              78

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          near the plant infrastructure. In some cases, landfills are located in relatively remote areas, which may be

          miles away from the plant operations. Given these settings, we encourage EPA to instead seek effective

          treatment systems with lower energy requirements and allow owners to reduce the leachate generated over

          time through appropriate landfill water management practices.


                  D.       EPA should not set CRL limits for closed landfills or landfills at retired

                           facilities.

          CRL discharges from retired facilities or from landfills capped and closed prior to or within five years after

          promulgation of the rule should be exempt from further regulation and remain subject to the limits currently

          applied. Research shows that closed landfills have reduced CRL flows due to less rainfall that percolates

          through or drains from the materials placed in the landfill.100 As the CRL flows decrease from closed

          landfills over time, the pollutant loadings decrease significantly. Likewise, in EPA’s TDD for the proposed

          2015 Rule, EPA provides the average CRL generation from active landfills is 65,500 gpd/plant, whereas

          the average CRL generation at retired landfills is 5,959 gpd/plant, less than 10% of active landfills.101


          Annual CRL pollutant loadings for a closed landfill are provided in Table 2. Using EPA’s flow rate for

          retired landfills and EPA’s untreated CRL water quality data,102 the pollutant loading per year for a closed

                   102 EPA, Technical Development Document for the Proposed Supplemental Effluent Limitations Guidelines

          landfill is 56,333 lbs/year and using EPA’s toxicity weighting factors,103 the loading per plant would be 38

          TWPE/year or toxic-weighed pounds per equivalent/year. These numbers are significantly different with

          EPA’s estimate of approximately 980,000 lbs/year at each operating plant.104 EPA states that the pollutant

          loadings were calculated as the sum of TDS and TSS. Most of the TDS constituents discharged from CRL

          include sulfate, chloride, calcium, and sodium, which are not considered toxic and have not been assigned

          toxic weighing factors by EPA. Therefore, the lower flows and smaller quantity of pollutant loadings in

          CRL at closed landfills does not justify substantial capital cost investments for chemical precipitation.


          In addition, when developing ELGs, the CWA requires EPA to consider the age of facilities involved and

          the cost of achieving effluent reduction. The costs of achieving the proposed BAT limits for CRL

          discharges at retired facilities would be much higher than compliance costs at operating facilities. EPA’s

          cost estimates for CRL BAT (chemical precipitation), assuming an average flow rate of 63 gallons per

          minute (gpm), is $11.2 million capital, $0.65 million annual O&M, and $1.7 million annualized cost.105 At

          a retired facility, the cost of power, labor, and residuals management and disposal is expected to be higher

          due to additional costs to bring power to the facility where no power is being generated onsite, the cost of

          a wastewater treatment operator who will work exclusively on the treatment system, and higher

          transportation and disposal costs for residuals management.106


                   103 EPA, Regulatory Impact Analysis for the Effluent Limitations Guidelines and Standards for the Steam
          Electric Power Generating Point Source Category, EPA-821-R-15-004, at Appendix F (Sept. 2015) (DCN SE07620)
          (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2009-0819-7549).
                   104 EPA, 2023 Technical Development Document, supra note 102, at 63, Table 20 (baseline 67,700,000
          lbs/year divided by 69 plants).
                  105 EPA assumed 7% interest rate and 20-year life for annualized cost.

          But EPA has not considered these costs. Therefore, in recognition of the age of the facilities and the cost of

          chemical precipitation, EPA should exclude retired facilities from the new CRL BAT limits or develop a

          new proposal that adequately assesses the potential regulatory impact on retired facilities.


                  E.       EPA should update its population of landfills that collect and discharge CRL

                           and the total industry costs to comply with the proposed CRL limits based on

                           chemical precipitation.

          EPA has underestimated the number of landfills that collect and discharge CRL and the total industry costs

          to treat CRL with chemical precipitation technology to meet proposed mercury and arsenic limits. Table

          12, Estimated Cost of Implementation for Combustion Residual Leachate by Regulatory Option (in Millions

          of Pre-tax 2021 Dollars), in the 2023 TDD107 includes 69 facilities that EPA has identified as the

          population of landfills containing CCRs that collect and discharge CRL to surface waters or POTWs. Also,

          Table 10 in EPA’s memorandum, Generating Unit-Level Costs and Loadings Estimates by Regulatory

          Option for the 2023 Proposed Rule (SE10381), provides costs for chemical precipitation treatment of CRL

          for 69 facilities. Later in its analysis, EPA found 65 additional facilities that have constructed new landfills

          since 2015 using data from utilities’ “CCR Rule Compliance Data and Information” websites108 but

          apparently did not include these facilities in their industry cost estimates. EPA needs to include these

          additional 65 landfills in its overall costs to the industry. The addition of these 65 facilities to EPA’s cost

          estimates is more than likely to double the costs of CRL treatment to the industry. EPA needs to add these


                  107 EPA, 2023 Technical Development Document, supra note 102, at 52, Table 12.

                  108 Memorandum from U.S. EPA, Evaluation of Potential CRL in Groundwater, supra note 96.


                                                                82

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


              costs into its total industry costs and rerun all its models to account for these additional costs, including the

              missing costs identified for FGD wastewater Option 3 compliance.


       VII.       CONCLUSION

              Southern Company is committed to building the future of energy for the advancement of our customers and

              communities. We are focused on transitioning our generating fleet to net zero greenhouse gas emissions

              and making the necessary related investments in our transmission and distribution grids, while maintaining

              reliability and affordability for our customers. EPA’s recently proposed Supplemental ELG Rule threatens

              to disrupt the orderly fleet transition by increasing risks to reliability while burdening customers with undue

              costs. While The Southern Company is committed compliance with environmental laws, the realities of

              cost and reliability concerns in serving our customers cannot be ignored. We encourage EPA to finalize a

              Supplemental ELG Rule that can protect the environment, promote resiliency and reliability of the electric

              power system, and help to alleviate a significant cost burden to customers. We look forward to engaging

              constructively with EPA on this and future rulemakings.
