          Technical Proposal
          Design Basis
          The objective of this document is to provide Southern Company Services with a conceptual design and
          budgetary level cost estimate of certain deliverables associated with converting Alabama Power
          Company’s existing flue gas desulfurization (FGD) wastewater treatment system at Plant Miller to
          comply with revised discharge limits for the treatment of FGD wastewater expected in EPA’s
          forthcoming Effluent Limitations Guideline (ELG) Supplemental Rule. Alabama Power previously installed
          “chemical precipitation + low hydraulic residence time biological treatment” at Plant Miller for the
          treatment of FGD wastewater. The treatment system is designed to comply with EPA’s 2015 and 2020
          ELGs.
          This document assumes EPA’s new FGD wastewater discharge limits will be identical to the Voluntary
          Incentives Program (VIP) limits included in the agency’s 2020 ELG rule and delineates a cost estimate for
          certain elements necessary for the installation of membrane filtration technologies (i.e., the “Process
          Island Costs”).

          Process Description
          Membrane Treatment System
          Stage 1 VSEP Feed Tank
          The influent for the system goes into the Stage 1 VSEP Feed Tank. The Stage 1 VSEP Feed Tank is fed by
          the existing Multimedia Filter effluent. The Tank also receives flow from the concentrate of the Stage 3
          Reverse Osmosis (RO) membrane. Acid is added to the Stage 1 Tank for any necessary pH adjustment.
          Anti-scalant and bisulfite are dosed in the header to prevent scaling and reduce chlorine respectively.
          The Stage 1 Low Pressure VSEPs pull from the Stage 1 VSEP Feed Tank. To prevent cavitation of the VSEP
          Feed Pumps, a Booster Pump on the feed line starts when both low pressure VSEP membranes are
          active.
          Stage 1 Low Pressure VSEP
          The Low Pressure VSEP Membranes use membrane filtration to separate suspended and dissolved
          solids. They employ a unique vibrating filter pack that produces a high shear rate on the membrane
          surface which inhibits membrane surface fouling and induces greater filtrate flow rates during the
          filtration process.


          Figure 1. New Logic Vibratory Shear Enhanced Processing Membrane leaf element tangential vibration process. Courtesy of
                                                    https://www.vsep.com/technology/

          The Stage 1 Low Pressure VSEPs discharge two streams: permeate (filtrate or product) and concentrate
          (brine or retentate). The VSEP concentrate is sent to the Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP Feed Tank. The
          permeate is sent to the Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank.
          The membranes will need to be cleaned occasionally to remove accumulated foulants or scaling. There
          are two modes of cleaning, flush and CIP. Flush is a lower pressure single pass step where heated RO
          permeate is sent to the system for removal of foulants and/or scaling. CIP is a lower pressure
          recirculation step where heated RO permeate mixed with cleaning chemicals is sent to the system for
          removal of more stubborn foulants.


                                                                Project: 24877_Rev2                                                 27

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP Feed Tank
          The Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP Feed Tank receives flow from the Low Pressure VSEP membranes
          concentrate. This Tank is the feed tank to the Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP membranes for further volume
          reduction. Antiscalant is dosed after the Feed Tank to prevent scaling.
          Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP
          The High Pressure VSEP membranes use membrane filtration to separate suspended and dissolved
          solids. They employ a unique vibrating filter pack that produces a high shear rate on the membrane
          surface which inhibits membrane surface fouling and induces greater filtrate flow rates during the
          filtration process. Stage 2 membranes operate at a higher pressure than Stage 1 due to the higher
          dissolved solids loading in the brine feed that must be rejected at the membrane surfaces.
          The Stage 2 High Pressure VSEPs discharge two streams: permeate (filtrate or product) and concentrate
          (brine or retentate). The Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP concentrate is sent to the Concentrate Storage
          Tank. The permeate is sent to the Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank.
          The membranes will need to be cleaned occasionally to remove accumulated foulants or scaling. There
          are two modes of cleaning, flush and CIP. Flush is a lower pressure single pass step where heated RO
          permeate is sent to the system for removal of foulants and/or scaling. CIP is a lower pressure
          recirculation step where heated RO permeate mixed with cleaning chemicals is sent to the system for
          removal of more stubborn foulants.
          Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank
          The Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank receives flow from the Stage 1 Low Pressure VSEP permeate, Stage 2
          High Pressure VSEP permeate, and Stage 4 Spiral RO concentrate. This tank is the feed tank to the Stage
          3 Spiral RO membranes for further polishing.
          Stage 3 Spiral RO
          The Stage 3 Spiral RO is the first stage of polishing after the VSEP membranes. There are 3 stages of RO
          (Stages 3, 4, and 5) total. The last stage is required to lower the mercury concentration to the required
          effluent quality. The same principles of operation apply to this membrane as the Stage 1 Low Pressure
          VSEP membranes. The feed stream is separated into 2 discharge streams: permeate and concentrate.
          The permeate is sent to the Stage 4 Spiral RO Feed Tank. The concentrate is recycled back to the Stage 1
          Low Pressure VSEP Feed Tank for additional processing. The Stage 3 Spiral RO is cleaned in a similar
          manner to the Stage 1 and 2 VSEP membranes.
          Stage 4 Spiral RO Feed Tank
          The Stage 4 Spiral RO Feed Tank receives flow from the Stage 3 Spiral RO permeate, and Stage 5 Spiral
          RO concentrate. This tank is the feed tank to the Stage 4 Spiral RO membranes.
          Stage 4 Spiral RO
          The Stage 4 Spiral RO is the second stage of polishing after the VSEP membranes. The same principles of
          operation apply to this membrane as the Stage 3 Spiral RO membranes. The feed stream is separated
          into 2 discharge streams: permeate and concentrate. The permeate is sent to the Stage 5 Spiral RO Feed
          Tank. The concentrate is recycled back to the Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank for additional processing. The
          Stage 4 Spiral RO is cleaned in a similar manner to the previous system membranes.


                                                          Project: 24877_Rev2                                         28

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          Stage 5 Spiral RO Feed Tank
          The Stage 5 Spiral RO Feed Tank receives flow from the Stage 4 Spiral RO permeate. This tank is the feed
          tank to the Stage 5 Spiral RO membranes.
          Stage 5 Spiral RO
          The Stage 5 Spiral RO is the third and final stage of polishing after the VSEP membranes. The same
          principles of operation apply to this membrane as the previous spiral RO membranes. The feed stream is
          separated into 2 discharge streams: permeate and concentrate. The permeate is sent to the Permeate
          Forwarding Storage Tank. This permeate water will meet the effluent limits assumed from the 2020 ELG
          VIP. The concentrate is recycled back to the Stage 4 Spiral RO Feed Tank for additional processing. The
          Stage 5 Spiral RO is cleaned in a similar manner to the previous system membranes.
          Permeate Forwarding Storage Tank
          The Permeate Forwarding Storage Tank will receive flow from the Stage 5 Spiral RO membranes and the
          AVARA distillate. The Permeate Forwarding Storage Tank supplies the Permeate Forwarding Pump Skid
          that sends water to the FGD Effluent Tank located in the existing Phys/Chem Treatment Area. Contents
          of the FGD Effluent Tank are pumped to the river for final discharge.
          Concentrate Storage Tank
          The Concentrate Storage Tank will receive the concentrate flow from the Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP
          membranes. It will feed the AVARA system.
          Thermal Evaporator (AVARA)
          There will be 3 Thermal Evaporators in parallel in this process. The thermal evaporators will be AVARA
          systems. AVARAs use advanced vapor recompression technology for thermal evaporation and to
          concentrate a brine stream. AVARA systems are fully automated and come as a fully skidded solution.
          The Thermal Evaporators will operate as 3x33%. The AVARAs will be fed by the Concentrate Storage
          Tank. The brine of the 3 AVARAs will go to the Brine Storage Tank while the distillate will be fed to the
          permeate forwarding tank.
          The Thermal Evaporator is used to concentrate brine from the High Pressure VSEP membranes to the
          point just before saturation. It is expected that the concentration of TDS could reach up to 262,000 ppm.
          The Thermal Evaporators will heat the feed concentrate to the point of boiling. Water is pumped
          through a 500-mesh self-cleaning filter and split into two streams. One stream is sent through the
          distilled heat-exchanger while the other is sent through the brine heat exchanger. The streams
          recombine and are sent to the core tank section of the AVARA.


                                                           Project: 24877_Rev2                                        29

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                     Figure 2. AVARA Advanced Vapor Recompression Process Schematic – Heat Exchange. Courtesy of
                                                  www.purestream.com/project-2

          In the core tank section, water is boiled to create a saturated vapor. Vapor is compressed to between 3
          and 7.5 PSI with a blower. The compressed vapor is then forced through dimpled plates. As the vapor
          moves through the plates, it condenses. The condensed and distilled water is then pumped through the
          feed heat exchangers and out of the system as effluent to the Permeate Forwarding Storage Tank.


                      Figure 3. AVARA Advanced Vapor Recompression Process Schematic – Vaporization. Courtesy of
                                                  www.purestream.com/project-2


                                                              Project: 24877_Rev2                                   30

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


                      Figure 4. AVARA Advanced Vapor Recompression Process Schematic – Condensation. Courtesy of
                                                   www.purestream.com/project-2

          Operators watch the pressures within the AVARA. Changes in pressure can change production rate and
          temperature making it a key process condition. Operators can adjust relief valves, heater temperature,
          blower speed, and the heat exchanger by-pass valve to optimize system pressures.
          With much of the feed water evaporated, condensed, and discharged, the brine left in the AVARA will
          continue to recirculate through the heat exchanger. Once it is concentrated to near saturation, it is
          pumped out of the system. A control valve will control brine discharge flowrate and will be set to
          maintain the desired brine concentration. Brine will be sent to the Brine Storage tank and then
          processed through the Solidification Batch Plant.
          Brine Solidification Batch Plant
          The solidification plant will collect, store, and meter dry solidification materials and brine for loading
          into a cement mixer. These solidification materials are Flyash, Lime, and standard concrete conditioning
          additives. Flyash with small amounts of lime will be used as the primary solidification material. If Flyash
          is not readily available Cement and lime can be used as an alternative. These materials will be stored in
          silos above a weigh hopper. These materials will be metered into the weigh hopper at a known quantity.
          This hopper will feed the dry material into cement trucks followed by brine for mixing. The solidification
          plant will be designed for fugitive dust control. The cement truck will transport the mixed material for
          disposal. The solidified brine mixture will pass both the paint filter test and the Toxicity Leaching
          Characteristic Procedure prior to being landfilled in an off-site facility.

          Design Assumptions:
          Design Case 1:
          The VSEP Stage 1 modules are designed for a total flow rate of 792 gpm. This includes 608 gpm of
          phys/chem effluent at a TDS concentration of 10,000 mg/L and 184 gpm of recycled reject from the
          Stage 3 Spiral RO Membranes. A membrane efficiency factor of 130% is applied to the design flux to
          reflect the decrease in membrane throughput over time. The operating flux is expected to decline to
          100% of the design flux after three years of operation.

          Membrane cleaning frequency is estimated on a per day basis at roughly 8% of an operational day. It is
          important to note that this is not the actual cleaning/maintenance frequency and is an estimated
          average value.

          The third stage of the spiral RO is required due to the high influent mercury levels of 10,000 to 15,000
          ng/L. The Second Stage Spiral RO can achieve approximately 30 ng/L, and the additional third stage is
          needed to achieve the required effluent value of 10 ng/L.
          Design Case 2:
          Design Case 2 assumes a majority of phys/chem effluent is recycled back to the FGD scrubbers as
          makeup water. The remaining water is sent to the membrane treatment system (150 gpm, 35,000 pm


                                                           Project: 24877_Rev2                                       40

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          TDS, 15,000 ng/L Hg, total). This flow may be routed directly to the Stage 2 HP VSEP membranes for
          treatment and achieve identical effluent values with Design Case 1 feeding the Stage 1 LP VESP
          membranes. Stage 2 HP VSEP permeate is sent through the Spiral RO Membrane stages with reject from
          those stages recycled back to the Stage 2 HP VSEP influent.

          Item B – AVARA: Advanced Vapor Recompression System

                   Table 12. Advanced Vapor Recompression System (AVARA) System Design Overview
                                             System Design Overview
           Parameter                                                          Value
           Total Influent Flow Rate                                          89 gpm
           Total Estimated Evaporation                                      65.9 gpm
           Total Estimated Brine                                            23.1 gpm
           Feed TDS                                                        68,211 ppm
           Target Brine TDS                                               262,000 ppm
           Nominal Operating Electricity                                    4,140 kW
           Required Electricity                                480V / 3 Phase / 4140 Service Amps


          AVARA features patented submerged core technology. Feed water is pumped into a tank and heated
          with immersion heaters. As steam is generated, compressors force the steam back into the submerged
          heat exchanger (core) where the steam recondenses into a clean distillate. The AVARA is capable of
          concentrating the residual brine in the tank up to 300,000 ppm TDS before being discharged from the
          system for disposal or beneficial use. AVARA can significantly reduce the amount of wastewater
          requiring disposal while providing a distilled water byproduct.

          Engineering & Design Services
          Scope of Services
          Deliverables developed during the engineering and design phase will serve as the basis of design for the
          project. The following engineering tasks and deliverables are included in this bid:
              •   Design Criteria
              •   Process Flow Diagram
              •   Process & Instrumentation Diagrams
              •   Mass Balance
              •   Hydraulic Profile
              •   Equipment Descriptions (GA drawings & Datasheets)
              •   Control Narrative
              •   Equipment Layout
              •   3D Plant Modeling
              •   Site Civil Design
              •   HVAC Design
              •   Design & Construction Schedule


          Process Flow Diagram (PFD)
          WesTech offers a wide range of treatment equipment that can be implemented in multiple process
          configurations and we will refine the approach with input from the finalized Design Criteria.
          The PFD will identify the major pieces of equipment, their position in the process and the main control
          loops operating the process. They will indicate the main process streams and utility lines.
          Deliverable:
              • Process Flow Diagram


          Process & Instrumentation Diagrams (P&IDs)
          After the Process Flow Diagram is finalized, WesTech will develop preliminary P&IDs for the process. The
          P&IDs will portray the components needed to run, monitor, control specific processes and will depict
          their relationship with each other. P&IDs will show equipment, piping that connects the equipment,
          instrumentation, and valves. The information compiled in the P&ID will provide the blueprint for the
          system and set the scope of the final project, define the process parameters and the level of controls.
          The P&IDs and supporting documentation are the most important document when establishing the
          details of the project.
          P&IDs will be generated following ISA S5.1 and the owner’s specifications. P&IDs typically include, but
          are not limited to the following information:
              •   Equipment names, tag and design conditions
              •   Relief valve location, tag numbers, sizes and pressure. Relief valve interlocks


                                                           Project: 24877_Rev2                                       52

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


              •   Venting, draining, maintenance, shutdown and start-up requirements are indicated
              •   Type of manual valves are identified, specialty piping items are tagged, and piping notes are
                  added
              •   Control valves size, fail position, tags, and interlocks
              •   Vessel nozzles, details, and levels
              •   Process and utility lines
              •   Line sizes, line numbers, pipe specifications and product designation are indicated
              •   All instrumentation is shown with alarm and switch set points
              •   Instrument signals to control system are detailed
              •   Scope of supply, system boundaries
          Deliverable:
              • P&IDs based on finalized PFD


          Mass Balance
          WesTech will perform mass balance calculations based on the finalized Design Criteria and PFD. Mass
          balance values will be used as inputs for specific equipment sizing.
          Deliverable:
              • Mass Balance calculations based on finalized PFD


          Equipment Descriptions (General Arrangement Drawings & Datasheets)
          WesTech will provide detailed equipment descriptions including General Arrangement (GA) drawings,
          equipment datasheets, and other lists as required.
          Deliverables:
              • Equipment datasheets
              • GA drawings


          Hydraulic Profile
          WesTech will perform hydraulic calculations for the treatment system within the specified boundaries
          given in the Battery Limits Table of the Design Basis.
          Deliverables:
              • Hydraulic profile drawing


          HAZOP Assistance
          WesTech will provide personnel for one (1) trip up to five (5) working days to participate in a hazard and
          operability study (HAZOP) workshop that will be conducted by others. Our process and controls
          engineers will assist in identifying and evaluating potential risks to personnel or equipment and
          operability issues.

          interactions between individual unit processes. The control narrative will provide the basis for PLC logic
          programming.

          shipment days, payment terms, and escalation clause shall be negotiated at order placement, otherwise
          the proposal terms and conditions contained herein shall apply.
          Paint: If your equipment has paint included in the price, please take note to the following. Primer paints
          are designed to provide only a minimal protection from the time of application (usually for a period not
          to exceed 30 days). Therefore, it is imperative that the finish coat be applied within 30 days of shipment
          on all shop primed surfaces. Without the protection of the final coatings, primer degradation may occur
          after this period, which in turn may require renewed surface preparation and coating. If it is impractical
          or impossible to coat primed surfaces within the suggested time frame, WesTech strongly recommends
          the supply of bare metal, with surface preparation and coating performed in the field. All field surface
          preparation, field paint, touch-up, and repair to shop painted surfaces are not by WesTech.
          Escalation: If between the proposal date and actual procurement and through no fault of the Seller, the
          relevant cost of labor, material, freight, tariffs, and other Seller costs combined relating to the contract,
          increase by greater than 2.5% of the overall contract price, then the contract price shall be subject to
          escalation and increased. Such increase shall be verified by documentation and the amount of contract
          price escalation shall be calculated as either the actual increased cost to the Seller or, if agreed by the
          Parties, the equivalent increase of a relevant industry recognized third-party index, and in both cases
          without any additional profit or margin being added.
          USA Tariffs and Current Trade Laws: All prices are based on current USA and North America tariffs and
          trade laws/agreements at time of bid. Any changes in costs due to USA Tariffs and trade laws/
          agreements will be passed through to the purchaser at cost.

          Design Basis
          The objective of this document is to provide Southern Company Services with a conceptual design and
          budgetary level cost estimate of the deliverables associated with potentially converting Georgia Power
          Company Plant Bowen flue gas desulfurization (FGD) wastewater treatment system to utilize membrane
          technology, considering the 2020 ELG Rule’s Voluntary Incentives Program (VIP) compliance option and
          the 2023 Proposed ELG Rule.

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          Process Description
          Physical / Chemical Treatment (Existing)
          Softening to Lower TDS
          Precipitation of solids by caustic and soda ash softening lowers the hardness and therefore Total
          Dissolved Solids (TDS) will be lowered as well. Dosage of caustic and soda ash will be in reaction tanks
          upstream of the clarifier. Metals precipitation can be improved by the addition of organosulfide. The
          clarifier is followed by continuous backwash sand filters. pH adjustment with acid takes place in the
          Stage 1 VSEP Feed Tank which also serves as an attenuation tank.
          Membrane Treatment System
          Stage 1 VSEP Feed Tank
          The influent for the system goes into the Stage 1 VSEP Feed Tank. The Stage 1 VSEP Feed Tank is fed by
          the multimedia filter effluent. The tank also receives flow from the concentrate of the Stage 3 Reverse
          Osmosis (RO) membrane. Acid is added to the Stage 1 tank for any necessary pH adjustment. Antiscalant
          and bisulfite are dosed in the header to prevent scaling and reduce chlorine respectively.
          The Stage 1 Low Pressure VSEPs pull from the Stage 1 VSEP Feed Tank. To prevent cavitation of the VSEP
          feed pumps, a booster pump on the feed line starts when both low pressure VSEP membranes are
          active.
          Stage 1 Low Pressure VSEP
          The Low Pressure VSEP Membranes use membrane filtration to achieve liquid/solid separation. They
          employ a unique vibrating filter pack that produces a high shear rate on the membrane surface which
          inhibits membrane surface fouling and induces greater filtrate flow rates during the filtration process.
          The Stage 1 Low Pressure VSEPs discharge two streams: permeate (filtrate or product) and concentrate
          (brine or retentate). The VSEP concentrate is sent to the Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP Feed Tank. The
          permeate is sent to the Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank.
          The membranes will need to be cleaned occasionally to remove accumulated foulants or scaling. There
          are two modes of cleaning, flush and CIP. Flush is a lower pressure single pass step where heated RO
          permeate is sent to the system for removal of foulants and/or scaling. CIP is a lower pressure
          recirculation step where heated RO permeate mixed with cleaning chemicals is sent to the system for
          removal of more stubborn foulants.
          Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP Feed Tank
          The Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP Feed Tank receives flow from the Low Pressure VSEP membranes
          concentrate. This tank is the feed tank to the Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP membranes for further volume
          reduction. Antiscalant is dosed after the Feed Tank to prevent scaling.
          Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP
          The High Pressure VSEP membranes use membrane filtration to achieve liquid/solid separation. They
          employ a unique vibrating filter pack that produces a high shear rate on the membrane surface which
          inhibits membrane surface fouling and induces greater filtrate flow rates during the filtration process.


                                                           Project: 24926_Rev1                                       17

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          Stage 2 membranes operate at a higher pressure than Stage 1 due to the higher dissolved solids loading
          in the brine feed that must be rejected at the membrane surfaces.
          The Stage 2 High Pressure VSEPs discharge two streams: permeate (filtrate or product) and concentrate
          (brine or retentate). The Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP concentrate is sent to the Concentrate Storage
          Tank. The permeate is sent to the Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank.
          The membranes will need to be cleaned occasionally to remove accumulated foulants or scaling. There
          are two modes of cleaning, flush and CIP. Flush is a lower pressure single pass step where heated RO
          permeate is sent to the system for removal of foulants and/or scaling. CIP is a lower pressure
          recirculation step where heated RO permeate mixed with cleaning chemicals is sent to the system for
          removal of more stubborn foulants.
          Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank
          The Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank receives flow from the Stage 1 Low Pressure VSEP permeate, Stage 2
          High Pressure VSEP permeate, and Stage 4 Spiral RO concentrate. This tank is the feed tank to the Stage
          3 Spiral RO membranes for further polishing.
          Stage 3 Spiral RO
          The Stage 3 Spiral RO is the first stage of polishing after the VSEP membranes. There are 3 stages of RO
          (stage 3,4, and 5) total. The last stage is required to lower the mercury concentration to the required
          effluent quality. The same principles of operation apply to this membrane as the Stage 1 Low Pressure
          VSEP membranes. The feed stream is separated into 2 discharge streams: permeate and concentrate.
          The permeate is sent to the Stage 4 Spiral RO Feed Tank. The concentrate is recycled back to the Stage 1
          Low Pressure VSEP Feed Tank for additional processing. The Stage 3 Spiral RO is cleaned in a similar
          manner to the Stage 1 and 2 VSEP membranes.
          Stage 4 Spiral RO Feed Tank
          The Stage 4 Spiral RO Feed Tank receives flow from the Stage 3 Spiral RO permeate, and Stage 5 Spiral
          RO concentrate. This tank is the feed tank to the Stage 4 Spiral RO membranes.
          Stage 4 Spiral RO
          The Stage 4 Spiral RO is the second stage of polishing after the VSEP membranes. The same principles of
          operation apply to this membrane as the Stage 3 Spiral RO membranes. The feed stream is separated
          into 2 discharge streams: permeate and concentrate. The permeate is sent to the Stage 5 Spiral RO Feed
          Tank. The concentrate is recycled back to the Stage 3 Spiral RO Feed Tank for additional processing. The
          Stage 4 Spiral RO is cleaned in a similar manner to the previous system membranes.
          Stage 5 Spiral RO Feed Tank
          The Stage 5 Spiral RO Feed Tank receives flow from the Stage 4 Spiral RO permeate. This tank is the feed
          tank to the Stage 5 Spiral RO membranes.
          Stage 5 Spiral RO
          The Stage 5 Spiral RO is the third and final stage of polishing after the VSEP membranes. The same
          principles of operation apply to this membrane as the previous spiral RO membranes. The feed stream is
          separated into 2 discharge streams: permeate and concentrate. The permeate is sent to the Permeate
          Forwarding Storage Tank. This permeate water will meet the effluent limits assumed from the 2020 ELG


                                                         Project: 24926_Rev1                                         18

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          VIP. The concentrate is recycled back to the Stage 4 Spiral RO Feed Tank for additional processing. The
          Stage 5 Spiral RO is cleaned in a similar manner to the previous system membranes.
          Concentrate Storage Tank
          The Concentrate Storage Tank will receive the concentrate flow from the Stage 2 High Pressure VSEP
          membranes. It will feed the AVARA system.
          Thermal Evaporator (AVARA)
          Parallel thermal evaporators will be used to reach the appropriate flow rate. The thermal evaporators
          will be AVARA systems. AVARAs use advanced vapor recompression technology for thermal evaporation
          and to concentrate a brine stream. AVARA systems are fully automated and come as a fully skidded
          solution.
          The AVARAs will be fed by the Concentrate Storage Tank. The brine from the AVARAs will go to the Brine
          Storage Tank while the distillate will be fed to the permeate forwarding tank.
          The Thermal Evaporator is used to concentrate brine from the High Pressure VSEP membranes to the
          point just before saturation. It is expected that the concentration of TDS could reach up to 250,000 ppm.
          The Thermal Evaporators will heat the feed concentrate to the point of boiling. Water is pumped
          through a 500 mesh self-cleaning filter and split into two streams. One stream is sent through the
          distilled heat-exchanger while the other is sent through the brine heat exchanger. The streams
          recombine and are sent to the core tank section of the AVARA.
          In the core tank section, water is boiled to create a saturated vapor. Vapor is compressed to between 3
          and 7.5 PSI with a blower. The compressed vapor is then forced through dimpled plates. As the vapor
          moves through the plates, it condenses. The condensed and distilled water is then pumped through the
          feed heat exchangers and out of the system as effluent to the Permeate Forwarding Storage Tank.
          Operators watch the pressures within the AVARA. Changes in pressure can change production rate and
          temperature making it a key process condition. Operators can adjust relief valves, heater temperature,
          blower speed, and the heat exchanger by-pass valve to optimize system pressures.
          With much of the feed water evaporated, condensed, and discharged, the brine left in the AVARA will
          continue to recirculate through the heat exchanger. Once it is concentrated to a point just before
          saturation, it is pumped out of the system. A control valve will control brine discharge flowrate and will
          be set to maintain the desired brine concentration. Brine will be sent to the Brine Storage tank where it
          will then be processed through the Solidification Batch Plant.
          Permeate Forwarding Storage Tank
          The Permeate Forwarding Storage Tank will receive flow from the Stage 5 Spiral RO membranes and the
          AVARA distillate. The Permeate Forwarding Storage Tank supplies the Permeate Forwarding Pump Skid
          that sends water to the FGD Effluent Tank located in the existing Phys/Chem Treatment Area.


                                                           Project: 24926_Rev1                                         19

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


          Solidification Plant
          The solidification plant will work to collect and meter dry solidification materials and brine for loading
          into a cement mixer. These solidification materials are Flyash, Lime, and standard concrete conditioning
          additives. Flyash with small amounts of lime will be used as the primary solidification material. If Flyash
          is not readily available, Cement and lime can be used as an alternative. These materials will be stored in
          silos above a weigh hopper. These materials will be metered into the weigh hopper at a known quantity.
          This hopper will feed the dry material into cement trucks followed by brine for mixing. The solidification
          plant will be designed for fugitive dust control. The cement truck will transport the mixed material for
          disposal. The solidified brine mixture will pass both the paint filter test and the Toxicity Leaching
          Characteristic Procedure prior to being landfilled in an on-site facility.

          Design Assumptions:
          Design Case 1:
          The VSEP Stage 1 modules are designed for a total flow rate of 1867 gpm. This includes 1500 gpm of
          phys/chem effluent and 367 gpm of recycled reject from the Stage 3 Spiral RO Membranes and an
          influent TDS value of 10,000 mg/L. A membrane efficiency factor of 130% is applied to the design flux to
          reflect the change in membrane throughput over time. This factor would correlate to 100% throughput
          effectiveness in year three of operation.

          Redundancy and cleaning frequency is estimated on a per day basis at roughly 8% of an operational day.
          It is important to note that this is not the actual cleaning/maintenance frequency and is an average
          assumed value.

          Item B – AVARA: Advanced Vapor Recompression System
                            Table 12. Advanced Vapor Recompression System (AVARA) System Design Overview
                                                System Design Overview
           Parameter                                                                Value
           Total Influent Flow Rate                                               467 gpm
           Total Estimated Evaporation                                            383 gpm
           Total Estimated Brine                                                   84 gpm
           Feed TDS                                                              45,000 ppm
           Target Brine TDS                                                     250,000 ppm
           Nominal Operating Electricity                                          7910 kW
           Required Electricity                                             480V / 3 Phase / 60 hz

          AVARA features patented submerged core technology. Feed water is pumped into a tank and heated
          with immersion heaters. As steam is generated, compressors force the steam back into the submerged
          heat exchanger (core) where the steam recondenses into a clean distillate. The AVARA is capable of
          concentrating the residual brine in the tank up to 300,000 ppm TDS before being discharged from the
          system for disposal or beneficial use. AVARA can significantly reduce the amount of wastewater
          requiring disposal while providing a distilled water byproduct.

          Engineering & Design Services
          Scope of Services
          Deliverables developed during the engineering and design phase will serve as the basis of design for the
          project. The following engineering tasks and deliverables are included in this bid:
              •   Design Criteria
              •   Process Flow Diagram
              •   Process & Instrumentation Diagrams
              •   Mass Balance
              •   Hydraulic Profile
              •   Equipment Descriptions (GA drawings & Datasheets)
              •   Control Narrative
              •   Equipment Layout
              •   3D Plant Modeling
              •   Site Civil Design
              •   HVAC Design
              •   Design & Construction Schedule
          Process Flow Diagram (PFD)
          WesTech offers a wide range of treatment equipment that can be implemented in multiple process
          configurations and we will refine the approach with input from the finalized Design Criteria.
          The PFD will identify the major pieces of equipment, their position in the process and the main control
          loops operating the process. They will indicate the main process streams and utility lines.
          Deliverable:
              • Process Flow Diagram
          Process & Instrumentation Diagrams (P&IDs)
          After the Process Flow Diagram is finalized, WesTech will develop preliminary P&IDs for the process. The
          P&IDs will portray the components needed to run, monitor, control specific processes and will depict
          their relationship with each other. P&IDs will show equipment, piping that connects the equipment,
          instrumentation, and valves. The information compiled in the P&ID will provide the blueprint for the
          system and set the scope of the final project, define the process parameters and the level of controls.
          The P&IDs and supporting documentation are the most important document when establishing the
          details of the project.
          P&IDs will be generated following ISA S5.1 and the owner’s specifications. P&IDs typically include, but
          are not limited to the following information:
              •   Equipment names, tag and design conditions
              •   Relief valve location, tag numbers, sizes and pressure. Relief valve interlocks
              •   Venting, draining, maintenance, shutdown and start-up requirements are indicated
              •   Type of manual valves are identified, specialty piping items are tagged, and piping notes are
                  added


                                                          Project: 24926_Rev1                                        38

STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment


              •   Control valves size, fail position, tags, and interlocks
              •   Vessel nozzles, details, and levels
              •   Process and utility lines
              •   Line sizes, line numbers, pipe specifications and product designation are indicated
              •   All instrumentation is shown with alarm and switch set points
              •   Instrument signals to control system are detailed
              •   Scope of supply, system boundaries
          Deliverable:
              • P&IDs based on finalized PFD
          Mass Balance
          WesTech will perform mass balance calculations based on the finalized Design Criteria and PFD. Mass
          balance values will be used as inputs for specific equipment sizing.
          Deliverable:
              • Mass Balance calculations based on finalized PFD
          Equipment Descriptions (General Arrangement Drawings & Datasheets)
          WesTech will provide detailed equipment descriptions including General Arrangement (GA) drawings,
          equipment datasheets, and other lists as required.
          Deliverables:
              • Equipment datasheets
              • GA drawings
          Hydraulic Profile
          WesTech will perform hydraulic calculations for the treatment system within the specified boundaries
          given in the Battery Limits Table of the Design Basis.
          Deliverables:
              • Hydraulic profile drawing
          HAZOP Assistance
          WesTech will provide personnel for one (1) trip up to five (5) working days to participate in a hazard and
          operability study (HAZOP) workshop that will be conducted by others. Our process and controls
          engineers will assist in identifying and evaluating potential risks to personnel or equipment and
          operability issues.
          Control Narrative
          WesTech process engineers will provide control narratives in paragraph form describing functionality of
          each unit process. Descriptions will include an overall description of the piece of equipment and how it
          is operated via pumps, blowers, valves, instruments, control logic, etc. Descriptions will also outline
          interactions between individual unit processes. The control narrative will provide the basis for PLC logic
          programming.

          on all shop primed surfaces. Without the protection of the final coatings, primer degradation may occur
          after this period, which in turn may require renewed surface preparation and coating. If it is impractical
          or impossible to coat primed surfaces within the suggested time frame, WesTech strongly recommends
          the supply of bare metal, with surface preparation and coating performed in the field. All field surface
          preparation, field paint, touch-up, and repair to shop painted surfaces are not by WesTech.

===== DKT 55378 STF-PIA-10 PD/STF-PIA-10-6/STF-PIA-10-6.docx =====

STF-PIA-10-6

Question:
Please refer to the proposed Supplemental Effluent Limitations Guidelines and Standards for the Steam Electric Power Generating Point Source Category, 88 Fed. Reg. 18824 (Mar. 29, 2023) (the “Proposed 2023 ELG Rule”).
Does the Company anticipate incurring costs for retrofits at the Bowen and Scherer coal units between now and 2029 to comply with the zero-discharge limitation for all pollutants in flue gas desulfurization (FGD) wastewater under the Proposed 2023 ELG Rule? If yes, please describe the capital projects that are required, and the estimated costs associated with them. If not, please explain why not.
Does the Company anticipate incurring costs for retrofits at the Bowen and Scherer coal units between now and 2029 to comply with the zero-discharge limitation for all pollutants in bottom ash transport water (BATW) under the Proposed 2023 ELG Rule? If yes, please describe the capital projects that are required, and the estimated costs associated with them. If not, please explain why not.
Will the Proposed 2023 ELG rule require any capital expenditures at the Bowen and Scherer coal units between now and 2029 to comply with the numeric discharge limitations for combustion residual leachate (CRL)? If yes, please describe the capital projects that are required, and the estimated costs associated with them. If no, please explain why not.
Response:
If the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) finalizes the Proposed 2023 ELG Rule, the Company anticipates incurring additional capital costs if Plant Bowen is required to install membrane-based wastewater treatment and meet a zero-liquid discharge (“ZLD”) requirement for flue gas desulfurization (“FGD”) wastewater. See STF-PIA-10-6 Attachment for Southern Company’s comments on the Proposed 2023 ELG Rule submitted to EPA on May 30, 2023, which includes a screening level estimate of approximately $580M for membrane-based FGD wastewater treatment at Plant Bowen. This does not include costs for a ZLD system, which would likely include additional storage tanks, pumps, and piping to reuse the permeate/distillate as make-up water to the boiler or FGD. 
The Company does not anticipate incurring additional costs at Plant Scherer beyond the membrane-based FGD wastewater treatment project that is currently underway, because the proposed rule did not indicate changing the requirements for the Voluntary Incentives Program that is applicable to Plant Scherer. 
The Company does not anticipate incurring additional capital costs for retrofits at Plants Bowen and Scherer for bottom ash transport water under the Proposed 2023 ELG Rule. Both facilities already meet the requirements of the proposed ELG requirements for bottom ash transport water with systems that were installed by 2019 to facilitate ash pond closure and meet existing ELG requirements. 
If EPA finalizes the Proposed 2023 ELG Rule, the Company anticipates incurring additional capital costs for retrofits if physical-chemical wastewater treatment systems are required for combustion residual leachate at coal combustion residual landfills. The Company does not yet have capital cost estimates for these treatment systems, and site-specific studies for the landfills at Plants Bowen and Scherer are currently underway to prepare for cost estimating activities once the final rule is released. 

===== DKT 55378 STF-PIA-10 PD/STF-PIA-10-7.docx =====
STF-PIA-10-7

Question:
Please refer to the proposed New Source Performance Standards for Greenhouse Gas Emissions from New, Modified, and Reconstructed Fossil Fuel-Fired Electric Generating Units; Emission Guidelines for Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Existing Fossil Fuel-Fired Electric Generating Units; and Repeal of the Affordable Clean Energy Rule, 88 Fed. Reg. 33240 (May 23, 2023) (the “Proposed 2023 GHG Rule”).
Has the Company evaluated the four different compliance options for compliance with the Proposed 2023 GHG Rule at the Bowen and Scherer coal units? If yes, please provide all documents supporting this evaluation. If not, please explain why not.
Does the Company anticipate retiring the Bowen and/or Scherer coal units prior to 2032 to avoid compliance with the Proposed 2023 GHG Rule?
Does the Company anticipate retiring the Bowen and/or Scherer coal units prior to 2035 and accepting an operational limit of 20% of full capacity starting in 2030 as one of the compliance options under the Proposed 2023 GHG Rule?
Has the Company analyzed the cost of installing carbon capture and storage with a 90% capture rate to comply with the Proposed 2023 GHG Rule? If yes, please provide all such analysis. If not, state whether the Company plans to issue any updates to the IRP that evaluate the impact that the Proposed 2023 GHG Rule on the cost to operate the system.
Response:
The Company has not evaluated the existing coal unit compliance options for the United States Environmental Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) Proposed 2023 GHG Rule for Plants Bowen and Scherer, such as the early retirement by 2032 or 2035 and carbon capture and sequestration options. Even if the rule is finalized as proposed, a compliance evaluation cannot be completed at this time, because uncertainty remains in the compliance options and requirements for existing facilities until the development of the Georgia state plan required by the rule. EPA has indicated that it plans to finalize the Proposed 2023 GHG Rule in 2024 and proposed that the state plan would be due two years later. The Company will work with the Georgia Environmental Protection Division to evaluate the final 2023 GHG Rule and compliance options for affected existing facilities in the development of the Georgia state plan, which then must also be reviewed and approved by EPA. 
As stated generally in comments submitted by Southern Company to EPA on August 8, 2023 (see STF-JKA-2-14 Attachment C), more time and compliance flexibility are required in the case of all four existing coal unit options presented in the proposal. The Company will update the Commission through a future Environmental Compliance Strategy and IRP process when sufficient information becomes available to complete the compliance evaluation.

STF-PIA-10-8

Question:
Has the Company evaluated the cost of installing carbon sequestration and storage, hydrogen conversion, or gas dual firing or conversion at any of its existing fossil plants (coal or gas-fired)? If so, please provide the Company’s cost estimates. If not, please explain. 


Response:
Georgia Power has not evaluated the cost of installing carbon sequestration and storage, hydrogen conversion, or gas fuel firing or conversion at any of the Company’s existing fossil plants (coal or gas-fired). However, at the direction of counsel, in 2021, Southern Company Services conducted a system level pre-screening analysis related to the installation of carbon sequestration and storage at fossil plants across the system. This is a confidential technical and legal analysis that is protected under the attorney client privilege and attorney work product doctrines and has been withheld from this response.

           1. Introduction
           On October 23, 2023, Georgia Power Company (GPC) filed with the Georgia Public Service Commission
           (PSC) an update to its integrated Resource Plan (IRP) to address Georgia’s rapidly growing energy needs.
           Since filing the last IRP in 2022, Georgia’s economy has continued to thrive, bringing rapid economic growth
           and an unprecedented increase in the demand for energy to the state. As part of ensuring that we can meet
           these energy needs, GPC is proposing to construct three (3) advanced class, dual-fuel REDACTED
           REDACTED REDACTED simple-cycle combustion turbine (CT) units at Plant Yates (“the Plant”), located in
           Coweta County, Georgia. Construction of the proposed CT units will include installation of new associated
           equipment, such as an emergency generator, an emergency fire water pump engine, and three fuel gas
           heaters. The proposed CT units, designated as Combustion Turbine Units 8, 9, and 10, along with all
           associated equipment, will be hereinafter referred to as the “Project” (f/k/a Project Peregrine). The proposed
           CT units will be capable of being fueled with either pipeline quality natural gas or ultra-low sulfur (i.e., 15 ppm)
           distillate oil. When natural gas is available, the proposed CT units will provide up to approximately
           REDACTED MW of capacity. If gas is unavailable, the proposed CT units will run on distillate oil and provide
           approximately REDACTED MW of capacity. Each proposed CT unit will be equipped with a dilution selective
           catalytic reduction (SCR) to minimize nitrogen oxide (NOX) emissions and an oxidation catalyst to minimize
           carbon monoxide (CO) and volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions.

           Plant Yates is an existing “major source” of criteria air pollutants, and the Project constitutes a “major
           modification” under Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) permitting requirements. As such, GPC is
           applying to the Georgia Environmental Protection Division (EPD) for an air permit authorizing construction and
           operation of the Project. The Project will be subject to PSD requirements for emissions of NOX, particulate
           matter (PM), particulate matter (PM) less than 10 microns in diameter (PM10), PM less than 2.5 microns in
           diameter (PM2.5), CO, VOC, sulfuric acid mist (SAM, or H2SO4), and greenhouse gases (GHG).

           This Introduction and the other components of this document constitute the application for an air permit
           authorizing construction and operation of the Project under Ga. Comp. R & Regs. Rule 391-3-1-.03. This
           application and supporting analyses address the applicable permitting requirements for the Project and
           demonstrate the Project will comply with all applicable state and federal air quality regulations.


           1.1 Facility Description
           Plant Yates is located at 708 Dyer Road, on approximately 2,400 acres on the east bank of the Chattahoochee
           River in Coweta County, Georgia, approximately eight miles northwest of the city of Newnan. Originally, seven
           coal-fired steam generating units were operated at Plant Yates. Units 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 were retired in 2015 and
           Units 6 and 7 were converted from coal to natural gas in 2015 as part of GPC’s compliance strategy for the
           Georgia Multipollutant Rule and federal Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS).

           A facility location map is provided in Figure 1-1 and Figure 1-2.

                •     North American Datum (NAD): 1983;
                •     Elevation Above Mean Sea Level (AMSL): Approximately 740 feet AMSL.

           Existing emissions sources at Plant Yates include Units 6 and 7 (Emission Unit IDs SG06 and SG07) and a
           natural gas-fired water bath heater (Emission Unit ID WBH1). Existing emissions sources that are categorized

                      (Emission Units IDs WBH2, WBH3, and WBH4.


           1.3 Project Location
           The proposed CT units and associated equipment will be located at Plant Yates, which is located in Coweta
           County on the Chattahoochee River, approximately 35 miles southwest of Atlanta, Georgia. Figure 1-1 and

           stationary source.”

           2. Process Description
           As stated in Section 1, GPC plans to construct Combustion Turbine Units 8, 9, and 10 (Emission Units IDs
           CT8, CT9, and CT10) and associated equipment. The primary equipment of the Project includes:

                •     Three (3) REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED simple-cycle CTs, each with an ISO base rating of
                      REDACTED MW (natural gas) and REDACTED MW (ultra-low sulfur distillate oil),

                      REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED
                      REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED REDACTED

           Associated equipment associated with the Project includes:

                •     One (1) ULSD fuel-fired emergency generator with an output capacity of 3250 kW,

                •     One (1) ULSD fuel-fired water pump engine with an output rating of approximately 350 bhp,
                •     One (1) ULSD fuel storage tank with a nominal capacity of 5.72 million gallons, and

                •     Three (3) natural gas-fired fuel gas heaters each with a heat input rating of less than 10 MMBtu/hr.


           2.1 Combustion Turbines
           The proposed CT units will provide between 1,000 to 1,400 MW of capacity, depending on the fuel source
           being utilized. Annual operation of each proposed CT unit will be limited to a capacity factor based on its
           design efficiency for purposes of compliance with NSPS Subpart TTTT. Each proposed CT unit is comprised
           of three major sections: the compressor, the combustor, and the power turbine, as described below:


                 •    In the compressor section, ambient air is drawn through a filter (and under certain meteorological
                      conditions, the evaporative cooler) to clean (and cool) the air. The air is then compressed and
                      directed to the combustor section.
                 •    Each proposed CT unit will be capable of firing either natural gas or ultra-low sulfur distillate oil,
                      hereinafter referred to as distillate oil or just oil. During natural gas firing, the proposed CT units will
                      utilize dry low- NOX (“DLN”) combustors to reduce NOX formation. During distillate oil firing, water
                      injection will be used to minimize peak flame temperature and reduce NOX formation.
                 •    In the combustor section, a fuel and air mixture is introduced and combusted. Hot gases from
                      combustion are mixed with additional air from the compressor section and directed to the power
                      turbine section at high temperature and pressure.
                 •     In the power turbine section, the hot exhaust gases expand and rotate the turbine blades, which are
                       coupled to a shaft. The rotating shaft drives the compressor and the generator, which generates
                       electricity.

           In addition to DLN and water injection, the emission control technologies for the proposed CT units include
           dilution selective catalytic reduction (SCR) to control NOX emissions, as well as an oxidation catalyst to control
           CO, VOC, and organic HAP emissions.


           2.2 Diesel-Fired Emergency Generator
           The proposed Project will include one (1) ULSD-fired emergency generator with a standby rating of 3,250 kW
           certified to Tier 2 emission standards. The generator will be operated for emergency purposes for a maximum
           of 200 hours per year, including 100 hours per year for maintenance and readiness testing, 50 hours of which
           may be used in non-emergency situations.

           2.3 Diesel-Fired Fire Water Pump Engine
           The proposed Project will include one (1) ULSD-fired fire water pump engine rated at approximately 350 bhp
           certified to Tier 3 emission standards. The engine will be operated for emergency purposes for a maximum of
           500 hours per year, including 100 hours per year for maintenance and readiness testing, 50 hours of which
           may be used in non-emergency situations.


           2.4 Diesel Fuel Storage Tank
           The Project will include a fixed roof storage tank with a nominal capacity of 5.72 million gallons for on-site
           storage of fuel for the proposed CT units to provide reliability and resiliency benefits to the electric system. The
           tank will be approximately 160’ in diameter and equipped with a submerged fill system to reduce evaporative
           VOC emissions during filling operations.


           2.5 Fuel Gas Heaters
           The Project will include three (3) natural gas-fired fuel gas heaters, each with a heat input capacity of <10
           MMBtu/hr, which will be used to warm up the incoming natural gas fuel to prevent freezing of the gas regulating
           valves under certain gas system operating conditions. The heaters will fire natural gas exclusively and use
           ultra-low NOX burners to control NOX emissions.

           3. Project Emissions Summary
           This section presents a summary of the Project emissions and a discussion of the methodologies used to
           calculate emissions. Within each emission source subsection below, the methods used to calculate emissions
           are discussed, followed by a summary of the emission estimates for each specific emission unit, and, for the
           proposed CT units, the mode of operation and fuel option. Section 3.1 below provides a summary of the
           potential hourly and annual emissions associated with the proposed Project for both fuel options.

           The procedures used in determining the potential emissions from the Project are based on information
           provided by the turbine manufacturer, other equipment vendor data, emission limitations specified by the
           applicable New Source Performance Standards, emission factors documented in EPA’s “Compilation of Air
           Pollution Emission Factors, AP-42,” and proposed Best Available Control Technology (BACT) emission limits.
           Operational limitations (as appropriate) have been accounted for in estimating potential annual emissions.

           Detailed emissions calculations for each emission source are presented in Appendix C.


           3.1 Combustion Turbines
           The main sources of emissions for the Project are the three proposed CT units. The following section presents
           the potential emission rates of these units. Additional emissions information at various loads, ambient
           temperatures, and operating conditions (e.g., evaporative cooling), as provided by the turbine manufacturer,
           are provided in Appendix C (Tables C-1 to C-4 and C-8 to C-9).

           Annual operation of each proposed CT unit will be limited to a capacity factor based on its design efficiency for
           purposes of compliance with NSPS Subpart TTTT. The design efficiency of each proposed CT unit is
           approximately 41.5% based on an overall net efficiency on a lower heating value (LHV) basis of REDACTED
           Btu/kW at ISO conditions, which is equivalent to an annual heat input of 14,483,434 MMBtu on a higher
           heating value (HHV) basis.

           Table 3-1 and Table 3-2 present the maximum hourly emissions rate (lb/hr) and the maximum annual
           emissions (tons/year) during normal operations for each proposed CT unit for natural gas and distillate oil fuel
           combustion, respectively.

           3.2.1 Emergency Engines
           The Project will include one 3,250 kW emergency generator and a 350 bhp emergency fire water pump engine.
           The ULSD-fired emergency generator and fire water pump engine will meet the emission requirements in
           EPA’s Standards of Performance for Stationary Compression Ignition Internal Combustion Engines, 40 CFR
           Part 60, Subpart IIII. The engines will also meet the applicable requirements of 40 CFR Part 63, Subpart
           ZZZZ.

           The fire water pump engine and the emergency generator will operate for emergency purposes and for limited
           periods of routine testing, maintenance, and other non-emergency purposes. The fire water pump engine is
           considered an emergency engine and will be operated for no more than 500 hours per year, and the
           emergency generator will be operated for no more than 200 hours per year. Emissions of criteria pollutants
           and HAPs from the emergency engine are presented in Table 3-5 and detailed emissions calculations can be
           found in Appendix C (Tables C-6, C-7, C-11, & C-12).


           3.2.2 Diesel Fuel Storage Tank
           One 5.72 million-gallon distillate oil fuel storage tank will be installed to provide fuel for the proposed CT units.
           VOC emissions from the storage tank will be minimized using submerged fill piping and a light-colored surface
           coating to reduce solar absorptance. Emissions of criteria pollutants from the fuel storage tank are also
           presented in Table 3-5 and detailed emissions calculations are presented in Table C-13 of Appendix C.


           3.2.3 Natural Gas-Fired Fuel Gas Heaters
           The Project will also include three natural gas-fired fuel gas heaters, each with a heat input rating of 10
           MMBtu/hr, to support the proposed CT units. Emissions of criteria pollutants from the natural gas-fired fuel gas
           heaters are also presented in Table 3-5 and detailed emissions calculations are presented in Tables C-5 and
           C-10 of Appendix C.

           4. Applicable Regulations
           This section identifies the federal and state air quality regulations and standards that will govern construction
           and operation of the proposed Project. Specifically, the following regulations and standards were reviewed for
           applicability to the proposed Project:

                •      National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS)
                •      Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) requirements
                •      Good Engineering Practice (GEP) Stack Height regulations
                •      New Source Performance Standards (NSPS)
                •      National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP)
                •      Compliance Assurance Monitoring (CAM) requirements
                •      Acid Rain Program (ARP)
                •      Risk Management Program (RMP)
                •      Cross-State Air Pollution Rule (CSAPR) requirements
                •      Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP)
                •      Georgia EPD regulations
                •      Georgia State Implementation Plan

           The following subsections review the key elements of the identified regulatory programs and requirements and
           the impact of each on the permitting and operation of the proposed Project.


           4.1 Ambient Air Quality Classification
           The CAA authorizes EPA to establish National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS), and EPA has
           established a NAAQS for six air pollutants, which are presented in Section 6, Table 6-1. Newnan, Coweta
           County, Georgia, in which Plant Yates is located, is currently designated as attainment or unclassifiable for all
           of these NAAQS. See 40 CFR 81.311.


           4.2 Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD)
               Program
           4.2.1 PSD Applicability
           Since Plant Yates is located in an area that has been designated as attainment or unclassifiable for all NAAQS,
           the Project must be evaluated to determine whether it constitutes a major modification at a major stationary
           source under PSD regulations. Plant Yates is a major stationary source because it is in one of the 28 major
           source categories listed in 40 CFR 52.21(b)(1)(iii) and referenced in Ga. Comp. R & Regs. 391-3-1-.02(7)(2)
           and has the potential to emit more than 100 tons per year of at least one regulated NSR pollutant. A major
           modification is defined as a physical change or change in the method of operation at a major source that
           results in a significant emissions increase and a significant net emissions increase in emissions that is greater
           than the PSD significant emission rates, as identified in Table 4-1.

           4.2.2 PSD Program Requirements
           The following sections provide a summary of the requirements for projects subject to PSD permitting.

           4.2.2.1 Best Available Control Technology

           Major sources conducting a major modification must meet the Best Available Control Technology (BACT) for all
           pollutants for which PSD permitting is required. Guidelines for the evaluation of BACT can be found in EPA’s
           Draft New Source Review Workshop Manual (EPA 1990) and other guidance documents. EPA has also
           published guidance on BACT for greenhouse gas emissions.

           The BACT analysis for the Project is presented in Section 5.

           4.2.2.2 Ambient Air Quality Analysis Requirements

           In accordance with the requirements of 40 CFR 52.21(m), a PSD permit application must contain an analysis
           of existing ambient air quality data in the affected area for all regulated pollutants for which PSD permitting is
           required. The analysis of existing air quality can be based on air monitoring data from either a state-operated
           or private network, or a pre-construction monitoring program that is specifically designed to collect data in the
           vicinity of the proposed source.

           The requirements for the ambient air quality analysis are discussed in Section 6.9.

           4.2.2.3 Source Impact Analysis

           In accordance with the requirements of 40 CFR 52.21(k), a source impact analysis must be performed for a
           proposed project for each pollutant that triggers PSD review to demonstrate that the project will not cause or
           contribute to an exceedance of any NAAQS and PSD increments. This is first demonstrated by assessing
           project-modeled concentrations relative to Significant Impact Levels (SILs) as an initial screening step,
           assuming the use of the SILs can be justified for the proposed project. Justification for the use of the SILs for
           the proposed project is provided in Section 7.2. For those pollutants that have modeled concentrations
           greater than the SILs, a cumulative analysis including nearby background sources is required to demonstrate
           that the project will not cause or contribute to an exceedance of the NAAQS or PSD increments.

           PSD regulations specify that new major sources or modifications to existing major sources may impact
           baseline air quality only by a defined amount known as a PSD increment. PSD increments have been
           established for PM10, PM2.5, SO2, and NO2 (see Section 6, Table 6-1). The increment is dependent on the
           classification of the area (Class I, Class II, or Class III) in which the action is to take place. Class I areas are
           federally protected areas and include specifically defined national parks, national forests, and wilderness
           areas. The remainder (and vast majority) of the country (including Coweta County) is designated as a Class II
           area. To date, no Class III areas have been designated.

           The PSD regulations require the use of atmospheric dispersion modeling to perform source impact analyses,
           estimate baseline and future air quality levels, and compare the results to NAAQS and PSD increments.
           Designated EPA models are used to perform these air quality analyses. Guidance for the use and application
           of dispersion models is presented in the EPA publication Guideline on Air Quality Models (GAQM), 40 CFR
           Part 51, Appendix W. In most circumstances, the source impact analysis requirement may be satisfied by
           demonstrating that the impact from the Project will not result in an impact above the SILs presented in Section
           6, Table 6-1.

           Various periods of meteorological data can be utilized for an impact analysis. A minimum period of one year of
           onsite data or five years of representative meteorological data is typically required. The result of the source
           impact analysis is presented in Sections 7 and 8.

           In addition to the source impact analysis, 40 CFR 52.21 of the PSD regulations requires applicants to conduct
           an analysis of the impairment to visibility and the effects on soils and vegetation that would occur as a result of
           construction and operation. The application must also address impacts due to commercial, residential,
           industrial, and other growth in the vicinity of the project to the extent this growth is a result of the project.
           These additional requirements are addressed in Section 9 of this application.


           4.3 Good Engineering Practice (GEP) Stack Height
               Analysis
           The CAA requires that the degree of emission limitation required for control of any pollutant must not be
           affected by a stack which exceeds the GEP height (EPA 1985). This analysis is described in more detail in
           Section 6.3.

           4.4.1 Subpart A – General Provisions
           All affected sources which are subject to a NSPS under 40 CFR Part 60 are subject to the general provisions
           of 40 CFR Part 60 Subpart A, unless those provisions are specifically excluded by an applicable source-
           specific NSPS. Since the Project will be subject to at least one NSPS, the permittee will be required to comply
           with applicable provisions of Subpart A. Subpart A contains initial notification, performance testing, monitoring,
           and recordkeeping requirements for the subparts, as applicable.


           4.4.2 Subpart Kb – Volatile Organic Liquid Storage Vessels
                 (Including Petroleum Liquids Storage Vessels) for
                 Which Construction, Reconstruction, or Modification
                 Commenced After July 23, 1984
           As part of the proposed Project, the new facility will have storage tanks for the distillate oil that will be used in
           the proposed CT units, emergency generator, and fire water pump engine. 40 CFR Part 60, Subpart Kb
           regulates storage vessels with a capacity greater than 75 cubic meters (m3) (19,813 gallons) that are used to
           store volatile organic liquids for which construction, reconstruction, or modification is commenced after July 23,
           1984. However, Subpart Kb does not apply to storage vessels of any size storing a liquid with a maximum true
           vapor pressure less than 3.5 kPa (0.5 psia).

           The maximum true vapor pressure of distillate oil stored at the Project will be less than 0.5 psia (~0.01 psia
           typ.). Therefore, the diesel fuel storage tanks at the facility will not be subject to this subpart.

           EPA proposed NSPS Subpart Kc on October 4, 2023. If finalized as proposed, the diesel fuel storage tanks at
           the facility will not be subject to that subpart.


           4.4.3 Subpart IIII – Standards of Performance for Stationary
                 Compression Ignition Internal Combustion Engines
           The emergency generator and fire water pump engine are subject to the emission standards in 40 CFR Part
           60, Subpart IIII - Standards of Performance for Stationary Compression Ignition Internal Combustion Engines.
           GPC will comply with the emission standards by purchasing an engine certified by the manufacturer to the
           emission standards in 40 CFR 60.4202, as applicable, for the same model year and maximum engine power.
           The emergency generator will be subject to Tier 2 standards and the fire water pump engine will be subject to
           Tier 3 standards under Subpart IIII and 40 CFR Part 1039. GPC will comply with all applicable Subpart IIII
           monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. Since the engines will be designated and operated as
           emergency engines, they will only be operated in emergency circumstances and for a maximum of 100 hours
           per year for maintenance and readiness testing, 50 hours of which may be used in non-emergency situations.

           4.4.4 Subpart KKKK – Stationary Combustion Turbines
           The proposed CT units will be subject to 40 CFR Part 60, Subpart KKKK, which establishes NOX and SO2
           emission limits for stationary combustion turbines that commence construction, modification, or reconstruction
           after February 18, 2005 and have a heat input at peak load equal to or greater than 10 MMBtu/hr based on the
           higher heating value.

           4.4.4.1 Emission Limits for NOX

           Under Subpart KKKK, the proposed CT units are subject to NOX emission standards of 15 ppm, corrected to
           15% O2, or 0.43 lb/MWh, when firing natural gas, and 42 ppm, corrected to 15% O2, or 1.3 lb/MWh, when firing
           distillate oil, based on a 30-operating day rolling average.

           As discussed in the BACT analysis in Section 5.0, the proposed CT units will reduce NOX emissions using
           DLN, water injection, and SCR to comply with Subpart KKKK. Compliance with the Subpart KKKK emissions
           standards will be verified based on CEMS data.

           4.4.4.2 Emission Limits for SO2

           The proposed CT units will be subject to either an emission limit of 0.9 lb/MWh gross output or a limit on the
           use of any fuel that contains the total potential sulfur emissions in excess of 0.06 lb SO2/MMBtu heat input.

           GPC will comply with the input-based emission standard for SO2 by utilizing natural gas and distillate oil in the
           proposed CT units. Both fuels have a sulfur content lower than needed to meet the 0.06 lb SO2/MMBtu limit.


           4.4.5 Subpart TTTT – Standards of Performance for
                 Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Electric Utility
                 Generating Units
           The proposed CT units will be subject to 40 CFR Part 60, Subpart TTTT, which applies to each electric utility
           generating units with a heat input greater than 250 MMBtu/hr of fossil fuel that serves a generator capable of
           selling greater than 25 MW of electricity to a utility power distribution system that commences construction on
           or after January 8, 2014. GPC will comply with Subpart TTTT by limiting the capacity factor of each proposed
           CT unit to less than its design efficiency on a 12-operating month and 3-year rolling average basis and being
           permitted to burn only pipeline quality natural gas and distillate oil (see 40 CFR 60.5520(d)(1)).


           4.4.6 Subpart TTTTa – Proposed Rule: Standards for
                 Greenhouse Gas Emissions from New, Modified, and
                 Reconstructed Fossil Fuel-Fired Electric Utility
                 Generating Units
           EPA proposed 40 CFR Part 60, Subpart TTTTa on May 23, 2023. If this rule is promulgated as proposed,
           combustion turbines for which construction commences after the proposal date and that meet the relevant
           applicability criteria would be subject to the requirements of Subpart TTTTa rather than Subpart TTTT.

           The proposed rule would be implemented in phases. For Phase I, the proposed emission standard for new
           intermediate load combustion turbines (less than 35-40 percent capacity factor, depending on efficiency level)
           is 1,150 lb CO2/ MWhr gross and the proposed emission standard for low load or peaking combustion turbines
           (less than 20 percent capacity factor) is 120 – 160 lb CO2/MMBtu of heat input, similar to the standard
           established under Subpart TTTT. For Phase II, intermediate load turbines would become subject to a more

           4.6 40 CFR Part 63 NESHAP
           Plant Yates is currently classified as an existing major source of HAPs, and the emission units constructed as
