           5.3.3 Carbon Monoxide
           5.3.3.1 Formation

           CO emissions from the proposed emergency generator and fire water pump engine are influenced by engine
           design and operational features which promote fuel combustion efficiency and complete combustion.

           5.3.3.2 Step 1 – Identify CO Control Options

           As discussed above, available control options for CO emissions from the proposed emergency generator and
           fire water pump engine are limited to those that are included with purchasing a Tier 2 emergency generator
           and a Tier 3 fire water pump engine, or purchasing a Tier 4 non-emergency engine and operating it as if it were
           an emergency generator or fire water pump engine. Based on the RBLC search results provided in Appendix
           E, Table E-16, there is one case in which Tier 4 was listed as BACT for an emergency engine. Therefore, Tier
           4 is considered further for the purposes of BACT. It should be noted, however, that the CO emission standard
           for Tier 2, 3, and 4 engines for the same engine category and model year with similar power ratings are
           identical (3.5 g/kW-hr). 43

           5.3.3.3 Step 2 – Eliminate Technically Infeasible CO Control Options

           Purchasing a Tier 2 emergency generator and a Tier 3 fire water pump engine is inherent to the Project and
           technically feasible. Tier 4 engines with similar power ratings appear to be commercially available based on a
           review of EPA’s annual certification database for nonroad CI engines. Therefore, Tier 4 is also considered
           technical feasible.

           5.3.3.4 Step 3 – Rank Remaining CO Control Options

           In EPA’s phased approach to regulating emissions from nonroad engines, each tier requires more stringent
           emissions reductions than the previous one. However, in the case of CO, the emissions standard for each tier
           is the identical.

           5.3.3.5 Step 4 – Evaluation of CO Control Options

           In the 2005 NSPS Subpart IIII proposal, EPA generally stated that the use of add-on controls for emergency
           stationary CI ICE could not be justified due to the cost of the technology relative to the emission reduction that
           would be obtained. 44 EPA has previously estimated the cost effectiveness of Tier 4 control strategies for CO to
           be between ~$10,000 and $24,000 per ton when applied to non-emergency engines with similar power ratings
           that operate for at least 1,000 hours per year. 45 The cost per ton will increase as operating hours decrease
           because capital costs remain unchanged, while emission reductions decrease with operating hours. This is
           especially true for the proposed emergency generator and fire water pump engine, which will be operated for a
           maximum of 200 and 500 hours per year, respectively. Therefore, Tier 4 is eliminated from this BACT analysis
           for both the proposed emergency generator and fire water pump engine based on the unreasonable estimated
           annual cost of control.

           5.3.5 Particulate Matter
           5.3.5.1 Formation

           PM emissions from the proposed emergency generator and fire water pump engine may consist of inorganic
           matter present in the fuel (e.g., ash, metals, etc.) and high molecular weight unburned hydrocarbons (soot).
           Generally, the use of clean fuels with negligible ash and sulfur content, such as ULSD, in conjunction with
           engine design and operational features to promote complete fuel combustion, minimizes PM emissions.

           5.3.5.2 Step 1 – Identify PM Control Options

           As discussed above, in addition to use of ULSD, available control options for PM emissions from the proposed
           emergency generator and fire water pump engine are limited to those that are included with purchasing a Tier
           2 emergency generator and a Tier 3 fire water pump engine, or purchasing a Tier 4 non-emergency engine and
           operating it as if it were an emergency generator or fire water pump engine. Based on the RBLC search
           results provided in Appendix E, Table E-18, there were no cases in which Tier 4 was identified as BACT for
           PM. GPC has nonetheless evaluated technical feasibility and other factors for this control option.

           5.3.5.3 Step 2 – Eliminate Technically Infeasible PM Control Options

           Purchasing a Tier 2 emergency generator and a Tier 3 fire water pump engine and exclusive use of ULSD is
           inherent to the Project and technically feasible. Tier 4 engines with similar power ratings appear to be
           commercially available based on a review of EPA’s annual certification database for nonroad CI engines.
           Therefore, Tier 4 is also considered technically feasible.

           5.3.5.4 Step 3 – Rank Remaining PM Control Options

           In EPA’s phased approach to regulating emissions from nonroad engines, each tier requires more stringent
           emissions reductions than the previous one. Tier 4 has the highest level of control effectiveness, whereas Tier
           2 has the lowest.

           In the 2005 NSPS Subpart IIII proposal, EPA estimated the cost effectiveness of Tier 4 control strategies for
           PM to be between ~$160,000 and $970,000 per ton when applied to emergency engines with similar power

           5.3.6 Greenhouse Gases
           5.3.6.1 Formation

           As with the proposed CT units, GHG emissions that result from the combustion of ULSD in the proposed
           emergency generator and fire water pump engine include CO2, CH4, and N2O.

           5.3.6.2 Step 1 – Identify GHG Control Options

           While some engine-based technologies may promote fuel efficiency, EPA’s tiered emission standards for CI
           ICE do not address GHG emissions directly. Based on the RBLC search results provided in Appendix E,
           Table E-19, no add-on control options were identified that would reduce GHG emissions from the proposed
           emergency generator and fire water pump engine. Instead, many facilities listed some variation of use of clean
           fuels (natural gas and distillate oil), good combustion practices, and limiting annual operating hours as BACT
           for GHG emissions.

           Potential control options not considered in this BACT analysis included use of natural gas and CCS. Relative
           to ULSD, natural gas inherently results in lower GHG emissions on a heat input basis. However, natural gas
           cannot be stored onsite and may not be available during an emergency, including when the emergency itself is
           unavailability of natural gas. Because natural gas is less likely to be available in the emergency circumstances
           during which the emergency engines and fire pump are needed, that option will not be considered further in
           this analysis, as it would interfere with the intended function of the units.

           Additionally, CCS should not be considered as a potentially available control option since GHG emissions from
           the proposed emergency generator and fire water pump engine are insignificant. CCS should only be
           considered as an available control option for facilities that emit CO2 in larger amounts, or for industrial facilities
           with high-purity CO2 steams, consistent with past EPA guidance. 48 GPC’s analysis of CCS for the proposed
           CT units found CCS to be technically infeasible and the annual cost of control to be unreasonable. Applying
           CCS to these sources alone or in combination with the proposed CT units cannot reasonably be expected to
           change the outcome of that analysis. Accordingly, use of ULSD, good combustion practices, and limiting
           annual operating hours are the only potentially available control options for GHG emissions from the proposed
           emergency generator and fire water pump engine.

           5.4 Diesel Storage Tank BACT Review
           5.4.1 Volatile Organic Compounds
           5.4.1.1 Characterization of Emissions

           VOC emissions from storage tanks result from two mechanisms: evaporative losses during storage (referred to
           as breathing or standing losses) and losses during tank filling (known as working losses). Standing losses
           occur when organic compounds contained in the vapor headspace above the stored liquid expand are emitted
           from tank vents due to changes in temperature and barometric pressure. Emissions from working losses occur
           due to the change in tank liquid level that accompanies tank filling operations. As the liquid level increases, the
           vapor headspace is displaced from the tank vent. In both cases, emissions vary as a function of the vapor
           pressure of the stored liquid and atmospheric conditions at the tank location.

           5.4.1.2 Step 1 – Identify VOC Control Options

           GPC searched EPA’s control technology database and considered relevant existing and proposed federal and
           state emission standards to identify potential control options for VOC emissions from the proposed diesel
           storage tank. Based on the RBLC search results provided in Appendix E, Table E-20, no add-on control
           options were identified. Many facilities listed work practice standards such as submerged filling and tank
           design, including the specific external surface color of the tank, as BACT for VOC emissions. Submerged filling
           reduces working losses from liquid storage tanks by eliminating splashing and reducing vapor displacement in
           the tank headspace. The use of light or reflective tank surface colors decreases breathing losses by reducing
           tank inventory temperature changes caused by solar energy absorptance through the tank shell.

           5.4.1.5 Step 4 – Evaluation of VOC Control Options

           The top control options – use of submerged filling and light or reflective tank surface colors – are being
           proposed for emissions of VOC from the proposed diesel storage tank. Therefore, no evaluation of the VOC
           control options is required. 51

           5.4.1.6 Step 5 – Select VOC BACT for Diesel Storage Tank

           VOC BACT for the proposed diesel storage tank is use of submerged filling and light or reflective tank surface
           colors. Submerged filling will minimize emissions of VOC resulting from splashing of product loaded. A fill pipe
           opening will be submerged below the tank’s liquid surface level, ensuring that liquid turbulence is mitigated
           during loading, resulting in minimal emissions into the vapor space above the liquid surface. A light-colored or
           reflective paint for the tank shell and roof will be used to minimize product temperature. Evaporative losses
           have a strong correlation with temperature of liquid product stored and reducing liquid product temperature can
           minimize evaporative losses.

           5.5 Fuel Gas Heater BACT Review
           Associated equipment associated with the Project includes:

                •     Three (3) natural gas-fired fuel gas heaters, each with a heat input rating of less than 10 MMBtu/hr.


           5.5.1 Nitrogen Oxides
           5.5.1.1 Formation

           NOX formation mechanisms for fuel-burning equipment such as the proposed fuel gas heaters are generally
           the same as those discussed above for the proposed CT units, although thermal NOX is expected to be the
           basis for the majority of NOX emissions from such heaters.

           5.5.1.2 Step 1 – Identify NOX Control Options

           GPC searched EPA’s control technology database and considered relevant existing and proposed federal and
           state emissions standards to identify potential control options for NOX emissions from the proposed fuel gas
           heaters. Generally, NOX emissions from fuel burning equipment can be controlled through two types of
           emission control strategies: combustion controls and add-on controls. Combustion controls address thermal
           NOX directly by reducing peak flame temperature by, for example, staging combustion and/or recirculating flue
           gas to reduce the oxygen content of the combustion air. Add-on controls employ various strategies to reduce
           NOX emissions to water and nitrogen, which often includes the use of reagents in the presence of a catalyst.
           Based on the RBLC search results provided in Appendix E, Table E-21, no add-on control options were
           identified. Many facilities listed some variation of use of clean fuels (such as natural gas), good combustion
           practices (e.g., tune-ups), and combustion controls (such as low or ultra-low NOX burners), as BACT. Add-on
           controls potentially applicable to the proposed fuel gas heaters include SCR, selective non-catalytic reduction
           (SNCR), and non-selective catalytic reduction (NSCR).

           5.5.1.3 Step 2 – Eliminate Technically Infeasible NOX Control Options

           Use of Clean Fuels, Good Combustion Practices, and Combustion Controls

           Use of natural gas, good combustion practices, and ultra-low NOX burners are inherent to the Project and
           technically feasible.

           Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR), Selective Non-catalytic Reduction (SNCR), Non-selective catalytic
           reduction (NSCR)

           As discussed in the BACT analysis for the proposed CT units, SCR, SNCR, and NSCR are all forms of post-
           combustion add-on controls that reduce NOX emissions to water and nitrogen, as follows:

                •     SCR – Injection of nitrogen-based reagent (e.g., ammonia or urea) in the presence of a catalyst

                •     SNCR – Similar to SCR, except no catalyst is used and higher operating temperatures are required

                •     NSCR – Catalyst reaction without use of a reagent in exhaust gas with low oxygen content

           GPC is unaware of any case in which these add-on controls have been installed and operated successfully on
           small fuel-burning equipment similar to the proposed fuel gas heaters. Combustion controls such as low or
           ultra-low NOX burners, with or without flue gas recirculation, are the most effective controls that can be
           obtained through commercial channels for such units. Therefore, add-on controls are not considered available.
           Additionally, both SNCR and NSCR are not applicable based on the physical and chemical characteristics of
           the exhaust gas from the proposed fuel gas heaters. For SNCR, the exhaust gas is not hot enough for this
           add-on control to be effective. For NSCR, the oxygen content of the exhaust gas is too high for this add-on

           5.5.2.1 Formation

           CO emissions from the proposed fuel gas heaters may result from incomplete conversion of carbon-containing
           compounds during combustion and are principally influenced by equipment operating conditions.

           5.5.2.2 Step 1 – Identify CO Control Options

           state emissions standards to identify potential control options for CO emissions from the proposed fuel gas
           heaters. Like NOX, CO emissions from fuel burning equipment can be controlled through two types of
           emission control strategies: good combustion practices and add-on controls. For sources such as the
           proposed fuel gas heaters, there is typically a trade-off between emissions of NOX and CO. For example,
           higher combustion temperatures and residence times may lead to more complete fuel combustion and thus
           lower CO emissions, but these control techniques may result in excessive NOX emissions. Good combustion
           practices strive to optimize emissions for both pollutants. Add-on controls may employ various types of
           catalysts to oxidize CO emissions to CO2. Based on the RBLC search results provided in Appendix E, Table
           E-22, no add-on control options were identified. Many facilities listed some variation of use of clean fuels such

           5.5.4 Particulate Matter
           5.5.4.1 Formation

           PM emissions from fuel-burning equipment such as the proposed fuel gas heaters generally occur in the same
           manner as those discussed above for the proposed CT units, except that sulfates are expected to have a
           negligible contribution to the condensable portion of PM.

           5.5.4.2 Step 1 – Identify PM Control Options

           GPC searched EPA’s control technology database and considered relevant existing and proposed federal and
           state emissions standards to identify potential control options for PM emissions from the proposed fuel gas
           heaters. Based on the RBLC search results provided in Appendix E, Tables E-24 (PM), 25 (PM10), and 26
           (PM2.5), no add-on control options were identified. Generally, conventional add-on controls often applied to
           solid fuel boilers, such as baghouses, electrostatic precipitators, and scrubbers, have not been applied to gas-
           fired fuel-burning equipment like the fuel gas heaters since combustion of natural gas inherently results in low
           levels of emissions. 54 Instead, many facilities listed some variation of use of clean fuels such as natural gas
           and good combustion practices as BACT. Accordingly, these control options are the only options considered
           further.

           Use of natural gas and good combustion practices are inherent to the Project and technically feasible.

           5.5.4.4 Step 3 – Rank Remaining PM Control Options

           No ranking of control options is required, as use of natural gas and good combustion practices are the only
           available and technically feasible control options for PM emissions from the proposed fuel gas heaters.

           5.5.4.5 Step 4 – Evaluation of PM Control Options

           The top control options are being proposed for PM emissions from the proposed fuel gas heaters. Therefore,
           no evaluation of the PM control options is required.

           5.5.4.6 Step 5 – Select PM BACT for Fuel Gas Heaters

           No BACT floor exists for emissions from the proposed fuel gas heaters since they are too small to be regulated
           under NSPS Subpart Dc.

           PM BACT for the proposed fuel gas heaters is based on the exclusive use of natural gas and good combustion
           practices. Based on the RBLC search results, PM emission limits for natural gas-fired fuel gas heaters with a
           heat input rating of less than 10 MMBtu/hr range from 0.007 to 0.010 lb/MMBtu.

           Vendor information indicates that PM emissions from the proposed fuel gas heaters should not exceed 0.007
           lb/MMBtu. However, instead of a numerical BACT limit, GPC is proposing exclusive use of natural gas as
           BACT.


           54
             When EPA proposed national standards for small industrial, commercial, and institutional boilers and process heaters in
           NSPS Subpart Dc, EPA stated that “[b]ecause of [the] low uncontrolled PM emission levels, the application of any type of PM
           control technology to small natural gas-fired… units would impose significant costs for no benefit. Consequently, the use of
           any conventional PM control technology to reduce PM emissions from small natural gas-fired… units is considered
           unreasonable…” 54 Fed. Reg. 24798 (June 9, 1989).

           5.5.5 Greenhouse Gases
           5.5.5.1 Formation

           As with the proposed CT units, GHG emissions that result from the combustion of natural gas in the proposed
           fuel gas heaters include CO2, CH4, and N2O.

           5.5.5.2 Step 1 – Identify GHG Control Options

           Based on the RBLC search results provided in Appendix E, Table E-27, no add-on control options were
           identified that would reduce GHG emissions from the proposed fuel gas heaters. Instead, many facilities listed
           some variation of use of clean fuels (natural gas and distillate oil) and good combustion practices as BACT for
           GHG emissions.

           As explained above, CCS should not be considered as a potentially available control option for sources with
           insignificant GHG emissions. Accordingly, use of natural gas and good combustion practices are the only
           potentially available control options for GHG emissions from the proposed fuel gas heaters.

           5.5.5.3 Step 2 – Eliminate Technically Infeasible GHG Control Options

           Exclusive use of natural gas and good combustion practices for the proposed fuel gas heaters are inherent to
           the Project and technically feasible.

           5.5.5.4 Step 3 – Rank Remaining GHG Control Options

           No ranking of control options is required, as the exclusive use of natural gas and good combustion practices
           are the only available and technically feasible control options for GHG emissions from the proposed fuel gas
           heaters.

           5.5.5.5 Step 4 – Evaluation of GHG Control Options

           The top control options are being proposed for emissions of GHG from the proposed fuel gas heaters.
           Therefore, no evaluation of the control options is required.

           5.5.5.6 Steps 5 – Select GHG BACT for Fuel Gas Heaters

           No BACT floor exists for emissions from the proposed fuel gas heaters.

           GHG BACT for the proposed fuel gas heaters is based on the exclusive use of natural gas as fuel and good
           combustion practices. GPC is proposing the exclusive use of natural gas and performing biennial tune-ups
           required by the Industrial Boiler MACT as GHG BACT.

           6. Class II Area Air Quality Modeling
              Analysis Procedures
           This section presents the approach to the dispersion modeling analysis conducted to assess the Project’s
           impacts with respect to applicable state and federal ambient air quality regulations and guidelines. This
           analysis was conducted in accordance with the EPD PSD Guidance Document (EPD 2017) and US EPA’s
           Guideline on Air Quality Models (US EPA 2017) (GAQM), which is contained in 40 CFR Part 51, Appendix W,
           as well as the modeling protocol submitted on October 11, 2023, and addresses comments on the protocol
           provided by EPD on November 21, 28, and 30, 2023, and by EPA Region 4 to EPD on November 9, 2023.

           The Project is subject to PSD review for NOX, PM, PM10, PM2.5, CO, VOC, H2SO4, and GHG. Therefore,
           associated dispersion modeling analyses were conducted for these pollutants, except for VOC and GHG
           emissions, as there are no direct modeling requirements for these pollutants. However, the impact of Project
           VOC emissions as a precursor to ozone is addressed in Section 6.8. The modeling analysis also addresses
           impacts associated with secondary PM2.5 as described further in Section 6.8.

           The EPA has determined that the permitting process can be streamlined without compromising air quality if the
           EPA and permitting authorities are able to identify a quantitative threshold or dividing line between an
           insignificant and a significant impact on air quality. Using a quantitative threshold for this purpose is
           permissible as long as the EPA or the appropriate permitting authority provides a reasoned explanation for why
           impacts below that value do not cause or contribute to a violation in a particular context. 55 Accordingly, US EPA
           has defined concentrations, called “significant impact levels” (SILs), that are used as a tool to streamline the
           evaluation of whether a major new source or modification may cause or contribute to a violation of a NAAQS or
           exceedance of a PSD increment for any pollutant subject to PSD review. For those pollutants which have
           modeled concentrations at or below the applicable SIL, that result indicates the Project will not cause or
           contribute to a NAAQS violation or an exceedance of a PSD increment, so long as the values and their use are
           justified in the administrative record. In particular, EPA guidance indicates that the SILs may be justified unless
           an area is currently in violation of the NAAQS, multiple sources may impact the same area, or the permitting
           authority is aware that a significant portion of the NAAQS or increment has already been consumed. 56 This
           justification can be provided demonstrating that the difference between background concentrations in a
           particular area and the NAAQS is greater than the SIL values. 57 On the other hand, if modeling indicated that
           SILs for some pollutants and averaging periods are exceeded, then a cumulative impact modeling assessment
           was performed. The results of the cumulative modeling were compared to the NAAQS and PSD increments
           (see Table 6-1), as applicable.

           All model input and output files are included with this application submittal to Georgia EPD in the modeling
           archive contained in Appendix G.

           6.1 Modeling Source Approach and Configurations
           The air dispersion modeling analysis was conducted with emission rates and flue gas exhaust characteristics
           (flow rate and temperature) determined to represent the worst-case parameters among the range of possible
           operating conditions for the proposed Project. The air dispersion modeling analysis was performed
           considering both normal operations and startup/shutdown of the proposed CT units, which were each modeled
           as point sources.

           characteristics for the proposed CT units at a given operating load vary as a function of ambient temperature
           and data was derived for a range of operating conditions as follows:

                    •        3 operating loads (100%, 75%, and minimum emission compliance (MECL))

           The modeling for startup/shutdown is comprised of a composite hourly profile of emissions that accounts for a
           single startup or shutdown event per hour. Since each one of these events does not last a full hour, the
           balance of the hour assumes the CT units are operating at full load. This creates a matrix of four (4) scenarios
           assessing short-term startup and shutdown emissions. Those scenarios include:

            1. Startup natural gas 32 minutes + 100% load natural gas for 28 minutes,
            2. Shutdown natural gas 5 minutes + 100% load natural gas for 55 minutes,
            3. Startup distillate oil 49 minutes + 100% load distillate oil for 11 minutes, and
            4. Shutdown distillate oil 15 minutes + 100% load distillate oil for 45 minutes.

           Since the startup/shutdown emissions occur under different stack parameters (compared to normal
           operations), the modeled hourly profile of emissions includes a startup or shutdown event using two co-located
           stacks. Stack 1 consists of the startup or shutdown stack depending on the scenario modeled and uses the
           total emissions from a single event as input to the model. Stack 2 reflects the normal operating emission rate
           at 100% load for the balance of the hour that the CT unit is not operating in startup or shutdown mode. The
           modeled emissions for Stack 2 are scaled based on the portion of the hour that the turbine is operating under
           normal conditions. Table 6-7 provides the emissions for each scenario modeled for each pollutant.

           Stack 1 (startup or shutdown stack) stack parameters consist of those shown in Table 6-4 and Table 6-5 for
           the MECL scenario. Stack 2 (normal operations stack) stack parameters consist of those shown in Table 6-4
           and Table 6-5 for the 100% load scenario.

           Each of these four (4) scenarios was included as part of the load analysis described in Section 7.1. The
           hourly profile of emissions was conservatively assumed to be occurring every hour of the year modeled,
           however, the modeling assumed that there would be only one (1) event per hour. One event is defined as
           either:

            1. 3 CT units start up on natural gas simultaneously and operate at 100% load for the balance of the hour,
            2. 3 CT units shut down on natural gas simultaneously and operate at 100% load for the balance of the hour,
            3. 3 CT units start up on distillate oil simultaneously and operate at 100% load for the balance of the hour,
               and
            4. 3 CT units shut down on distillate oil simultaneously and operate at 100% load for the balance of the hour.

           6.2 Model Selection and Options
           The suitability of an air quality dispersion model for a particular application is dependent upon several factors.
           The following selection criteria were evaluated:

                 •      stack height relative to nearby structures;
                 •      dispersion environment;
                 •      representative meteorological data; and
                 •      local terrain.

           The US EPA GAQM prescribes a set of approved models for regulatory applications for a wide range of source
           types and dispersion environments. AERMOD is US EPA’s recommended refined dispersion model for simple
           and complex terrain for receptors within 50 kilometers (km) of a modeled source and is capable of handling the
           source geometry, terrain, and dispersion environment associated with this Project. Representative
           meteorological data with suitable data capture for various meteorological parameters is needed to run
           AERMOD.

           Based on a review of the factors described in the following sections, the latest version of AERMOD (version
           23132) (US EPA 2023) was used to assess air quality impacts for the proposed Project. AERMOD was used to
           assess air quality impacts of NO2, PM10, PM2.5, and CO at receptors located within 20 km of the proposed
           Project site. AERMOD was run with default model options in the CONTROL pathway, unless otherwise noted
           or discussed with EPD. AERMOD was also applied without using any urban source options as discussed in
           Section 6.4.

           6.3 Building Downwash and GEP Height Analysis
           US EPA modeling guidelines require the evaluation of the potential for physical structures to affect the
           dispersion of emissions from point sources. The exhaust from stacks that are located within specified
           distances of buildings, and whose physical heights are below specified levels, may be subject to “aerodynamic
           building downwash” under certain meteorological conditions. If this is the case, a model capable of simulating
           this effect must be employed.

           The analysis used to evaluate the potential for building downwash is referred to as a physical “Good
           Engineering Practice” (“GEP”) stack height analysis. Stacks with heights below physical GEP are considered
           to be subject to building downwash. In the absence of influencing structures, a “default” GEP stack height is
           creditable up to 65 meters (213 feet) per the Guideline for Determination of Good Engineering Practice Stack
           Height (US EPA, 1985). Any portion of a stack above the maximum of the physical or default GEP height
           cannot be used in the dispersion modeling analysis for purposes of comparison to US EPA’s ambient impact
           criteria.

           A GEP stack height analysis was performed for all point sources included in the modeling in accordance with
           US EPA’s guidelines (US EPA, 1985). Per the guidelines, the physical GEP height (“HGEP”) is determined from
           the dimensions of all buildings that are within the region of influence using the following equation:

                      HGEP = H + 1.5L

           where:

                      H = height of the structure within 5L of the stack which maximizes HGEP, and

                      L = lesser dimension (height or projected width) of the structure.

           For a squat structure (i.e., height less than projected width), the formula reduces to:

                      HGEP = 2.5H

           Both the height and width of the structure are determined from the frontal area of the structure projected onto a
           plane perpendicular to the direction of the wind. In all instances, the GEP stack height is based on the plane
           projections of any nearby building which result in the greatest justifiable height. For purposes of the GEP
           analysis, nearby refers to the “sphere of influence,” defined as five times the height or width of the building,
           whichever is less, downwind from the trailing edge of the structure.

           The current Project design has all modeled stacks less than 65 meters. As such, all Project stacks were
           modeled using their actual stack height. In addition, the EPA’s Building Profile Input Program (BPIP-Version
           04274) version that is appropriate for use with PRIME algorithms in AERMOD was used to incorporate wind-
           direction-specific building dimensions for input to AERMOD. Building coordinates and stack locations were
           developed using site plan drawings, aerial photographs, and GIS software. All relevant new and existing
           building structures were included in the BPIP modeling for both new and existing stacks at Plant Yates. PRIME
           addresses the entire structure of the wake, from the cavity immediately downwind of the building, to the far
           wake.

           In addition, cumulative modeling required the inclusion of the two existing units (Unit 6 and Unit 7) at Plant
           Yates, which share a common 805-ft actual stack height. The GEP formula height for the common stack is 495
           feet. The controlling structure in determining the GEP formula height is the boiler building, with a height of 198
           feet. This structure is wider than it is tall so the GEP formular height is 198 feet times 2.5 = 495 feet. The
           cumulative modeling was conducted using the GEP stack height of 495 ft for Plant Yates Unit 6 and Unit 7
           (model IDs GWP1 and GPW2).

           Figure 6-1 provides an illustration of the point sources and buildings used as input to BPIP.

           6.4 Dispersion Environment
           6.4.1 Land Use Analysis
           The application of AERMOD requires characterization of the local (within 3 km) dispersion environment as
           either urban or rural based on prevalent land use. According to US EPA modeling guidelines (US EPA 2017), if
           more than 50 percent of an area within a 3-km radius of the proposed project is classified as rural, then a rural
           modeling application is required. Conversely, if more than 50% of the area is urban, an urban dispersion
           adjustment can be used.

           Using the Auer method recommended by the US EPA (US EPA 2017), urban land use types are classified as
           categories I1, I2, C1, R2, and R3. Table 6-9 describes these categories and maps them to reasonably
           equivalent USGS 2016 National Land Cover Database (NLCD) categories. While the Auer method and NLCD
           do not use the same terms to define their categories, the similarities between the five Auer categories and
           NLCD categories 23 and 24 are apparent. Thus, it is reasonable to classify NLCD categories 23 and 24 as
           urban land use. A visual comparison of the 2016 (the most recent version) NCLD land use types to recent
           aerial imagery from Google™ indicates only insignificant changes to the land use within 3 km since 2016.
           Figure 6-2 displays the 2016 NLCD data superimposed over aerial imagery within 3 km of the Plant.

           The NLCD data were processed with US EPA’s AERSURFACE processor (version 20060) to determine the
           different land use types within 3 km of the Plant. AERSURFACE is typically used to process NLCD data for
           input to AERMET, the AERMOD model’s meteorological data processor. In this case, AERSURFACE output in
           the form of the pixel count for each of NLCD’s land use types was used to determine the total pixel count of
           urban land use types within 3 km.

           As noted above, urban land use types were assumed to be NLCD categories 23 and 24: “Developed, Medium
           Intensity” and “Developed, High Intensity”, respectively. The pixel count for these categories was 1.83% of the
           total pixel count for all categories. Thus, a majority (>98%) of the 3 km area around the Plant can be classified
           as rural land use and AERMOD will not be applied with any urban source options. Table 6-10 provides the
           pixel counts as reported in the AERSURFACE output along with respective percentages.

           6.4.2 Terrain
           US EPA’s GAQM requires that the differences in terrain elevations between the stack base and model receptor
           locations be considered in the modeling analyses. There are three types of terrain:

                 •      simple terrain – locations where the terrain elevation is at or below the exhaust height of the stacks
                        to be modeled;
                 •      intermediate terrain – locations where the terrain is between the top of the stack and the modeled
                        exhaust “plume” centerline (this varies as a function of plume rise, which in turn, varies as a function
                        of meteorological conditions);
                 •      complex terrain – locations where the terrain is above the plume centerline.

           Figure 6-3 provides a topographic map of the area in the vicinity of the proposed Project site. The area near
           the Plant is characterized as consisting of simple terrain relative to the modeled stacks.

           6.5 Meteorological Data
           The modeling analysis was conducted using 5 years (2017-2021) of surface data from Hartsfield-Jackson
           Atlanta International Airport (KATL) and upper air meteorological data from Atlanta Regional Airport – Falcon
           Field (KFFC). Pre-processed meteorological data, processed with the AERMET ADJ_U* option, was obtained
           from EPD. The Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is located approximately 29 miles northeast of
           the proposed Project site and was deemed to be the most representative from a meteorological and land use
           perspective. A wind rose of the airport is presented in Figure 6-4.

           EPD guidelines, consistent with US EPA’s AERMOD Implementation Guide (AIG) (US EPA 2022), specify that
           the determination of representativeness of meteorological data should include a comparison of surface
           characteristics; specifically, the surface roughness, albedo, and the Bowen ratio between the monitoring site
           and the project site. Therefore, a comparison of the surface characteristics in the area surrounding KATL and
           the Project site was conducted using US EPA’s AERSURFACE processor (version 20060).

           The most recent version of AERSURFACE (20060) uses digital land cover data from the USGS National Land
           Cover Data 2016 archives and is commonly applied to derive surface land use characteristics for input to
           AERMET. As such, this tool was utilized to compare the surface characteristics between KATL and the
           proposed Project site. Specifically, AERSURFACE was applied with a 1-km radius (AERSURFACE default) for
           the surface roughness determination for each location to determine an annual average set of surface
           characteristics. The 1-km radius around KATL was partitioned into two site-specific sectors. Sector 1 was
           classified as non-airport land use and Sector 2 was classified as airport land use. For this analysis, the 1-km
           radius around the proposed Project site was also split into two sectors, with Sector 1 classified as non-airport
           and Sector 2 classified as airport for comparison purposes. Table 6-11 presents the AERSURFACE results for
           albedo, Bowen ratio, and surface roughness. The AERSURFACE results show that the albedo, Bowen ratio,
           and surface roughness results are similar, with the largest difference occurring with the Bowen ratio. Because
           surface roughness is typically the most influential in dispersion modeling, that similarity outweighs the
           difference in Bowen ratio results. Therefore, the surface characteristics used to process the meteorological
           data at KATL are representative of the surface characteristics at the proposed Project site, making the
           meteorological data from KATL acceptable for use in dispersion modeling at the proposed Project site.

           Far-field and near-field views of the receptor grid and ambient air boundary are shown in Figure 6-5 and
           Figure 6-6, respectively. All maximum model concentrations were resolved to 100-m grid spacing.

           Figure 6-6 also shows the ambient air boundary modeled for this proposed Project, which is bounded by an
           internal access road parallel to a railroad spur to the north, the Chattahoochee River to the west, Dyer Road to
           the east, and an area designated as no hunting grounds to the south (and east of a transmission right-of-way).
           GPC owns additional property on all sides of the ambient air boundary, but is only using a portion of the
           property owned since the river and public roads bisect the property and form a convenient ambient air
           boundary for purposes of this application. The modeled ambient air boundary consists of security fencing to
           control public access along the western, northern, and the eastern boundary as depicted in Figure 6-6. The
           ambient air boundary to the south is comprised of other means to control public access, including areas with
           security cameras, posting of "No Trespassing" signs, security patrolling, and other physical barriers (e.g.,
           densely woody terrain with increasing levels of vegetation toward the river) consistent with US EPA’s
           December 2019 “Revised Policy on Exclusions from Ambient Air” 58. US EPA December 2019 Guidance states,

                       In setting forth this revised ambient air policy, the EPA is making a limited change to the way it applies
                       the "access" element in the regulatory definition of ambient air. while maintaining the level of public
                       health protection afforded by the original policy. This narrow change is that the EPA will no longer
                       consider a fence or other physical barriers to be the exclusive means by which public access may be
                       effectively precluded for purposes of excluding an area owned or controlled by the source from
                       ambient air under the regulatory definition. Accordingly, the EPA is replacing a concept in the 1980
                       letter with a broader concept of measures, which may include physical barriers, that are effective in
                       precluding access by the general public. Thus, the EPA's revised ambient air policy, consistent with
                       its discretion available under the regulatory definition of ambient air, is that the atmosphere over land
                       owned or controlled by the stationary source may be excluded from ambient air where the source
                       employs measures, which may include physical barriers, that are effective in precluding access to the
                       land by the general public.

           Additional physical barriers beyond the fencing and other measures to control public access delineated above
           include extensive property owned by the source operator, active and closed landfills, and forested areas.

           AERMAP (version 18081) (US EPA 2018b), the AERMOD terrain preprocessor program, was used to calculate
           terrain elevations and critical hill heights for the modeled receptors (NAD83 datum and zone 16) using USGS
           National Elevation Data (NED). The dataset downloaded with Lakes Environmental AERMOD View software
           consists of 1/3 arc second (~10 m resolution) NED. As per the AERMAP User’s Guide (US EPA, 2018b), the
           AERMAP domain was sufficient to ensure that all significant nodes were included such that all terrain features
           that exceed a 10% elevation slope from any given receptor were considered. The NED files are referenced to
           Datum NAD83 (note all source locations and receptors were also referenced to NAD83 UTM Zone 16). The
           NED files are included in the electronic modeling archive submitted with the final modeling report.

           6.7 NOx Modeling
           Based on current US EPA guidance, NO2 impacts can be determined by using a 3-tiered NOx-to-NO2
           conversion rate system, where:

                 •      Tier 1 assumes 100 percent conversion of NOx to NO2 conversion;
                 •      Tier 2 utilizes the Ambient Ratio Method 2 (ARM2);
                 •      Tier 3 allows the use of refined techniques such as the Ozone Limiting Method (OLM) or the Plume
                        Volume Molar Ratio Method (PVMRM). Both OLM and PVMRM are default options in AERMOD.
           For the Project, modeled concentrations were assessed using the US EPA default Tier 2 ARM2 methodology
           for estimating NO2 concentrations from total NOX emissions.


           6.8 Secondary PM2.5 and Ozone
           In April 2019, US EPA released the final “Guidance on the Development of Modeled Emission Rates for
           Precursors (MERPs) as a Tier 1 Demonstration Tool for Ozone and PM2.5 under the PSD Permitting Program”
           (EPA-454/R-19-003) (2019 EPA MERPs Guidance) (US EPA 2019). This guidance replaces the draft MERPs
           Guidance that was released in April 2016. Section 4 of the 2019 EPA MERPs Guidance provides several
           examples of MERPs Tier 1 demonstrations for sources subject to PSD review. The examples focus on both
           secondary PM2.5 and ozone precursor emissions and at what emission levels those precursors would result in
           an insignificant impact from a potential project, which would eliminate the need for project-specific modeling.
           Section 4.1.3 of the 2019 US EPA MERPs Guidance also illustrates how the US EPA-model data used to
           develop the MERPs could be used as a Tier 1 demonstration tool in a cumulative impact analysis for both
           PM2.5 and ozone. EPD’s “Guidance on the Use of EPA’s MERPs to Account for Secondary Formation of
           Ozone and PM2.5 in Georgia” (EPD MERPs Guidance) (EPD 2019) also requires that impacts associated with
           secondary PM2.5 and ozone be addressed in a PSD application, and EPD recommends the use of the MERPs
           in an analysis.


           6.8.1 Approaches
           For the Project, precursor emissions for both PM2.5 and ozone are shown in Table 6-12. Precursor emissions
           from the Project will be below the MERPs values for the most representative US EPA hypothetical sources,
           except for NOX as a precursor to 8-hour ozone. In addition, the Project will have modeled impacts of primary
           PM2.5 that exceed the PM2.5 SIL and a cumulative analysis will therefore need to be performed. The
           methodology described in Section 4.1.3 of the 2019 US EPA MERPs Guidance (which is consistent with EPD’s
           MERPs Guidance) was used to assess the Project and cumulative impacts for PM2.5 and ozone.

           To estimate the Project impact on ozone and secondary PM2.5, the list of hypothetical sources that were
           modeled by US EPA and provided as options in the EPD MERPs Guidance document were considered. There
           are three hypothetical sources situated on different sides of Georgia, with the Tallapoosa County, AL source
           being the closest to the Project site by more than 150 km over the Giles County, TN source and more than 200
           km over the Allandale County, SC source. Given the closer proximity of the Tallapoosa County site, it was the
           primary site considered, as it best represents the airshed of the Project source, being located in a similar
           climate regime and similarly exhibiting a warm and humid climate during the ozone season. For Tallapoosa
           County, climate summaries from the NWS / NOAA Online Weather products indicate very similar 30-year
           climate normals when compared to the location of the Project site. A comparison of 30-year (1991-2021)
           average, maximum, and minimum, temperatures and precipitation for the proposed Project site and the
           Tallapoosa County hypothetical source is provided in Table 6-13. Table 6-13 shows very similar annual
           average high temperatures in the low 70s°F, and low temperatures around 50°F, with average low
           temperatures for Tallapoosa County and the Project site within 1ºF. In addition, mid-summer (peak ozone
           season) higher temperatures were in the range of 89 – 91°F for both the Project site and Tallapoosa County,
           and precipitation averages are also close with approximately 55 inches of rain per year each.

           In addition, no significant terrain features are present that would differentiate the climate regimes between the
           Project and the hypothetical source location in Tallapoosa County. Both have similar elevations: 596 ft for
           Tallapoosa County and 740 ft for the Project site, and both are located in Piedmont area with gently rolling hills.
           The Tallapoosa County hypothetical source also exhibits similar land use to the Project area. The Project area
           consists of forested, industrial, and agricultural areas. The Tallapoosa source area consists of forested and
           agricultural areas. Both are primarily rural. Based on the similarities in land use, climate, and terrain, the data
           associated with US EPA’s hypothetical source in Tallapoosa, AL was used for assessing the impact on ozone

           6.9.1 Available Representative Ambient Air Quality Data
           Ambient air quality data are used to represent the contribution to total ambient air concentrations from non-
           modeled sources. The objective of reviewing this data is to develop representative background concentrations
           which, when added to modeled impacts, are used in the NAAQS analysis. This section summarizes the
           ambient background concentrations used in the NAAQS analysis. The monitored concentrations presented in
           this section were obtained from values provided by EPD. 60 While EPD’s website identifies a set of “Statewide”
           default concentrations for NO2 and PM2.5, the other locations provided on EPD’s website were also considered
           to determine the most representative monitors for the proposed Project location.

           6.9.4 Pre-construction Monitoring
           According to 40 CFR §52.21(m), an analysis of ambient air quality in the vicinity of the proposed Project for
           each pollutant subject to PSD review must be conducted. Air quality data are obtained from pre-construction
           monitoring or, under certain conditions, from existing monitoring data. Existing air quality monitoring data may
           be used in lieu of pre-constructing monitoring if:

           •     The data are representative of the proposed facility’s impact areas;

           •     The data are of similar quality as would be obtained if the applicant monitored according to the PSD
                 requirements; and

           •     The data are current; that is, the data have been collected during the two-year period preceding the permit
                 application, provided the data are still representative of current conditions.
           Existing ambient monitoring data from EPD’s monitoring network was used to satisfy the requirement for pre-
           construction monitoring, as described in previous sections.

           7.1 Load Analysis
           Prior to performing the Class II Area SIL analysis, a load analysis for the three CT units was performed to
           determine the worst-case operating load (normal operations, startup, or shutdown) in terms of ground-level
           concentrations. This analysis was performed using data in Table 6-4, Table 6-5, and Table 6-6 along with
           normalized emission rates assuming 90% conversion of NOX to NO2 (Tier 1 Option). Model results were
           estimated for each applicable averaging period, including 1-hour, 3-hour, 8-hour, 24-hour, and annual.

           The normalized concentrations associated with the load analysis run were used to calculate pollutant and
           averaging period-specific concentrations to determine which resulted in the highest modeled concentration.
           This modeling analysis was performed with AERMOD and the associated databases as described in Section
           6.

           and shutdown operations. These load conditions were used to complete the SIL modeling analyses presented

           7.2 SIL Analysis
           The Class II Area SIL analysis was conducted using AERMOD for the worst-case operating load on a pollutant
           and averaging period-specific basis (as determined in Section 7.1). In addition to the worst-case operating
           load for the proposed CT units, the SIL analysis also includes the fuel gas heaters for the short-term modeling,
           and fuel gas heaters, emergency generator, and fire pump for the annual modeling.

           The SIL modeling analysis was used as a tool in evaluating whether the emissions of NO2, CO, PM10, and
           PM2.5 from the Project may cause or contribute to a NAAQS or increment exceedance. The evaluation was
           made using the highest short-term and highest annual modeled concentration over the five years of
           meteorological data modeled. For 1-hour NO2, 24-hour PM2.5, and annual PM2.5, impacts were determined
           based on the highest 5-year average concentrations. Additionally, the modeled NO2 concentrations were
           assessed using the EPA default Tier 2 ARM2 methodology for estimating NO2 concentrations from total
           modeled NOX emissions.

           EPA guidance 63 indicates that use of the SILs may be justified provided that the difference between ambient
           background concentrations representative of the Project area and the NAAQS is greater than the SIL values.
           For the Project, all NO2, CO, PM10, and PM2.5 monitors in the State of Georgia were evaluated and show that
           the difference between the monitored design values and the NAAQS is greater than the SIL values, thus
           justifying the use of the SILs.

           Since the SIL values developed by EPA are justified for use in this case, no further modeling is needed to
           satisfy the required “cause or contribute” determination for those pollutants and averaging periods with
           modeled concentrations less than the SILs. For those pollutants and averaging periods with modeled
           concentrations that exceed the relevant SIL, a Class II Area cumulative impact analysis was performed to
           evaluate whether the Project may cause or contribute to an exceedance of the NAAQS or PSD increments.
           For PM2.5, the secondary PM2.5 concentrations estimated as described in Section 6.9 were added to modeled
           concentrations for comparison with the SILs.

           A comparison of the overall maximum modeled concentrations with the SILs is presented in Table 7-2 for the
           worst-case operating load. As is depicted in Table 7-2, all modeled concentrations are below their respective
           SILs with the exception of 1-hour NO2 and 24-hour PM2.5. As such, no further analyses were performed for
           annual NO2, CO, PM10, or annual PM2.5 standard. A Class II Area cumulative impact analysis for 1-hour NO2
           and 24-hour PM2.5 was conducted, as documented in Section 8.0.

           8. Class II Area Cumulative Impact
              Analysis Results
           8.1 Class II Area Air Quality Standards and PSD
               Increments
           The discussion below applies only to those pollutants and averaging periods for which a modeled impact is
           predicted with AERMOD to exceed the relevant SIL. The cumulative impact analyses were conducted using
           methods and data described in Sections 6 and 7 with the exception that the receptors were limited to those at
           which the Project has a significant modeled concentration.

           The evaluation of whether the Project may cause or contribute to an exceedance of the PSD increments and
           NAAQS is based on the sum of the following:

                •     Modeled concentrations attributable to the Project;
                •     Modeled concentrations from “nearby” sources; and
                •     Representative ambient background concentration (NAAQS only).

           Modeled concentrations attributable to the Project and “nearby” sources were estimated using AERMOD. An
           inventory of sources was developed based on information obtained from EPD to assess cumulative impacts.
           The modeled design short-term concentration from the Project, as well as influencing nearby emission
           sources, were compared with the NAAQS and PSD increments. Note that primary plus secondary PM2.5
           impacts were accounted for from the Project using the secondary PM2.5 concentrations estimated in Section
           6.8. For the NAAQS analysis, a conservative background concentration (see Section 6.9), as provided by
           Georgia EPD, was added to modeled design impacts.


           8.2 Nearby Source Inventory
           The NAAQS and PSD increment analyses include the new sources associated with the Project, along with
           regional inventory sources, including existing emission units at the Project site. For PSD increment analysis,
           only increment-consuming sources were included. For example, the 24-hour PM2.5 increment analysis does
           not include increment expansion associated with the seven coal-fired steam generating units that were once
           operated at Plant Yates but retired or converted to gas after the minor source baseline date.

           SIL modeling was used to establish the significant impact area (SIA) which denotes the maximum distance
           from the Project that the modeled concentrations are greater than their respective SILs. The SIAs for 1-hour
           NO2 and 24-hour PM2.5 are as shown in The Class II Area SIL analysis was conducted using AERMOD for the
           worst-case operating load on a pollutant and averaging period-specific basis (as determined in Section 7.1).
           In addition to the worst-case operating load for the proposed CT units, the SIL analysis also includes the fuel
           gas heaters for the short-term modeling, and fuel gas heaters, emergency generator, and fire pump for the
           annual modeling.

           The SIL modeling analysis was used as a tool in evaluating whether the emissions of NO2, CO, PM10, and
           PM2.5 from the Project may cause or contribute to a NAAQS or increment exceedance. The evaluation was
           made using the highest short-term and highest annual modeled concentration over the five years of
           meteorological data modeled. For 1-hour NO2, 24-hour PM2.5, and annual PM2.5, impacts were determined
           based on the highest 5-year average concentrations. Additionally, the modeled NO2 concentrations were
           assessed using the EPA default Tier 2 ARM2 methodology for estimating NO2 concentrations from total
           modeled NOX emissions.

           The regional source inventory was developed based on EPD’s PSD Permit Guidance Document (Section 5.3)
           for each pollutant with modeled concentrations that exceed the SIL. For 24-hour PM2.5, the modeled SIA is
           1.36 km. 50 km was added to the 24-hour PM2.5 SIA to determine which sources should be considered in the
           cumulative modeling for a distance of 51.36 km. For 1-hour NO2 (which has an SIA of 15.23 km), EPD’s
           guidance suggests use of US EPA guidance, which generally suggests a regional source inventory should not
           extend much beyond 20 km for 1-hour averaging periods since transport distances over 1 hour are more
           limited. Therefore, the regional source inventory for 1-hour NO2 was based on a 25-km distance from the
           Project site.

           The regional source inventory for Georgia was initially generated using EPD’s “PSD Modeling Tool” provided
           on EPD’s website, which provides an off-site inventory for the applicable pollutants based on the location of the
           subject source. The initial inventory was then screened using the “20D Rule” as recommended by EPD. The
           20D rule allows for the screening of inventory sources based on annual allowable emissions and distance from
           the Project site. As required by EPD, in employing the 20D rule, all sources located within 2 km from each
           other were identified. The emissions of these sources were then grouped together for the 20D evaluation.
           Sources located within the SIA were not excluded using the 20D rule and were included in the modeling.

           Individual sources or source groups within the screening area may be removed from the inventory if the
           source’s or grouped sources’ allowable emissions (in tons per year) are less than 20D, where D is the distance
           (in km) from the project source to the inventory source for short-term modeling.

           Once sources were screened based on the 20D rule, those that are required to be included in the background
           inventory were added to the model based on how they are represented in the AERMOD-ready files provided by
           EPD’s PSD Modeling Tool. For those sources that have “ND” as stack parameters, based on past experiences
           with EPD, the following default parameters were used:

                •     Stack Height – 10 meters
                •     Stack Temperature – 293 Kelvin
                •     Stack Velocity – 15 meters/second
                •     Stack Diameter – 0.5 meters

           In addition, secondary PM2.5 from nearby sources was accounted for in the cumulative NAAQS and PSD
           increment consumption analyses. Specifically, SO2 and NOX emissions from those nearby sources that were

           9. Other PSD Requirements
           9.1 Class I Area Impact Analysis
           PSD Class I areas are areas of special national or regional value from a natural, scenic, recreational, or
           historical perspective. The PSD program provides special protection for such areas. NO2, PM10, and PM2.5 are
           the only pollutants for which the Project is subject to Class I area review. According to 40 CFR §52.21(p),
           sources located within 300 km of a Class I area may be required to demonstrate that the proposed project will
           not cause or contribute to an exceedance of the PSD Class I increments or adversely affect certain air quality-
           related values (AQRVs) (including visibility and acid deposition). The five PSD Class I areas located within 300
           km of the Project site are pictured in Figure 9-1 and listed in Table 9-1.

           The Federal Land Managers’ Air Quality Related Values Work Group Phase 1 Report (Revised 2010) (FLAG
           2010) guidance document contains a screening approach that is designed to screen out projects with small
           impacts from the need to conduct an AQRV analysis for nearby Class I areas. The FLAG 2010 guidance
           states that a proposed source with a Q/D ratio less than 10 will likely not have an adverse impact on air quality
           related values, where ‘Q’ is the annual steady-state equivalent emission rate based on the sum of NOX, SO2,
           filterable PM10, and H2SO4 emissions (expressed in tons per year, based on maximum 24-hour emissions) and
           ‘D’ is the distance (km) to the closest Class I area. Since the proposed CT units will be fueled by natural gas,
           or distillate oil when gas is not available, the Project has a ‘Q’ value for each fuel. Note that all SO2 emissions
           from the Project are assumed to form H2SO4 prior to release, so no SO2 emissions were included in the Q/D
           calculation for the Project.

           Table 9-1 provides the distance (D) from the proposed Project to each Class I area along with the Q/D ratio.
           For natural gas, ‘Q’ is 746.4 tons per year based on the following calculation: 41.0 lb/hr (NOX) + 7.0 lb/hr
           (PM10, filterable) + 8.8 lb/hr (H2SO4) = 56.8 lbs/hr/CT x 3 CT units = 170.4 lbs/hr x 8,760 hrs/yr ÷ 2000 lbs/ton =
           746.4 tons/year. Relative to the Cohutta Wilderness Area, Q = 746.4 tons/year, d=156, and Q/D ratio = 4.8.
           For distillate oil, ‘Q’ is 1,544.0 tons per year based on the following calculation: 74.0 lb/hr (NOX) + 35.4 lb/hr
           (PM10, filterable) + 8.1 lb/hr (H2SO4) = 117.5 lbs/hr/CT x 3 CT units = 352.5 lbs/hr x 8,760 hrs/yr ÷ 2000 lbs/ton
           = 1,544.0 tons/year. Relative to the Cohutta Wilderness Area, Q = 1,544.0 tons/year, d=156, and Q/D ratio =
           9.9.

           As shown in Table 9-1, Project’s most conservative Q/D for natural gas is 4.8 and for distillate oil is 9.9, both
           below the screening threshold. GPC prepared a Request for Applicability of Class I Area Modeling Analysis
           which was submitted to the United States Forest Service (USFS) for review to confirm that an assessment of
           AQRVs will not be required. On November 20, 2023, the USFS FLM provided a waiver from the need to
           perform an AQRV analysis based on the submittal. The FLM correspondence is included as an attachment in
           Appendix H. Since the USFS has the closest Class I area to the proposed Project, it is considered the lead
           agency for this Project’s AQRV waiver request. As such, the National Park Service (NPS) was not contacted
           relative to an AQRV waiver request for the Great Smokey Mountains National Park, which is the closest Class I
           area managed by the NPS.


           9.1.1 Class I SIL Analysis
           In accordance with Appendix W (Section 4.2.c.i), because AERMOD (Version 23132) was used for the
           Project’s nearfield assessment, it can be utilized in a screening-level analysis to estimate the Project’s potential
           for a significant modeled impact at the PSD Class I areas listed above. As such, AERMOD was used as a
           screening tool with the meteorological data described in Section 6.5 and with a radial arc of receptors located
           50 km from the Project. Receptors along the 50-km arc were placed every 1 degree for 360 degrees.

           9.3 Growth-Related Impacts
           A qualitative evaluation of the general commercial, residential, industrial, and other growth associated with the
           Project was conducted. The Project is not expected to employ many new additional employees at this time.
           Therefore, secondary growth is not expected, and an analysis of such growth was not performed.


           9.4 Visibility Impairment
           The PSD regulations require an evaluation of the impact of the Project emissions on visibility. The primary
           pollutants responsible for visibility impairment are particulates, SO2, and NOx; however, since SO2 emissions
           from the Project are minimal, this analysis focuses primarily on PM and NOx. A visibility analysis was
           conducted with US EPA’s VISCREEN model for Chattahoochee Bend State Park in Georgia, approximately 5.4
           km to the west of the Project site and the nearest state park to the Project site.

           The analysis was conducted in accordance with US EPA’s Workbook for Plume Visual Impacts Screening and
           Analysis (Revised) (“Workbook”; US EPA, 1992). The VISCREEN model was applied to estimate two visual
           impact parameters, plume perceptibility (∆E) and plume contrast (Cp). Screening-level guidance indicates that
           values above 2.0 for ∆E and +/- 0.05 for Cp are considered perceptible.

           The VISCREEN model Workbook offers two levels of analysis. Level 1 screening analysis is the most
           simplified and conservative approach, employing worst-case default meteorological data. Level 2 analysis
           allows refinement of meteorological conditions as well as site-specific conditions such as complex terrain.
           Initially, the Level 1 analysis was conducted and indicated ∆E and Cp values were above the screening
           thresholds. Therefore, a Level 2 analysis was conducted.

           The Level 2 analysis was conducted with five years of surface observations from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta
           International Airport (KATL) and upper air data from Atlanta Regional Airport – Falcon Field (KFFC). Terrain
           elevation differences between the stack tops (187 m) and Chattahoochee Bend State Park maximum elevation
           (approximately 303 m) is less than 500 meters.

           have a σyσzu product with a cumulative probability of one percent. That is, the dispersion condition is selected
           such that the sum of all frequencies of occurrence of conditions worse than this condition totals one percent.
           Note that as recommended by the Workbook, dispersion conditions that result in greater than 12 hours of
           plume transport time are discounted from the analysis, since it is unlikely that steady-state plume conditions

           10. Toxics Impact Assessment
           10.1 Introduction
           An assessment of potential impacts of toxic air pollutants (TAP) following EPD’s Guideline for Ambient Impact
           Assessment of Toxic Air Pollutant Emissions 64 (“Guideline” hereinafter) was conducted for the Project. The
           basic steps in the air toxics impact assessment are as follows:

                1.    Quantify emissions of TAPs from each emission unit;
                2.    Determine the acceptable ambient concentrations (AAC) for each TAP;
                3.    Conduct a dispersion modeling analysis to compute an ambient air concentration; and
                4.    Compare the modeled concentration to the AAC.

           The following sections present the data and methodology used in the TAP analysis as well as comparison of
           modeled TAP concentrations to the AACs.


           10.2 Toxic Air Pollutant Emissions
           GPC quantified emissions of TAPs from the entire site (Project source and existing sources). To assess the
           potential impacts of TAPs, total site-wide emission rates for each TAP were evaluated first using a screening
           procedure. Per the Guideline, if a TAP’s total emission rate is below the associated Minimum Emission Rate
           (MER), no further analysis is required. The MER for each TAP is provided within Appendix A of the Guideline.
           For those TAPs with total emission rates above the MER, further analysis (modeling to compare against the
           AAC) is required. The following pollutants had emission rates above the associated MER and required
           modeling:

                •     Arsenic
                •     Beryllium
                •     Cadmium
                •     Chromium (Total)
                •     Lead
                •     Manganese
                •     Nickel
                •     Selenium
                •     Acetaldehyde
                •     Acrolein
                •     Ammonia
                •     Benzene
                •     1,3-Butadiene
                •     Formaldehyde
                •     Propylene Oxide
                •     Sulfuric Acid
                •     Naphthalene

           It is understood that if non-point source emissions account for more than 20 percent of the MER for a TAP,
           additional review of that TAP is also required (per Guideline, “If facility-wide emissions are mainly emitted as
           volume or area sources, MER should not be used for screening out of the modeling analysis.”). No additional
           pollutants were pulled into the analysis based on this step of the review.

           10.3 Acceptable Ambient Concentrations
           The Guideline provides the methodology for determining the AAC for TAPs based on various sources of toxicity
           data. EPD maintains a database of AACs for common TAPs 65. AACs for all TAPs considered in the analysis
           were obtained from the EPD database.


           10.4 Modeling Process
           The AERMOD dispersion model was used to determine the maximum short-term and annual modeled
           concentrations of arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium (total), lead, manganese, nickel, selenium,
           acetaldehyde, acrolein, benzene, 1,3-butadiene, formaldehyde, propylene oxide, sulfuric acid, and
           naphthalene, as applicable, for comparison to the AACs.

           AERMOD was applied with the same source data, receptor grid, meteorological data, building downwash file,
           and model options as used in the Class II air quality analysis described in Section 6. In addition to the Project
           sources, existing sources at the facility were included in the AERMOD dispersion model. These sources
           include existing Unit 6 and Unit 7 and the existing water bath heater.

           To simplify the modeling, a conservative screening level approach was used. All sources were individually
           modeled with a unit emission rate (1 g/sec). The maximum impact for each source over the five years of
           meteorological data was scaled by its respective air toxics emission rates (in g/sec). Then all scaled
           concentrations for each source were summed irrespective of time and space. Finally, the site-wide totals were
           evaluated relative to the appropriate toxic thresholds. This is a conservative approach since the highest
           impacts for each source likely do not occur at the same receptor or during the same time period.


           10.5 Dispersion Modeling Analysis Results
           Table 10-2 summarizes the results of the dispersion modeling for short-term averages and annual averages
           and compares the maximum modeled concentration per pollutant and averaging period to the applicable AAC.

      15. Description of general production process and operation for which a permit is being requested. If
          necessary, attach additional sheets to give an adequate description. Include layout drawings, as necessary,
          to describe each process. References should be made to source codes used in the application.


           GPC is proposing to construct and operate three (3) advanced class, dual-fuel simple-cycle combustion turbines
           (CTs) at Plant Yates to provide between 1,000 to 1,400 MW of capacity, depending on the fuel source being utilized.
           The proposed CT units will be equipped with dry low-NOx (DLN) combustors, water injection, selective catalytic
           reduction (SCR) systems and oxidation catalysts for air pollution control.

           Equipment associated with the proposed CT units includes one (1) 3250 kW emergency generator certified to Tier 2
           standards, one (1) 350 bhp fire water pump engine certified to Tier 3 standards, one (1) 5.72 million gallon distillate
           fuel oil storage tank equipped with submerged filling, and three (3) less than 10 MMBtu/hr natural gas-fired fuel gas
           heaters equipped with ultra-low NOx burners.
